content_chunk: uNK cells play a crucial role in spiral artery remodeling, which is necessary for establishing an adequate blood supply to the placenta. In preeclampsia, impaired uNK cell function disrupts the secretion of essential angiogenic factors such as vascular endothelial growth factor VEGF and placental growth factor PlGF , resulting in inadequate spiral artery transformation and poor placental perfusion. Additionally, dysfunctional IFN- γ and TNF- α signaling from uNK cells can create an inflammatory environment, further increasing vascular resistance 36,77. The interaction between KIRs on uNK cells and HLA-C on trophoblasts is also significant in preeclampsia, with specific KIR-HLA-C genotypes being linked to an increased risk of this condition 67,78. 4illustrates the molecular pathways involved in uNK- trophoblast interactions to enhance our understanding of how uNK cell dysfunction contributes to pregnancy complications. This visual highlights how variations in cytokine production, signaling pathways, and receptor-ligand interactions influence the processes critical for a healthy pregnancy, such as spiral artery remodeling and immune tolerance. Recurrent pregnancy loss RPL Recurrent pregnancy loss, defined as two or more consecutive pregnancy losses, has been associated with abnormalities in uNK cell populations and function within the decidua 79. Abnormal uNK cell activity can lead to an imbalance in cytokine production, disrupting immune tolerance and supporting an overly aggressive immune response that hinders fetal survival 40,77. Reduced levels of anti-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-10 and TGF- β compromise the immune-protective environment essential for early pregnancy estab - lishment 80,81. Moreover, inadequate KIR-HLA interaction impede proper trophoblast invasion, contributing to placental insufficiency and subsequent pregnancy loss 82. Studies indicate that an altered ratio of CD56bright and CD56dim uNK cells in the decidua could impact immune regulation, further emphasizing the role of uNK cells in maintaining pregnancy 27,83. Placenta accreta spectrum PAS disorders PAS disorders, including placenta accreta, increta, and percreta, involve abnormal invasion of the placenta into the uterine wall 84. uNK cells are essential for controlling trophoblast invasion; however, dysfunctions in uNK cell signaling pathways or cytokine production can lead to either excessive or insufficient trophoblast invasion 6,36,52. Imbalances in matrix metalloproteinases MMPs and their tissue in- hibitors TIMPs , regulated by uNK cells, are implicated in PAS disorders 85. The failure of uNK cells to modulate trophoblast operly can result in excessive tissue invasion, creating complications during delivery due to the inability to separate the placenta from the uterus 53,86. The molecular mechanisms underlying this dysregulation highlight the need for improved diagnostic and therapeutic strategies targeting uNK cell-trophoblast interactions in PAS disorders 19,87. Specific KIR-HLA-C genotypes influence the extent of uNK cell activation, affecting trophoblast invasion and immune tolerance 20, 36.

content_chunk: Applied to uNK cells, scRNA-seq has allowed researchers to identify previously unrecognized subtypes and functional states of these cells at the maternal-fetal interface 97. By analyzing gene expression at the single-cell level, scRNA-seq provides insights into the diversity of uNK cell populations and the specific roles they play throughout different stages of pregnancy 55,98. This technology has proven essential for mapping uNK cell heterogeneity, revealing distinct clusters based on cytokine production, receptor expression, and migratory properties, which contribute to maternal-fetal tolerance and placental development 99. Spatial transcriptomics While scRNA-seq provides detailed transcriptional profiles, it does not retain spatial information, which is crucial for understanding the functional context of cells within the tissue architecture. Spatial tran- scriptomics addresses this limitation by combining gene expression analysis with spatial localization, allowing researchers to examine how uNK cells are distributed and interact within the decidua 100. This technique offers a spatially resolved view of uNK cell heterogeneity, showing how specific subtypes cluster around trophoblast cells and blood vessels, thereby contributing to trophoblast invasion, spiral artery remodeling, and immune modulation. Spatial transcriptomics thus provides insights into how the tissue microenvironment influences uNK cell behavior 55,101. Molecular pathways of uNK-trophoblast interactions. IFN- γ released by uNK cells promotes spiral artery remodeling through the pro- duction of nitric oxide, other vasoactive substances, and PGE2 signaling. Through KIR-HLA-C interactions with trophoblasts, uNK cells modulate responses that either support trophoblast invasion and maternal-fetal tolerance, conducive to a successful pregnancy, or activate cytotoxicity, which can contribute to pregnancy com- plications such as abortion or recurrent miscarriage. TGF- α plays a role in promoting an inflammatory immune response during the early trimester, essential for pregnancy initiation. During the middle and late trimesters, TGF- α modulates immune responses to prevent excessive inflammation, balancing immune tolerance to support fetal development. Understanding uNK cell heterogeneity and function These emerging techniques have deepened our understanding of uNK cell heterogeneity, revealing complex functional distinctions among various uNK subtypes 14. For instance, combining scRNA-seq with spatial transcriptomics has highlighted differences in cytokine expression between CD56bright and CD56dim uNK cells, with implications for their distinct roles in immune regulation and placental development 55,104. Understanding these nuanced differences is crucial for eluci- dating the mechanisms by which uNK cells contribute to maternal-fetal tolerance and pregnancy health 59. Implications for clinical research and therapeutic development The application of these techniques extends beyond basic research, offering promising avenues for clinical translation. By identifying spe- cific uNK cell subtypes and pathways associated with pregnancy com- plications, these methods enable the development of targeted therapies aimed at modulating uNK cell function 25,53. For example, scRNA-seq data can inform potential biomarkers for early diagnosis of disorders like preeclampsia or recurrent pregnancy loss, while spatial transcriptomics may reveal critical microenvironmental factors that could be targeted to enhance uNK cell function 106. Advanced imaging techniques could also aid in evaluating the efficacy of novel therapeutics by visualizing their effects on uNK cell distribution and activity within the uterine environment 107. In summary, cutting-edge techniques such as single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and advanced imaging are trans - forming uNK cell research 108. By providing comprehensive insights into uNK cell heterogeneity and interactions within the decidua, these tools not only enhance our understanding of maternal-fetal immune tolerance but also pave the way for novel diagnostic and therapeutic strategies for managing pregnancy-related complications 5,104. Therapeutic targets and potential interventions The critical roles of uNK cells in maintaining maternal-fetal immune tolerance, supporting placental development, and modulating immune responses underscore their potential as therapeutic targets 5,7,109. Advances in understanding uNK cell function and their interactions with trophoblasts and other immune cells have paved the way for exploring therapeutic strategies aimed at modulating uNK activity 24,53. This section provides an overview of current and prospective therapies tar- geting uNK cell function, cytokine modulation, gene therapy, and monoclonal antibodies mAbs , along with relevant clinical trials and preclinical models. Current and prospective therapeutics 6. uNK cell function modulation Directly targeting uNK cell function offers an avenue for improving pregnancy outcomes in patients at risk of complications related to uNK dysfunction 110. Strategies focusing on enhancing or suppressing uNK activity could potentially correct the imbalance that contributes to conditions like preeclampsia and recurrent pregnancy loss 36,111. Small molecule inhibitors or activators that modulate uNK cell cyto- toxicity, cytokine production, or adhesion are promising approaches, yet they pose risks of unintended immune effects. For instance, excessive modulation of IFN-γ could either exacerbate inflammation or, if overly suppressed, reduce immune surveillance, potentially compromising maternal-fetal tolerance 11,112.

content_chunk: Cytokine modulation Cytokine signaling is vital for uNK cell function, with specific cyto- kines such as IL-10, TGF-β, and VEGF playing essential roles in main - taining immune tolerance and supporting angiogenesis 63,113. Therapeutic modulation of these cytokines has been proposed to restore balance in uNK-mediated immune responses. However, achieving pre- cise control over cytokine levels is challenging. Exogenously delivered IL-10 and TGF-β, for instance, may enhance an anti-inflammatory environment but carry risks of immune suppression, which could in- crease susceptibility to infections or other immune-related complica - tions 114. Additionally, VEGF-based therapies aimed at promoting placental vascularization may inadvertently promote abnormal vascular growth if not carefully controlled, raising concerns about potential im- pacts on placental structure and function 115. Gene therapy Gene-editing technologies such as CRISPR-Cas9 present promising opportunities to correct genetic variations influencing uNK cell function, specifically by modifying genes like KIR and HLA-C to optimize uNK cell-trophoblast interactions 116. While gene therapy holds potential for preventing complications arising from genetic imbalances, this approach also introduces significant ethical and safety concerns, particularly in the context of pregnancy 117. There is a risk of off-target effects, which could lead to unintended genetic changes with unpredictable impacts on both maternal and fetal health. Rigorous preclinical studies are essential to ensure the feasibility and safety of gene-editing interventions in pregnancy 118. Monoclonal antibodies Monoclonal antibody mAb therapies targeting specific pathways involved in uNK cell function offer another innovative therapeutic avenue 119. mAbs designed to modulate KIR-HLA-C interactions could theoretically enhance maternal-fetal tolerance by fine-tuning uNK cell activity 64,120. Additionally, antibodies targeting pro-inflammatory cytokines like TNF- α may help manage inflammation-related preg- nancy complications 121. Despite promising preclinical results, mAb therapies must be carefully evaluated for potential impacts on maternal-fetal immune dynamics. Safety profiles need to be rigorously tested to prevent unintended immune reactions that might disrupt the delicate balance of tolerance required during pregnancy 122. This figure serves as a visual summary of the therapeutic concepts discussed, followed by Table 2, which details the potential strategies and their status in research or clinical trials. Clinical trials and preclinical models 6. Relevant clinical trials Several clinical trials have been conducted or are ongoing to evaluate therapies that could indirectly influence uNK cell function and maternal- fetal tolerance 5,59. For instance, trials assessing the use of anti-inflammatory agents in managing preeclampsia may offer insights J. content_chunk: Addi- tionally, clinical trials on cytokine therapy in autoimmune or inflam - matory conditions may serve as models for pregnancy-specific interventions, although uNK-targeted therapies for pregnancy compli - cations remain limited 22,132. Preclinical models Animal models, particularly murine and rat models, have been invaluable in studying uNK cell function and potential interventions 133. Knockout models lacking specific genes like those encoding KIRs or cytokines e. , IL-10, TGF- β provide insights into how these mole- cules influence uNK cell function and pregnancy outcomes 7,50,104. Advances in humanized mouse models, where human uNK cells are introduced into immunocompromised mice, also offer new avenues for testing therapeutic interventions in a controlled environment 134. In summary, a variety of therapeutic strategies targeting uNK cell function, cytokine modulation, gene therapy, and mAbs are being explored for managing pregnancy complications associated with uNK dysfunction 135. Although still in early stages, these approaches hold promise for improving pregnancy outcomes by enhancing maternal-fetal immune tolerance and supporting placental health 136. Further clin- ical trials and refined preclinical models are essential to translate these therapeutic concepts into safe and effective treatments, ultimately aiming to optimize maternal-fetal immune interactions and promote healthy placental function 137. Future directions and knowledge gaps Significant advancements have been made in understanding the roles of uNK cells in maternal-fetal immune tolerance, yet critical knowledge gaps persist. Addressing these gaps is essential for a more comprehensive understanding of pregnancy complications associated with uNK cell dysfunction and could pave the way for novel therapeutic strategies. This section highlights key research needs and explores the potential for biomarker development and personalized interventions. Highlight research needs 7. Understanding uNK cell subtypes and their functions Although various uNK cell subtypes have been identified, such as CD56bright CD16dim and CD56dimt CD16bright, their precise functions and interactions within the uterine environment remain incompletely un- derstood 61,138. Each subtype appears to play distinct roles, including regulatory, angiogenic, or immune defense functions, yet how these roles evolve throughout pregnancy is still unclear 52,53,139. Detailed studies are necessary to elucidate how each uNK subtype contributes to placental development and immune tolerance, especially in high-risk pregnancies. Therapeutic approaches targeting uNK cells and immune modulation in pregnancy. A uNK cell function modulation: Strategies include 1 NK-specific chemokine activation, 2 immune checkpoint inhibition e. , PD-1, CTLA-4 , 3 receptor activation e. , CD16 , 4 adoptive transfer of modified cells e. , CAR-NK cells , 5 cytokine recruitment e. , IL-2 , and 6 tri-specific NK engagers for precise modulation. B Cytokine modulation: IL-10 and TGF- β support immune tolerance, while VEGF promotes placental vascularization. C Gene and antibody therapy: Gene-editing e. , CRISPR modifies KIR and HLA-C genes to optimize uNK-trophoblast interactions, with antibody therapies targeting these pathways for improved tolerance. D Functional or engineered uNK cell therapies: Engineered uNK cells secrete factors e. , CSF1, CSF2, CCL5, XCL1 and cytokines IFN- γ, IL-8 , and support vascular remodeling via VEGF and PlGF, aiding trophoblast invasion and spiral artery transformation.

Influence of environmental and maternal factors Environmental and lifestyle factors, including diet, stress, infection, and exposure to toxins, can impact maternal immune function and potentially alter uNK cell behavior 140. However, limited research has focused on how these external factors influence uNK cell function and interactions with trophoblasts 13,22,104. Furthermore, maternal health conditions, such as autoimmune disorders and metabolic syn- dromes, may affect uNK cells and exacerbate pregnancy complications 141. Future studies should explore the environmental and maternal factors affecting uNK cell functions and assess how these influences vary across populations with different genetic backgrounds. Longitudinal changes in uNK cells during pregnancy Most current research on uNK cells is limited to early pregnancy stages, with fewer studies examining their roles in mid-to-late pregnancy 142. Understanding the dynamic changes in uNK cell populations, phenotypes, and functions throughout pregnancy is essential for iden- tifying how they contribute to pregnancy maintenance and how dysre - gulation may lead to complications 143. Longitudinal studies tracking uNK cell characteristics from conception to delivery could reveal crucial insights into their temporal roles and adaptation within the uterine environment 52,104,144. Mechanistic pathways beyond KIR-HLA-C interactions While the KIR-HLA-C axis is well-studied in maternal-fetal tolerance, other molecular pathways may significantly influence uNK cell function 7,145. Pathways involving cytokines like IL-15, IL-10, and TGF-β, as well as non-HLA ligand-receptor interactions, have been suggested to influence uNK cell activity 7,146.

content_chunk: Further research into these less-studied pathways may reveal additional mechanisms that support immune tolerance and placental health, expanding our understanding of the immune microenvironment in pregnancy. Potential for biomarkers and personalized interventions 7. Development of non-invasive biomarkers Identifying biomarkers indicative of uNK cell activity could facilitate early detection of pregnancy complications, such as preeclampsia and recurrent pregnancy loss 21,40. Non-invasive biomarkers, particularly those detectable in maternal blood or urine, would offer clinicians a valuable tool for assessing uNK cell function and associated risks throughout pregnancy 147. Potential biomarkers may include cyto- kines, chemokines, and uNK-specific surface markers that correlate with abnormal immune responses 148. Validation of these biomarkers in large, diverse populations is essential to ensure their reliability and predictive accuracy. Potential for personalized interventions The diversity in uNK cell subtypes and their distinct roles in immune tolerance and placental support suggest a strong potential for person - alized approaches to treating pregnancy complications 149. Person - alized interventions could involve targeted modulation of specific uNK subtypes, or the use of cytokine therapies tailored to an individual s immune profile. For example, regulating cytokines, such as IL-10 or VEGF, based on a patient s specific needs could enhance treatment ef- ficacy by precisely addressing immune imbalances 150. Additionally, genetic screening for KIR-HLA mismatches may help identify women at higher risk for complications, allowing for early, targeted interventions aimed at improving maternal-fetal compatibility 151. Future research should prioritize developing these targeted therapies, focusing on ac- commodating individual variations in immune tolerance mechanisms to maximize therapeutic outcomes 21,152. Personalized approaches offer the promise of more effective, patient-specific care that addresses the unique immune environment of each pregnancy. In summary, advancing our understanding of uNK cells requires a multifaceted approach that includes studies on cellular diversity, environmental impacts, and longitudinal dynamics. Developing reliable biomarkers and personalized therapeutic strategies holds great promise for improving pregnancy outcomes and managing complications linked to uNK dysfunction 153. Bridging these knowledge gaps will be critical for translating basic research on uNK cells into clinical applications, ultimately enhancing maternal-fetal health 36,40. Conclusions and prospects 8. Summary of key insights This review has highlighted the multifaceted role of uNK cells in establishing and maintaining maternal-fetal immune tolerance, ensuring successful placental development, and supporting pregnancy health 7, 53. uNK cells contribute significantly to processes such as trophoblast invasion, spiral artery remodeling, and modulation of immune responses at the maternal-fetal interface 7,13,154. Their interaction with trophoblast cells, mediated through KIR-HLA-C and other molecular pathways, is essential for balancing immune tolerance and defense, thereby preventing adverse pregnancy outcomes 20,27. Additionally, the functional diversity of uNK cell subtypes, characterized by unique cytokine profiles and receptor expressions, underscores the complexity of their regulatory roles 63,77. Understanding the implications of uNK cell dysfunction has provided valuable insights into pregnancy complications, including preeclampsia, recurrent pregnancy loss, and PAS disorders 12,77. Genetic and epigenetic factors that influence uNK cell activity have also emerged as critical determinants of maternal-fetal tolerance, revealing potential risk markers for these conditions 7,55,145.

content_chunk: Advances in research tech- niques, particularly single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial tran- scriptomics, have further enhanced our understanding of uNK cell heterogeneity, opening up new avenues for targeted therapeutic ap- proaches 155. Potential clinical impact and future research The clinical implications of uNK cell research are vast, particularly in developing predictive biomarkers and personalized therapies for preg- nancy complications 104,156. Non-invasive biomarkers reflecting uNK cell activity could transform prenatal care by enabling early detection and intervention for high-risk pregnancies 157. Such bio- markers, combined with genetic screening for KIR-HLA mismatches, may facilitate individualized risk assessments, helping to tailor in- terventions for each patient s unique immunological profile 7,55,66. Future research should focus on exploring uncharted areas in uNK cell biology including their longitudinal behavior across different pregnancy stages and the influence of environmental factors 52,158. These studies could deepen our understanding of how uNK cells adapt to changes within the uterine environment and contribute to pregnancy maintenance over time. Further exploration into alternative ligand-receptor pathways and cytokine interactions will likely reveal additional layers of immune regulation essential for pregnancy health 159. In conclusion, recent advancements in uNK cell research have significantly expanded our understanding of their roles and interactions with trophoblasts 7,22,50,53. Despite remaining gaps in knowledge, these findings highlight the transformative potential of uNK cell research in reproductive immunology and maternal-fetal medicine 160. By continuing to explore molecular mechanisms and the impact of various factors on uNK cell functions, paving the way for innovative diagnostic tools, targeted treatments, and ultimately, improved preg- nancy outcomes. content_chunk: Maternal vaping and pregnancy adverse outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis Alexandre Vall eea, , Maha Eidb, Anis Fekic , Jean-Marc Ayoubib,d aDepartment of Epidemiology and Public Health, Foch Hospital, Suresnes, France bDepartment of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Medicine, Foch Hospital, 40 rue Worth, Suresnes 92150, France cDepartment of Obstetrics and Gynecology, HFR-Fribourg, Chemin des Pensionnats 2-6, Fribourg 1708, Switzerland dMedical School, University of Versailles, Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines UVSQ , Versailles, France Keywords: Electronic cigarettes Pregnancy Prenatal care Vaping, tobacco smoking Preterm birth Low birth weight Small-for-gestational-ageABSTRACT Background: The increasing use of vaping during pregnancy raises concerns due to known risks of nicotine exposure. This meta-analysis assesses the association between maternal vaping and preterm birth, low birth weight, and small-for-gestational-age, compared to non-smokers, tobacco smokers, and dual users both vaping and combastible tobacco use. Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library were searched for studies published from Auguts 1986 to December 2024. Eligible studies included pregnant women using vaping, with reported outcomes on preterm birth, low birth weight, or small-for-gestational-age. Odds ratios ORs with 95 confidence intervals CIs were pooled using fixed- or random-effects models. Results: Nine studies involving 423,680 pregnant women met the inclusion criteria. Compared to non-smokers, vaping use was associated with a 40 increased risk of preterm birth OR 1. 58 , a 49 increased risk of low birth weight OR 1. 69 , and a 32 increased risk of small-for- gestational-age OR 1. No significant difference was found between vaping users and smokers or dual users for preterm birth or low birth weight. However, vaping users had a 47 lower risk of small-for-gestational-age OR 0. 66 , and a 67 lower risk compared to dual users OR 0. Conclusion: Vaping during pregnancy is associated with a significantly higher risk of preterm birth, low birth weight, and small-for-gestational-age, compared to non-use of nicotine. Statement of significance Problem or issue The impact of maternal vaping on pregnancy outcomes remains poorly understood, despite the rising use of vaping during pregnancy. What is already known Tobacco use during pregnancy increases the risk of preterm birth, low birth weight, and small-for-gestational-age infants. Vaping is often marketed as a safer alternative, though they still contain harmful substances. What this paper addsThis study provides clear evidence that maternal vaping increases the risk of preterm birth, low birth weight, and small-for- gestational-age outcomes, even compared to non-smokers. These findings support the need for midwives to actively discourage vaping in pregnancy and for policymakers to strengthen public health messaging and regulation around nicotine use in expectant mothers. However, this method still exposes users to harmful substances such as nicotine, volatile organic compounds, heavy metals, and flavoring agents, all of which may adversely affect both maternal and fetal health 2,3. These toxicants can impair placental development, reduce utero - placental blood flow, and lead to fetal hypoxia and restricted growth 4 7. Such pathophysiological changes are strongly associated with preterm birth delivery before 37 weeks of gestation , low birth weight LBW D2500 g , and small-for-gestational-age SGA infants birth weight below the 10th percentile for gestational age , all of which are major contributors to neonatal morbidity, mortality, and long-term developmental complications 8,9. Tobacco smoking during pregnancy is a well-established risk factor for these outcomes, with clear dose-response associations: greater fre- quency and duration of smoking lead to increased risk of LBW, SGA, and preterm birth 4,10 12. Although vaping is often perceived as less harmful, emerging data suggest that similar risks may apply, especially among frequent users or those who engage in dual use vaping combined with combustible tobacco 13 15. Moreover, other modifiable factors such as inadequate prenatal care, nutritional deficiencies, psychosocial stress, and concurrent use of alcohol or other substances further amplify these risks 16. Recent studies estimate that 5 7 of pregnant women report vaping during pregnancy, either exclusively or in combination with conven - tional cigarettes 17 19. Human and animal research has shown that prenatal exposure to vaping aerosols may impair fetal growth, alter placental structure and function, and negatively affect postnatal lung and neurodevelopment 7,18,20 27. Despite this growing evidence, the use of vaping during pregnancy remains poorly regulated and inadequately addressed in clinical guidance. Several systematic reviews have attempted to evaluate the impact of maternal vaping on pregnancy outcomes 21,28 , but their conclusions are often inconsistent due to variations in study design, exposure defi- nitions, and comparator groups. Most reviews do not simultaneously assess exclusive vaping, smoking, dual use, and nicotine-free controls. This systematic review and meta-analysis therefore aims to clarify the association between maternal vaping and preterm birth, low birth weight, and small-for-gestational-age, compared to non-smokers, to- bacco smokers, and dual users. Methods Study design and eligibility criteria We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis by following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta- Analyses PRISMA guidelines 29 , and in line with the suggestions provided by the Cochrane Collaboration 30. The protocol was regis- tered with PROSPERO CRD42024594752.

content_chunk: Eligibility criteria Studies were eligible for inclusion if they investigated populations of pregnant women and included at least one exposure group using vaping either exclusively or in combination with tobacco cigarettes , with a comparator group comprising non-smokers, exclusive tobacco smokers, or dual users. Studies that included only women who did not use either tobacco or vaping, without any exposed group for comparison, were excluded. Included studies had to report at least one of the following outcomes: preterm birth defined as delivery before 37 weeks of gestation , low birth weight birth weight D2500 g , or small-for-gestational-age birth weight below the 10th percentile for gestational age and sex. We included randomized controlled trials RCTs , cohort studies prospective or retrospective , case-control studies, and cross-sectional studies. We excluded case reports, editorials, commentaries, narrative reviews, animal or in vitro studies, studies not reporting extractable data e. , odds ratios or raw event counts , studies in languages other than English, and duplicate publications only the most complete version was retained. Research questions Is maternal use of vaping during pregnancy associated with increased risks of preterm birth, low birth weight, and small-for- gestational-age, when compared to non-smokers, tobacco smokers, and dual users. Primary outcomes The primary outcomes of interest were: Preterm birth: Defined as delivery before 37 completed weeks of gestation. Low birth weight LBW : Defined as a birth weight less than 2500 g. Small-for-gestational-age SGA : Defined as birth weight below the 10th percentile for gestational age and sex. Secondary outcomes Differences in outcome risk between vaping users and tobacco smokers or dual users. Exploration of heterogeneity in risk estimates across studies. Exposure categories Exposure categories were defined as follows: Vaping users: Pregnant individuals who reported exclusive use of vaping during pregnancy. Tobacco smokers: Individuals who reported exclusive use of combustible cigarettes during pregnancy. Dual users: Individuals who reported concurrent use of both vaping and combustible tobacco products during pregnancy. Non-smokers: Individuals who reported no use of nicotine- containing products including vaping and cigarettes during pregnancy. Search strategy and study selection Information sources We conducted a systematic research on PubMed, Web of Science and Cochrane library for studies published from database Auguts 1986 to December 2024. Search strategy The search strategy used MeSH terms and following the search equation: birth outcome OR pregnancy OR Miscarriage OR pre- term birth OR low birth weight OR Unfavorable Birth OR small-for- gestational-age OR growth restriction OR intra-uterine development OR neonatal morbidity OR stillbirth AND combustible cigarette OR electronic cigarette OR vaping OR e-cigarette. We only considered English-language studies, and we performed a thorough assessment of the references from the pertinent articles. Data extraction and quality assessment Data extraction Data from eligible studies were extracted independently by one reviewer ME and verified by a second reviewer AV to ensure accu- racy and consistency. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion.

Finally, 9 studies met all inclusion criteria and were included in the meta-analysis Fig. Quality assessment of included studies The methodological quality of each included study was indepen - dently assessed by two reviewers AV and ME using the Cochrane Collaboration s Risk of Bias Tool 31. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion, with arbitration by a third reviewer JMA when necessary. For randomized controlled trials, the evaluation considered domains such as random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and outcome assessors, completeness of outcome data, selective reporting, and other potential sources of bias. For non-randomized studies, including cohort, case-control, and cross-sectional designs, an adapted version of the Cochrane tool was applied, focusing on the selection of participants, accuracy of exposure and outcome assessment, control of confounding variables, and completeness of data reporting. Each domain was rated as having low, high, or unclear risk of bias. The overall quality of the included studies was summarized descriptively, and funnel plots were used to evaluate the presence of publication bias. Statistical analysis We extracted and summarized the following data: author, year of publication, country, number of patients, period of inclusion, type of study, epidemiology and physiology, main outcomes LBW, SGA, pre- term birth , and limits. We assessed the pregnancy outcomes number and percentage in each group of patients. We assessed the number, percentage, mean, standard deviation, median, interquartile range, and confidence interval CI for all measures of each study 32. We did not conduct formal sensitivity analyses, such as excluding studies at high risk of bias or testing the robustness of the pooled estimates by removing individual studies, which may be considered in future updates of this review. This approach is consistent with preliminary meta-analyses aimed at identifying overall patterns rather than confirming causal in- ferences in the presence of limited high-quality data 29. content_chunk: Nicotine crosses the placental barrier, leading to direct fetal exposure, disrupting development and increasing the risk of SGA, preterm birth, and LBW 47. However, the risks of vaping extend beyond nicotine. Vaping aerosols contain harmful substances, including heavy metals, volatile organic compounds, and flavoring agents, which induce oxidative stress and inflammation 48. Animal studies reveal that prenatal vaping exposure not only reduces birth weight but also impairs lung development and alters brain devel - opment due to oxidative stress and inflammation 6,49. Additionally, solvents like propylene glycol and glycerol in e-liquids have shown cytotoxic effects on placental cells, further contributing to adverse pregnancy outcomes 50. Implications for public health policy These findings are particularly timely given the ongoing debate regarding regulation of vaping use, especially among adolescents and young adults. In several countries, including the United States, Canada, and parts of Europe, youth vaping rates have increased substantially, often driven by aggressive marketing tactics, flavored products, and perceptions of reduced harm 51 53. The normalization of vaping among young women raises concern for future pregnancies, particularly in the absence of comprehensive regulation. The increasing prevalence of vaping among adolescents and young adults, particularly women of reproductive age, poses significant challenges for public health policy. Marketing strategies that promote flavored e-liquids and sleek device designs have contributed to the perception that e-cigarettes are a safer alternative to smoking, even during pregnancy. However, our findings align with growing evidence that vaping carries serious risks for fetal development and pregnancy outcomes. This underscores the urgency of integrating vaping into existing tobacco control and maternal health frameworks. Current regulatory approaches to vaping remain fragmented across countries. In many jurisdictions, flavored vaping products continue to be widely available, despite mounting evidence that these products disproportionately attract younger users and mask the harshness of nicotine inhalation. Without effective regulatory countermeasures, these trends are likely to continue contributing to nicotine exposure during future pregnancies. Although some argue that e-cigarettes play a role in harm reduction for adult smokers, their use in pregnant populations introduces unac- ceptable risks. Policymakers should consider stricter regulation of vap- ing devices and e-liquids, including bans on flavored products, warning labels specific to pregnancy, and age verification systems. Public awareness campaigns targeting reproductive-age women are also essential.

content_chunk: Importantly, our analysis reinforces the need to include pre- natal vaping in broader tobacco control strategies, integrating it into frameworks that address tobacco cessation, reproductive health, and maternal-child safety. Midwives, nurses, and public health professionals have a pivotal role to play in both practice and advocacy. Their direct engagement with pregnant populations uniquely positions them to identify early use, provide brief interventions, and support policy initiatives that limit youth access to harmful nicotine products. As the reproductive health landscape evolves, addressing the underestimated harms of e-cigarettes must become a core element of maternal and perinatal public health strategies. Clinical practice implications For midwives, nurses, and other maternity care providers, these findings underscore the need to routinely inquire about e-cigarette use during antenatal assessments, alongside questions about tobacco and alcohol. While patients may perceive vaping as a less harmful option, healthcare professionals should be equipped to explain the specific risks of prenatal vaping exposure, including placental dysfunction, fetal hypoxia, and growth restriction 56. Tailored smoking cessation sup- port should address e-cigarette dependence, and resources must emphasize complete nicotine abstinence during pregnancy, not just cessation of combustible tobacco 57. Additionally, clinical guidance documents and antenatal education materials should be updated to reflect the risks of vaping, avoiding any ambiguity about its safety in pregnancy 58. Gender-sensitive health promotion As pregnancy is a gendered experience, the development of public health strategies addressing e-cigarette use during pregnancy must explicitly consider the social, cultural, and structural determinants that affect women s health behaviors. Gender norms, socioeconomic vulnerability, and exposure to targeted marketing disproportionately shape women s risk environments and their engagement with nicotine products. Research has shown that pregnant individuals may be influ- enced by social expectations to maintain a healthy pregnancy, yet may Fig. Comparative Forest Plots of preterm birth among vaping Users, Non-Users, Smokers, and Dual Users. Furthermore, tobacco and vaping com- panies have historically used gender-specific advertising, framing e-cigarettes as tools for stress relief, weight control, or modernity, messages that can resonate powerfully with young women and pregnant individuals navigating complex life transitions. Effective health pro- motion must therefore go beyond biomedical risk messaging to include gender-responsive education, culturally appropriate counseling, and intersectional strategies that address the lived realities of pregnant in- dividuals 61. Community-based approaches that engage women as co-designers of interventions, as well as policies that confront com- mercial determinants of health e. , marketing and accessibility of flavored products , are essential to reduce prenatal exposure to vaping. content_chunk: Dual use significantly increases toxic exposure, as it combines the harmful effects of both vaping and combustible cigarettes, including additive exposure to nicotine, volatile organic compounds, and heavy metals 35. This combination leads to a higher risk of adverse preg- nancy outcomes, exceeding the risk caused by either product alone. Dual users consistently experience the most severe complications , with elevated rates of preterm birth, LBW, and SGA infants 62,63. The synergistic effects of nicotine, heavy metals, and volatile organic com- pounds VOCs exacerbate placental dysfunction, restricting oxygen and nutrients to the fetus, which contributes to growth restriction and hypoxia, as highlighted in recent research 21. Although vaping users are exposed to fewer toxins, the presence of VOCs and heavy metals still poses substantial risks 15. Thus, the biological mechanisms underlying adverse pregnancy-related outcomes associated with prenatal vaping use remain largely unclear, as do the factors contributing to the differing effects observed between vaping and tobacco smoking. Both e-liquids and the byproducts produced during the heating process, such as alde- hydes, may play a role in increasing these risks 8. Research on animal models has indicated that exposure to vaping aerosols containing nico- tine during pregnancy can impair blood flow in both the maternal uterine artery and the fetal umbilical cord. This disruption can poten - tially lead to intrauterine growth restriction and preterm birth 7. Moreover, substances other than nicotine in e-liquids have been found to interfere with trophoblast function in the placenta, resulting in struc- tural complications 22,23. These placental alterations may heighten the likelihood of preeclampsia, early miscarriage, preterm delivery, and even maternal or fetal mortality. However, they do not entirely account for the differences in effects between vaping and cigarettes users. Strengths and limitations This meta-analysis s strengths include its review of current literature and the inclusion of diverse studies, providing a broad perspective on the impact of vaping use during pregnancy. However, the heterogeneity across studies in terms of population characteristics, vaping usage pat- terns, and outcome measures may limit the generalizability of the findings. The reliance on self-reported data in many studies could introduce recall bias, and the cross-sectional design of most studies limits the ability to infer causality. Additional limitations include vari- ability in study design, sample size, and inconsistent control for con- founding factors. Furthermore, studies often lacked detailed information on nicotine dosage and did not differentiate between ex-smokers and current smokers. For example, while studies such as those by Ammar 2023 8 and Nanninga 2023 11 benefit from large sample sizes, they did not account for the duration and intensity of vaping use, which may influence outcomes. Conclusion Our study demonstrates a strong association between vaping use during pregnancy and an increased risk of SGA, preterm birth, and LBW, with dual users facing the highest risks. These findings have important implications for both public health and clinical practice. Vaping should not be considered a safe alternative for pregnant women.

content_chunk: Maternal vaping and pregnancy adverse outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis Alexandre Vall eea, , Maha Eidb, Anis Fekic , Jean-Marc Ayoubib,d aDepartment of Epidemiology and Public Health, Foch Hospital, Suresnes, France bDepartment of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Medicine, Foch Hospital, 40 rue Worth, Suresnes 92150, France cDepartment of Obstetrics and Gynecology, HFR-Fribourg, Chemin des Pensionnats 2-6, Fribourg 1708, Switzerland dMedical School, University of Versailles, Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines UVSQ , Versailles, France Keywords: Electronic cigarettes Pregnancy Prenatal care Vaping, tobacco smoking Preterm birth Low birth weight Small-for-gestational-ageABSTRACT Background: The increasing use of vaping during pregnancy raises concerns due to known risks of nicotine exposure. This meta-analysis assesses the association between maternal vaping and preterm birth, low birth weight, and small-for-gestational-age, compared to non-smokers, tobacco smokers, and dual users both vaping and combastible tobacco use. Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library were searched for studies published from Auguts 1986 to December 2024. Eligible studies included pregnant women using vaping, with reported outcomes on preterm birth, low birth weight, or small-for-gestational-age. Odds ratios ORs with 95 confidence intervals CIs were pooled using fixed- or random-effects models. Results: Nine studies involving 423,680 pregnant women met the inclusion criteria. Compared to non-smokers, vaping use was associated with a 40 increased risk of preterm birth OR 1. 58 , a 49 increased risk of low birth weight OR 1. 69 , and a 32 increased risk of small-for- gestational-age OR 1. No significant difference was found between vaping users and smokers or dual users for preterm birth or low birth weight. However, vaping users had a 47 lower risk of small-for-gestational-age OR 0. 66 , and a 67 lower risk compared to dual users OR 0. Conclusion: Vaping during pregnancy is associated with a significantly higher risk of preterm birth, low birth weight, and small-for-gestational-age, compared to non-use of nicotine. Statement of significance Problem or issue The impact of maternal vaping on pregnancy outcomes remains poorly understood, despite the rising use of vaping during pregnancy. What is already known Tobacco use during pregnancy increases the risk of preterm birth, low birth weight, and small-for-gestational-age infants. Vaping is often marketed as a safer alternative, though they still contain harmful substances. What this paper addsThis study provides clear evidence that maternal vaping increases the risk of preterm birth, low birth weight, and small-for- gestational-age outcomes, even compared to non-smokers. These findings support the need for midwives to actively discourage vaping in pregnancy and for policymakers to strengthen public health messaging and regulation around nicotine use in expectant mothers. However, this method still exposes users to harmful substances such as nicotine, volatile organic compounds, heavy metals, and flavoring agents, all of which may adversely affect both maternal and fetal health 2,3. These toxicants can impair placental development, reduce utero - placental blood flow, and lead to fetal hypoxia and restricted growth 4 7. Such pathophysiological changes are strongly associated with preterm birth delivery before 37 weeks of gestation , low birth weight LBW D2500 g , and small-for-gestational-age SGA infants birth weight below the 10th percentile for gestational age , all of which are major contributors to neonatal morbidity, mortality, and long-term developmental complications 8,9. Tobacco smoking during pregnancy is a well-established risk factor for these outcomes, with clear dose-response associations: greater fre- quency and duration of smoking lead to increased risk of LBW, SGA, and preterm birth 4,10 12. Although vaping is often perceived as less harmful, emerging data suggest that similar risks may apply, especially among frequent users or those who engage in dual use vaping combined with combustible tobacco 13 15. Moreover, other modifiable factors such as inadequate prenatal care, nutritional deficiencies, psychosocial stress, and concurrent use of alcohol or other substances further amplify these risks 16. Recent studies estimate that 5 7 of pregnant women report vaping during pregnancy, either exclusively or in combination with conven - tional cigarettes 17 19. Human and animal research has shown that prenatal exposure to vaping aerosols may impair fetal growth, alter placental structure and function, and negatively affect postnatal lung and neurodevelopment 7,18,20 27. Despite this growing evidence, the use of vaping during pregnancy remains poorly regulated and inadequately addressed in clinical guidance. Several systematic reviews have attempted to evaluate the impact of maternal vaping on pregnancy outcomes 21,28 , but their conclusions are often inconsistent due to variations in study design, exposure defi- nitions, and comparator groups. Most reviews do not simultaneously assess exclusive vaping, smoking, dual use, and nicotine-free controls. This systematic review and meta-analysis therefore aims to clarify the association between maternal vaping and preterm birth, low birth weight, and small-for-gestational-age, compared to non-smokers, to- bacco smokers, and dual users. Methods Study design and eligibility criteria We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis by following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta- Analyses PRISMA guidelines 29 , and in line with the suggestions provided by the Cochrane Collaboration 30. The protocol was regis- tered with PROSPERO CRD42024594752.

content_chunk: Eligibility criteria Studies were eligible for inclusion if they investigated populations of pregnant women and included at least one exposure group using vaping either exclusively or in combination with tobacco cigarettes , with a comparator group comprising non-smokers, exclusive tobacco smokers, or dual users. Studies that included only women who did not use either tobacco or vaping, without any exposed group for comparison, were excluded. Included studies had to report at least one of the following outcomes: preterm birth defined as delivery before 37 weeks of gestation , low birth weight birth weight D2500 g , or small-for-gestational-age birth weight below the 10th percentile for gestational age and sex. We included randomized controlled trials RCTs , cohort studies prospective or retrospective , case-control studies, and cross-sectional studies. We excluded case reports, editorials, commentaries, narrative reviews, animal or in vitro studies, studies not reporting extractable data e. , odds ratios or raw event counts , studies in languages other than English, and duplicate publications only the most complete version was retained. Research questions Is maternal use of vaping during pregnancy associated with increased risks of preterm birth, low birth weight, and small-for- gestational-age, when compared to non-smokers, tobacco smokers, and dual users. Primary outcomes The primary outcomes of interest were: Preterm birth: Defined as delivery before 37 completed weeks of gestation. Low birth weight LBW : Defined as a birth weight less than 2500 g. Small-for-gestational-age SGA : Defined as birth weight below the 10th percentile for gestational age and sex. Secondary outcomes Differences in outcome risk between vaping users and tobacco smokers or dual users. Exploration of heterogeneity in risk estimates across studies. Exposure categories Exposure categories were defined as follows: Vaping users: Pregnant individuals who reported exclusive use of vaping during pregnancy. Tobacco smokers: Individuals who reported exclusive use of combustible cigarettes during pregnancy. Dual users: Individuals who reported concurrent use of both vaping and combustible tobacco products during pregnancy. Non-smokers: Individuals who reported no use of nicotine- containing products including vaping and cigarettes during pregnancy. Search strategy and study selection Information sources We conducted a systematic research on PubMed, Web of Science and Cochrane library for studies published from database Auguts 1986 to December 2024. Search strategy The search strategy used MeSH terms and following the search equation: birth outcome OR pregnancy OR Miscarriage OR pre- term birth OR low birth weight OR Unfavorable Birth OR small-for- gestational-age OR growth restriction OR intra-uterine development OR neonatal morbidity OR stillbirth AND combustible cigarette OR electronic cigarette OR vaping OR e-cigarette. We only considered English-language studies, and we performed a thorough assessment of the references from the pertinent articles. Data extraction and quality assessment Data extraction Data from eligible studies were extracted independently by one reviewer ME and verified by a second reviewer AV to ensure accu- racy and consistency. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion.

The full text of 45 articles was then reviewed for eligibility. Finally, 9 studies met all inclusion criteria and were included in the meta-analysis Fig. Quality assessment of included studies The methodological quality of each included study was indepen - dently assessed by two reviewers AV and ME using the Cochrane Collaboration s Risk of Bias Tool 31. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion, with arbitration by a third reviewer JMA when necessary. For randomized controlled trials, the evaluation considered domains such as random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and outcome assessors, completeness of outcome data, selective reporting, and other potential sources of bias. For non-randomized studies, including cohort, case-control, and cross-sectional designs, an adapted version of the Cochrane tool was applied, focusing on the selection of participants, accuracy of exposure and outcome assessment, control of confounding variables, and completeness of data reporting. Each domain was rated as having low, high, or unclear risk of bias. The overall quality of the included studies was summarized descriptively, and funnel plots were used to evaluate the presence of publication bias. Statistical analysis We extracted and summarized the following data: author, year of publication, country, number of patients, period of inclusion, type of study, epidemiology and physiology, main outcomes LBW, SGA, pre- term birth , and limits. We assessed the pregnancy outcomes number and percentage in each group of patients. We assessed the number, percentage, mean, standard deviation, median, interquartile range, and confidence interval CI for all measures of each study 32. We did not conduct formal sensitivity analyses, such as excluding studies at high risk of bias or testing the robustness of the pooled estimates by removing individual studies, which may be considered in future updates of this review. This approach is consistent with preliminary meta-analyses aimed at identifying overall patterns rather than confirming causal in- ferences in the presence of limited high-quality data 29. content_chunk: Nicotine crosses the placental barrier, leading to direct fetal exposure, disrupting development and increasing the risk of SGA, preterm birth, and LBW 47. However, the risks of vaping extend beyond nicotine. Vaping aerosols contain harmful substances, including heavy metals, volatile organic compounds, and flavoring agents, which induce oxidative stress and inflammation 48. Animal studies reveal that prenatal vaping exposure not only reduces birth weight but also impairs lung development and alters brain devel - opment due to oxidative stress and inflammation 6,49. Additionally, solvents like propylene glycol and glycerol in e-liquids have shown cytotoxic effects on placental cells, further contributing to adverse pregnancy outcomes 50. Implications for public health policy These findings are particularly timely given the ongoing debate regarding regulation of vaping use, especially among adolescents and young adults. In several countries, including the United States, Canada, and parts of Europe, youth vaping rates have increased substantially, often driven by aggressive marketing tactics, flavored products, and perceptions of reduced harm 51 53. The normalization of vaping among young women raises concern for future pregnancies, particularly in the absence of comprehensive regulation. The increasing prevalence of vaping among adolescents and young adults, particularly women of reproductive age, poses significant challenges for public health policy. Marketing strategies that promote flavored e-liquids and sleek device designs have contributed to the perception that e-cigarettes are a safer alternative to smoking, even during pregnancy. However, our findings align with growing evidence that vaping carries serious risks for fetal development and pregnancy outcomes. This underscores the urgency of integrating vaping into existing tobacco control and maternal health frameworks. Current regulatory approaches to vaping remain fragmented across countries. In many jurisdictions, flavored vaping products continue to be widely available, despite mounting evidence that these products disproportionately attract younger users and mask the harshness of nicotine inhalation. Flavors such as fruit, mint, and dessert varieties are strongly associated with initiation and sustained use among adolescent Fig. Comparative Forest Plots of SGA among vaping Users, Non-Users, Smokers, and Dual Users. Without effective regulatory countermeasures, these trends are likely to continue contributing to nicotine exposure during future pregnancies. Although some argue that e-cigarettes play a role in harm reduction for adult smokers, their use in pregnant populations introduces unac- ceptable risks. Policymakers should consider stricter regulation of vap- ing devices and e-liquids, including bans on flavored products, warning labels specific to pregnancy, and age verification systems. Public awareness campaigns targeting reproductive-age women are also essential.

content_chunk: Importantly, our analysis reinforces the need to include pre- natal vaping in broader tobacco control strategies, integrating it into frameworks that address tobacco cessation, reproductive health, and maternal-child safety. Midwives, nurses, and public health professionals have a pivotal role to play in both practice and advocacy. Their direct engagement with pregnant populations uniquely positions them to identify early use, provide brief interventions, and support policy initiatives that limit youth access to harmful nicotine products. As the reproductive health landscape evolves, addressing the underestimated harms of e-cigarettes must become a core element of maternal and perinatal public health strategies. Clinical practice implications For midwives, nurses, and other maternity care providers, these findings underscore the need to routinely inquire about e-cigarette use during antenatal assessments, alongside questions about tobacco and alcohol. While patients may perceive vaping as a less harmful option, healthcare professionals should be equipped to explain the specific risks of prenatal vaping exposure, including placental dysfunction, fetal hypoxia, and growth restriction 56. Tailored smoking cessation sup- port should address e-cigarette dependence, and resources must emphasize complete nicotine abstinence during pregnancy, not just cessation of combustible tobacco 57. Additionally, clinical guidance documents and antenatal education materials should be updated to reflect the risks of vaping, avoiding any ambiguity about its safety in pregnancy 58. Gender-sensitive health promotion As pregnancy is a gendered experience, the development of public health strategies addressing e-cigarette use during pregnancy must explicitly consider the social, cultural, and structural determinants that affect women s health behaviors. Gender norms, socioeconomic vulnerability, and exposure to targeted marketing disproportionately shape women s risk environments and their engagement with nicotine products. Research has shown that pregnant individuals may be influ- enced by social expectations to maintain a healthy pregnancy, yet may Fig. Comparative Forest Plots of preterm birth among vaping Users, Non-Users, Smokers, and Dual Users. Furthermore, tobacco and vaping com- panies have historically used gender-specific advertising, framing e-cigarettes as tools for stress relief, weight control, or modernity, messages that can resonate powerfully with young women and pregnant individuals navigating complex life transitions. Effective health pro- motion must therefore go beyond biomedical risk messaging to include gender-responsive education, culturally appropriate counseling, and intersectional strategies that address the lived realities of pregnant in- dividuals 61. Community-based approaches that engage women as co-designers of interventions, as well as policies that confront com- mercial determinants of health e. , marketing and accessibility of flavored products , are essential to reduce prenatal exposure to vaping. content_chunk: Dual use significantly increases toxic exposure, as it combines the harmful effects of both vaping and combustible cigarettes, including additive exposure to nicotine, volatile organic compounds, and heavy metals 35. This combination leads to a higher risk of adverse preg- nancy outcomes, exceeding the risk caused by either product alone. Dual users consistently experience the most severe complications , with elevated rates of preterm birth, LBW, and SGA infants 62,63. The synergistic effects of nicotine, heavy metals, and volatile organic com- pounds VOCs exacerbate placental dysfunction, restricting oxygen and nutrients to the fetus, which contributes to growth restriction and hypoxia, as highlighted in recent research 21. Although vaping users are exposed to fewer toxins, the presence of VOCs and heavy metals still poses substantial risks 15. Thus, the biological mechanisms underlying adverse pregnancy-related outcomes associated with prenatal vaping use remain largely unclear, as do the factors contributing to the differing effects observed between vaping and tobacco smoking. Both e-liquids and the byproducts produced during the heating process, such as alde- hydes, may play a role in increasing these risks 8. Research on animal models has indicated that exposure to vaping aerosols containing nico- tine during pregnancy can impair blood flow in both the maternal uterine artery and the fetal umbilical cord. This disruption can poten - tially lead to intrauterine growth restriction and preterm birth 7. Moreover, substances other than nicotine in e-liquids have been found to interfere with trophoblast function in the placenta, resulting in struc- tural complications 22,23. These placental alterations may heighten the likelihood of preeclampsia, early miscarriage, preterm delivery, and even maternal or fetal mortality. However, they do not entirely account for the differences in effects between vaping and cigarettes users. Strengths and limitations This meta-analysis s strengths include its review of current literature and the inclusion of diverse studies, providing a broad perspective on the impact of vaping use during pregnancy. However, the heterogeneity across studies in terms of population characteristics, vaping usage pat- terns, and outcome measures may limit the generalizability of the findings. The reliance on self-reported data in many studies could introduce recall bias, and the cross-sectional design of most studies limits the ability to infer causality. Additional limitations include vari- ability in study design, sample size, and inconsistent control for con- founding factors. Furthermore, studies often lacked detailed information on nicotine dosage and did not differentiate between ex-smokers and current smokers. For example, while studies such as those by Ammar 2023 8 and Nanninga 2023 11 benefit from large sample sizes, they did not account for the duration and intensity of vaping use, which may influence outcomes. Conclusion Our study demonstrates a strong association between vaping use during pregnancy and an increased risk of SGA, preterm birth, and LBW, with dual users facing the highest risks. These findings have important implications for both public health and clinical practice. Vaping should not be considered a safe alternative for pregnant women.

Introduction Former ly known as monke ypox, mpo x is a re-emerging zoonotic disease caused by Monkeypo x virus MPXV , a species belonging to the genus Orthopo xvirus within the family Poxviridae 1,2.

content_chunk: Fol- lowing over three years of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic 3 , the World Health Organization WHO declaration of a new mpo x outbreak as a Public Health Emerge ncy of International Concern PHEIC under - scores the potential for heightened concern in response to reports of a novel virus spreading globally 4. The true burden and geo- graphical distribution of endemic mpo x remain unclear due to di- agnostic challenges and limitations in surveillance 5. How ever , mpo x has historicall y impacte d children and adolescents in rural, low-income areas of West and Central Africa, with data from the Democratic Republic of the Congo showing the highest incidence rate of 18. 1 per 100,000 among 5 9-y ear-olds 6. Throughout the years, limited epidemiological data on the im- pact of mpo x during pregnancy have been collected. A 2024 sys- tematic revie w of seven studies identified 32 pregnan t women infected with clade IIb MPXV between 6 and 31 weeks of gestat ion. Among the 12 pregnancies with reported outcomes, half result ed in intraut erine fetal demise 5. How ever , it remains unclear whether pregnant wom en are more susceptible to MPXV due to im- munomodulatory chang es in pregnancy , whether the infection is more sever e during pregnancy , what the fetal and newborns out- comes are and whether there are differences in the matern al and fetal health depend on the MPXV clade 7. Given this gap in know ledge , we undertook a narrat ive revie w of the most recent liter ature on mpo x in the conte xt of pregnancy , with particular focus on the new ly emerging mpo x variant. Epidemiology MPXV is now recognized to have two geneticall y distinct clades that originated in different geogr aphical regions of Africa: Clade I including sub-clades Ia and more recent ly Ib is endemic in Central Africa, while Clade II subdivided into IIa and IIb is endemic in West Africa 8 1 0. Since its isolation in monkey s in 1958 and the first human case in 1970 11 , sever al mpo x outbr eaks have occurred, primarily in rural rainfor ests areas of Central and West Africa, as a result of zoonotic spillov er events and, as a result, did not garner broad attention 12,13. Historicall y almost all mpo x cases report ed outside Africa were linked to international travel or the importation of exotic pets 14. In 2017, an mpo x outbreak in Nige ria, became one of the largest recor ded in Africa at that time, mainly caused by west African clade of the virus, with more than 120 confirmed cases and sever al deaths 15. This outbr eak raised concern due to a possible human-to- human tran smission in urban areas, but the sexual tran smission rout e of this outbr eak may have been underr eported 16.

content_chunk: Clade I MPXV predominat ed until 2022, with most documented cases occurring in Centr al Africa 17. How ever , the unprecedent global outbreak of 2022 was primarily associated with a new lineage , B1 of Clade IIb MPXV 18,19 with more than 87,000 mpo x cases report ed by 121 Countries across all 6 World Health Organization WHO regions 20. The multi-country outbr eak of mpo x rapidl y spread through human-to-human close contact and sexual transmission, affecting sever al countries where the virus had not previousl y been observed. On 23 July 2022, WHO Direct or-Gener al, Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebre yesus, declare d mpo x a Public Health Emergency of International Concern PHEIC 21. With a sustained global decline of cases, this PHEIC was lifted in May 2023. How ever , seven African Union Member States AU MS Cameroon, Central African Republic, Congo, Democrat ic Republic of the Congo, Ghana, Liberia, Nigeria continued to report cases in 2023, totaling 14,95 7 cases with 739 deaths, resulting in a case fatality rate CFR of 4. Phylog enetic studies have indicated that by the mid-Sept ember 2023, a new Clade Ib MPXV emerged in Kamituga, a densely populated mining town in Democratic Republic of the Congo DRC 9. DRC has since become the epicenter of this new epidemic, with the high tran smission rate of Clade Ib facilitating the rapid spread of the virus, particularl y due to the commercial nature of the mining town. By 2024, the DRC, which had report ed appro ximatel y 88 of mpo x cases in Africa in that year, had recorded 19,513 cases before the emergency declaration. To date, 59 467 suspected cases and 1300 deaths linked to mpo x since 2024 have been report ed within DRC 23. The epidemic also spread to neighboring countries including Rwanda, Burundi, Kenya, and Uganda, which had not previousl y reported mpo x 24. On 13 August 2024 Africa CDC declare the on- going MPO X Clade I outbreak a public health emergency of con- tinental security PHECS 25 , while the following day, the WHO declare d it a PHEIC 26. All documented transmission rout es of MPO X, both zoonotic and human-to-human whether sexual or not have been observed in the ongoing outbreak, although the relati ve contribution of each mode of tran smission remains unclear. A particular concern is the high incidence among children , who are disproportionat ely affected, likely due to household transmission and contact with small mam - mals 27,28. Although the true number of cases may be underestimat ed, the global number of confirmed mpo x cases has risen steadil y since 2022, reaching 124,753. As of 14 February 2025, more than 15 AU MS across all five regions of Africa have report ed a cumulativ e total of 21,113 confirmed cases since the beginning of 2024 29.

content_chunk: Starting from August, Sweden, Thailand and India reported the firsts import ed cases of mpo x due to MPXV Clade Ib outside Africa 30 32. As of 14 February , other sever al import ed travel-r elated cases have also been dete cted in German y seven cases , United Kingdom nine cases , the United States of America four cases , Canada one case , Pakistan one case , Belgium two cases , China seve n cases , Franc e one case , India one case , Oman one case , the United Arab Emirat es one case , and Ireland one case 29. Secondary tran smission among close contacts of imported cases within the EU EEA have been reported in the UK, German y, Belgium, China and Franc e 33. Pregnant women represent a neglecte d population in this con- text, due to the scarce resour ces and limited technical capacity for virus dete ction in deep rural regions of Africa, where much of the natural history of the infection has unfolded 34. Follo wing the 2022 global outbreak and the ongoing epidemic in Africa, the risk of vertical tran smission of mpo x has garnered increasing atten tion. Virology MPXV is a large, enveloped, double-str anded, linear DNA dsDN A virus of 190 kb with a diameter of appro ximat ely 200 250 nm that uniq uely replicates within the cytopl asm of the infected cells, independently of the host cell s cellular machinery 2. The virus is extremely comple x and contains more than 100 viral proteins, whose functions are not yet completel y known 2. As previously described, two clades have been identified: Clade I formerl y known as Congo Basin clade and Clade II formerl y know n as West African clade , with further classification into subclades Ia, Ib, IIa and IIb 35. These clades exhibit differen t epidemiological char acteristics and clinical outcomes. Clade Ia is endemic in animal reservoirs, primarily rodents and non-human primat es, and it has historic ally caused small outbreaks in humans, predominantly af- fecting children, who are at great er risk for sever e disease. Journal of Infection and Public Health 18 2025 102758 was first identified in 2023 during an outbreak in eastern Demo - cratic Republic of the Congo, where cases were primarily observed in adolescents and adults, with sexual tran smission being a key mode of spread, and subseq uently expanded to other African countries and travellers 30. Recent studies revealed that a novel Clade Ib has a deletion of the D14L OPG032 gene 36. The D14L gene encodes valosin-containing protein VCP -MPO X, which contribut es to viru- lence, together with inhibiting the complement cascade 37. Com - parati ve studies betwee n Clade I and II, with the D14L gene either deleted or inserted, show ed no differences in virulence. So, other factors besides VCP-MPO X are necessary to explain this aspect 38.

content_chunk: Subclade IIa is also a zoonosis with occasional spillov er from animal reservoirs to humans. In contrast, subclade IIb tran smission is primarily sustained through human-t o-human contact, pre- dominantly affecting men who have sex with men and their sexual networ ks. This subclade trigge red the global mpo x epidemic in 2022 20. A recent systematic revie w reported that Clade I is associated with a significantly higher mortality rate than Clade II OR 10. How ever , this comparison involved populations with different char acteristics in terms of age and did not account for potential disparities in re- porting practices, publication bias, access to medical care, or HIV status. Moreo ver, data from Clade I did not include the recently detect ed Clade Ib. The mortality rate of MPXV Clade Ib appears lower than that of Clade Ia, estimated at appro ximatel y 4. 9 , although it remains unclear whether this difference is attributable to the viru- lence of the variant or the fact that most infected individuals are adults, who are intrinsically at lower risk of sever e disease 40. Like smallpo x, MPXV can be trans mitted verticall y, although the exact mechanisms of intraut erine tran smission remain unknown 41. Four pathw ays of transmission have been theorized: 1 genital ascension: the virus could ascend from infected vagina and cervix, infecting the chorionic membranes; 2 hematog enous rout e: high viral loads up to 10⁶ copies per millilitre in one case can enter the fetal circulation from the maternal bloodstream through the ma- ternal-fetal interface at the chorionic villi; 3 direct infection of placenta: MPXV may directl y infect the placental syncytiotr opho - blast, through mechanisms like transcyt osis or membran e fusion; 4 inflammatory mediation: inflammation trigger ed by the virus could disrupt matern al immune responses, allowing viral invasion of fetal blood 42. Matern al-fetal transmission of Clade Ia mpo x has been demon - strat ed through the detection of the virus in fetal tissue biopsies and autopsies, amniotic fluid, and cord blood 43,4 4. Additionally , in a meta-analy sis and systematic review conducted by Clemente et at, mpo x-specific IgM has been identified in serum or cerebr ospinal fluid CSF in children within a few days of birth 5. While there are limited reports of fetal infection or intraut erine tran smission invol- ving Clades IIa and IIb, a recent nonhuman primates model research by Krabbe et al. suggests that Clade IIb can also be tran smitted from mother to fetus, with a similar pattern of infected tissues as pre- viously observed in human cases involving Clade Ia 45. Trans mission of mpo x from breastfeeding mothers to their in- fants can also occur , likely through close contact. How ever , it re- mains unknown whether MPXV is present in breast milk 46. Clinical manifestations To date, most of the available literatur e on mpo x MPX in pregnancy is limit ed to case reports.

content_chunk: To provide a compreh ensiv e analy sis of the clinical manifestations of MPX during pregnan cy, we conducted a liter ature revie w using MEDLINE, focusing exclusiv ely on original resear ch articles published in peer -review ed medical journals. Relevant studies were identified using a combination of the following sear ch terms: monkeypo x OR mpo x AND pregnancy OR fetus OR stillbirth OR miscarriage. A total of 65 articles were initially screened for eligibility; how ever , the majority 51 65, 78. 5 were excluded as they did not report original cases of MPX infection during pregnancy. The data extract ed from the 10 10 65, 15. 4 selecte d articles are summarized in Table 1. A total of 37 cases of MPX in pregnancy have been documented in the liter ature, with the majority described in North America 28 3 7, 75. 7 and Africa 8 37, 21. Clade assignment was infreq uentl y dete rmined 5 37, 13. 5 , with clade II infections confirmed in 4 out of 5 cases 80 and Clade I infection identified in 1 out of 5 cases 20. The median maternal age was 22 years rang e: 19 29 , and, based on the available data, most cases were report ed during the second trimester of pregnancy 11 22, 50. Most cases reported the char acteristic MPX rash 26 30, 86. Additionall y, a smaller pro- portion present ed with or without typical genital ulcers 3 30, 10 and lymphadenopath y 3 30, 10. In terms of fetal outcomes, there were three cases of stillbirth 3 37, 8. 1 and two cases of mis- carriage report ed 2 37, 5. Moreo ver, one case of fatal hydrops fetalis associated with hepatomegal y and peritoneal effusion was described. These findings align with the Centers for Disease Control and Prev ention CDC recommendations, which emphasize that the signs and sympt oms of MPXV infection in pregnant women may resemble those observed in the gener al population, including fever , headache, lymphadenopath y, malaise, sore throat, and cough 55. Distin - guishing MPXV infection during pregnancy can be challenging, as its sympt oms may overlap with other conditions, including dermatoses of pregnan cy, such as polymorphic eruption of pregnan cy, or more common infections like varicella zoster. Additionall y, sexually tran smitted infections STIs together with MPX have been reported and an inclusiv e diagnostic approach is recommended when testing for potential infections 55. It is important to ackno wledge that, beyond the 37 cases de- scribed here, additional instances of MPX in pregnancy have been mentioned in the literatur e 56. Moreo ver, the prev alence of the disease may be underest imated, particularl y in light of the emer - gence of the new Clade 1b, which is primarily spreading in Africa. Curren tly, there is no available data regar ding the impact of MPX Clade 1b on pregnancy or fetal outcomes.

content_chunk: Considering the physiological changes in the immune system during pregnancy , pregnant women are among the groups at higher risk of exposure to mpo x 57. How ever , due to the limited number of studies on mpo x in pregnancy , data on disease severity in this population remain scarce. Data from a recent systematic revie w conduct ed by Clemente et al. , reported that maternal primary out- comes were pret erm deliv ery, pregnancy loss, requirement for hos- pitalization or inten sive care, and maternal death 5. Moreo ver, existing know ledge of other orthopoxviruses confirm that smallpo x poses a great er risk of sever e illness in pregnan t women than in nonpregnan t individuals, with a higher case fatality rate, mostly in the third trimester of gestation 58,59. The primary congenital outcomes included mothe r-to-child mpo x tran smission, pret erm birth, small-for -gestational-ag e status, low birth weight, microcephal y, and hepatosplenomegal y. When comparing fetal outcomes with other orthopoxviruses, preterm birth, miscarriage and stillbirth are more frequentl y observed in pregnant women infected with smallpo x 58. Diagnosis Rapid diagnosis is crucial for managing mpo x, including isolation to prev ent transmission, minimizing outbreaks, and guiding treat - ment strat egies 60. Since mpo x sympt oms closely resemble those of other, mainly viral, infections 61 , diagnosis must be supported B.
