The WHO classifies mpo x cases as suspected, proba ble, or confirmed, based on these criteria 62. Diagnosis of mpo x infection in obst etric and pediatric popula - tions is challenging, since the curr ent diagnostic criteria do not specifically addres s testin g among pregnant women and chil- dren 56. The gold standar d for confirming mpo x is real-time polymer ase chain reaction RT-PCR or conv entional PCR targeting MPXV, which can be used alone or in combination with sequencing to dete rmine the viral clade 63. Depending on clinical presentation, RT-PCR can be performed on various biological samples 64 6 6. As report ed in sever al case reports, PCR has also proven effectiv e in cases of vertical tran smission, dete cting MPXV in amniotic fluid, peritoneal fluid, placental tissue from mpo x infect ed mothe rs and in fetal tissue, and umbilical cord blood 44,67. Whether MPXV is present in breast milk is still unknown, because PCR performed on breast milk from one MPXV-infected woman tested negati ve for MPO X DNA 51. Serologica l tests, such as enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay ELISA , later al flow assay s LFAs , immunofluor escence assay IFA , and immunohistochemistry , are important in seropr evalence and vaccine efficacy studies 68 , but have limited value in diagnosing acute mpo x due to cross -reacti vity with other orthopoxviruses OPV 69. suggest ed that an ELISA may guide appropriat e deliv ery decisions for women with recent mpo x infection 43. De- tecting serocon version of specific IgM and IgG antibodies in un- vaccinate d pregnant women, appro ximatel y 4 days after the onset of rash, may allow for the deferral of deliv ery 68. This could enable the tran splacental transfer of maternal IgG antibodies against MPXV to the fetus, in analogy to the management approac h for var- icella 70. Moreo ver, as described in a recent systematic revie w of maternal and congenital mpo x infection, serology was used in two cases to confirm a mpo x congenital diagnosis 41. Histopathology and immunohistoche mistry analy ses using anti- body to vaccinia virus on placental tissue have proved to be useful for determining mpo x infection. Basal hemorr hages, visible on both the maternal and fetal side, can be observed, along with a pattern of extensiv e and diffuse positiv e staining in chorionic villous stromal cells 71. Real-time PCR remains the fastest, cheapest and most sensitiv e assay to detect, distinguish and monit or MPXV outbr eaks. devel oped, validated and implemented a new RT-PCR assay dD1 4 16 to dete ct the novel MPXV Clade Ib 72. Until now , identification of the MPXV genetic clade has been primarily based on genome sequences of the detect ed virus.

content_chunk: Additionally , the PCR assa ys recommended by the CDC for distinguishing MPXV from other or- thopoxviruses, but also betwee n Clade I and Clade II MPXV strains, may result in false negati ves 73 , because of the large 1 kbp de- letion in MPXV genome, specifically in the OPG032 gene 9,36. Treatment The majority of patients do not require antivir al treatment, as mpo x is typically a self-limiting illness. For immunocompete nt pa- tients with mild disease, pain control and supportiv e care are usually sufficient. How ever , antivir al treatment should be considered for specific groups, including vulner able populations and individuals with activ e skin diseases at high risk of dissemination or those with life-threat ening mpo x. Vulner able groups include sever ely im- munocompromised patients, as well as pregnant, recently pregnant or breastfeeding wom en 74. The only treatment appro ved by the European Medicines Agency EMA for mpo x diseases is teco virimat 75 , although other options have been used in the last years, as outlined in Table 2. Due to the alter ed immune status, pregnancy and breastfeeding are considered indications for prioritized treatm ent in patients with mpo x. Given the limit ed data on efficacy , medical managem ent should be tailored based on the stage and severity of the illness 94. If treatment is indicated, teco virimat is recommended as the first- line antiv iral by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prev ention CDC to prevent vertic al transmission, despite not being authorized for use during pregnancy and the absence of clear guidelines 80. Animal studies to date have shown no embryo toxic or teratog enic effects, and pregnant and breastfeeding women are eligible for en- rollment in the open-label Study of Tecov irimat for Human Mon - keypox Virus STOMP 43,81. Additionall y, a CDC report on pregnan t persons noted that 11 pregnant wom en who recei ved te- covirimat experienced no adverse effects 51. The use of cidofov ir and brincidofovir in treating mpo x during pregnan cy is contro versial, as animal reproduction studies have demonstra ted teratog enic effects. Thus, these medications must be avoide d, particularl y in the first trimester of pregnancy 83. Limited data also exist regarding vaccinia immune globulin intra venous VIGIV , and its effects on fetal health and on fertility remain unclear. How ever , since immune globulins have been widely used during pregnan cy without any specific negativ e effect on repr oductiv e health, VIGIV may be considered for selected cases 95. Medical managem ent should be integr ated with obstet ric guidance to ensure approp riate fetal surveillance and dete rmine optimal deliv ery timing 43. Prev ention Early dete ction of cases, combined with vaccination, are critical pillars for the prev ention and control of global mpo x outbreaks.

content_chunk: Timely identification of confirmed cases is essential to imple - ment primary prev ention measures aimed at disruption transmis - sion chain. Control interv entions, applicable in both hospital and domestic settings, include patient isolation, strict adherence to hand hygiene practices, and the use of approp riate personal protectiv e equipment 96,9 7. Vaccination serves as another important tool to reduce viral tran smission and can be used as pre-e xposure prophylaxis PrEP or post-e xposure proph ylaxis PEP 98,99. To date, two vaccines licensed for smallpo x have demonstra ted cross-pr otection against the MPXV: the ACAM20 00 vaccine, a live, replication-competent vaccinia virus, and JYNNEOS MVA-BN , a non-re plicating modified vaccinia Ankara virus vaccine. Their use in pregnancy has been debated for years, as most clinical trials do not include pregnan t women 100. If indicated, and following a thorough assessment of the benefits and potential ad- verse effects of vaccination, a PEP should be offered to reduce the risk of vertical transmission and protect the fetus. Like other live vaccines, ACAM 2000 is contrai ndicated during pregnan cy due to the risk of transplacental transmission, which can negativ ely affect pregnancy outcomes 43,101. In contrast, MVA-BN, a highl y attenuat ed, non-replicating vaccine, has not shown vaccine- related fetal malformations in animal studies 102. Alongside infection control and prev entiv e measures, pregnant and breastfeeding women who have been exposed to mpo x and are at risk may be vaccinated with the MVA-BN, which has proven ef- ficacy in prev enting infection. How ever , the MVA-BN vaccine is gener ally not recommended during pregnancy unless the benefits of prev enting mpo x outwei gh any potential unknown risks 103. Journal of Infection and Public Health 18 2025 102758 Conclusions This narrati ve revie w highlights the know ledge gaps regar ding mpo x infection during pregnancy , particularl y with the emergen ce of new MPXV clades such as Clade Ib. While existing data suggest that mpo x poses significant risks to both maternal and fetal health, including miscarriage, stillbirth, and neonatal complications, the limited number of reported cases hinders a comprehensi ve under - standing of these outcomes. The scarcity of clade-specific informa - tion, especially concerning Clade Ib, further complicates efforts to assess the relati ve virulence and transmission dynamics in pregnant women. Pregnant women appear equally susceptibl y to MPXV in- fection compared to non-pregnant individuals although whether it is more sever e in pregnancy remains unclear. Recommendations and future directions Diagnostic challenge s persist, with curr ent methodologies not fully adapt ed to the needs of obstet ric populations. While teco vir- imat appears promising for managing mpo x in pregnancy , its safety and efficacy remain undere xplored in this conte xt. Decisions about treatment, mode of deliv ery or other obstetrics interv entions in pregnancy should be individualized based on available resources, gestational age of fetus and clinical severity. Ongoing research and surveillance are essential to better inform clinical and public health strat egies, particularl y for vulnerable populations such as pregnant women. Masseye, Sharlene Newmanf, Vidya Rajagopalang, Lynne M. Smithh, Anna Zilverstandi, Gretchen Bandolij, The HBCD Pregnancy Exposures, Including Substances Workgroup aUniversity of Florida, PO Box 100231, Gainesville, FL 32610-0231, USA bChildren s Hospital of Philadelphia, University of Pennsylvania, 734 Schuylkill Ave, Room 19363, Philadelphia, PA 19146, USA cOklahoma State University, 116 Psychology Building, Stillwater, OK 74074, USA dEmory University School of Medicine, 12 Executive Park Drive, Atlanta, GA 30329, USA eMassachusetts General Hosptial, Harvard Medical School, 55 Fruit Street, Boston, MA 02114, USA fUniversity of Alabama, NE Medical Building, Box 870328, Tuscaloosa, AL 35487, USA gChildren s Hospital Los Angeles, Keck School of Medicine, University of Southern California, 4650 Sunset Blvd, Los Angeles, CA 90703, USA hHarbor-UCLA Medical Center, 1124 West Carson Street, Box 17, Torrance, CA 90502, USA iUniversity of Minnesota, 717 Delaware Street, Minneapolis, MN 55414, USA jUniversity of California San Diego, 9500 Gilman Drive, MC 0828, La Jolla, CA 92093, USA Keywords: Brain Child development HBCD Maternal health Pregnancy Prenatal exposure delayed effects Substance-related disordersABSTRACT The Healthy Brain and Child Development HBCD Study, a multi-site, prospective, longitudinal cohort study, will examine human brain, cognitive, behavioral, social, and emotional development beginning prenatally and planned through early childhood. Prenatal exposures, including substances of abuse, impact fetal development and have effects across the life course. During the development of the HBCD Study, the Pregnancy Exposures, Including Substances Workgroup WG-PRG was charged with characterizing maternal health and behavior during pregnancy into the childhood years. Maternal physical and mental health, including substance use, and pregnancy and birth complications and outcomes were prioritized. Pregnancy, chronic and acute health con- ditions, family mental health, and healthcare utilization were assessed using existing and novel measures. Maternal mental health was assessed with the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale, select items in the DSM-5 Self-Rated Level-1 and 2 Cross-Cutting Symptom Measures, and the National Stressful Events Survey-PTSD Short Scale. Finally, participants reported lifetime, recent, and current use of substances using a modified- ASSIST during pregnancy and postpartum. Quantities and frequencies of reported substances were collected for select periods prior to and during pregnancy through an interview or web application using the timeline- followback method. HBCD will advance our understanding of the impact of the intrauterine environment on early development. Introduction The Healthy Brain and Child Development Study HBCD https : hbcdstudy. org is the largest study of brain development from birth into middle childhood in the United States US. Launched in 2023, the HBCD study is enrolling from 27 sites and plans to follow a na- tionally representative sample of over 7000 pregnant individuals and their offspring beginning in the second trimester of pregnancy through the first decade of life.

Located in every region of the US, study sites map available at hbcdstudy. org recruitment-sites enroll participants from catchment areas that collectively represent the US population of individuals aged 15 50 years who have recently given birth. To ensure the study pop- ulation reflects the population of childbearing individuals nationally, the consortium developed site-specific enrollment goals based on the characteristics of this population, including race, Hispanic ethnicity, educational attainment, household income, and the urbanicity and area deprivation index for the location of residence. In addition, because use of certain substances during pregnancy is relatively rare, the HBCD Study over-samples participants who have or continue to use alcohol, cannabis, nicotine, or opioids during the current pregnancy 25 of the overall sample to ensure sufficient power to investigate the impact of prenatal exposure to opioids and other substances on later brain development. The rationale for this innovative study, its goals and the overall approach taken to develop the protocol is described in detail elsewhere Nelson et al. , 2024 ; Volkow et al. Briefly, the HBCD protocol was designed by a collection of Workgroups WGs , each comprising intramural scientists from the NIH and extramural scientists from the coordinating centers and study sites with expertise in specific domains. Each WG worked independently to ensure its respective domain was well specified and collectively to ensure its domain was incorporated cohesively into the protocol with the other domains. Investigators serving on multiple workgroups with interrelated domains served as liaisons between the WGs to minimize redundancy. This paper focuses on the portion of the protocol developed by the Pregnancy Exposures, Including Substances Workgroup WG-PRG for the first four visits of the HBCD Study, which span pregnancy and the first fifteen months following the estimated due date.

content_chunk: The specific focus of the WG-PRG was to characterize a range of protective and adverse prenatal influences on neurodevelopment, while balancing measure quality with participant burden. Within the domain of pregnancy exposures, the constructs of interest include 1 maternal physical health, 2 maternal mental health, 3 maternal substance use, and 4 pregnancy and birth complications and outcomes. This paper describes the scientific rationale for assessing each of these constructs, and the measures selected to assess them during the first four study visits. Not all pregnant individuals identify as mothers; the term maternal is used only to distinguish the birth parent enrolled during pregnancy from other parents or caregivers of the child participant. Domain of interest An overarching goal of the consortium was to develop a protocol for the HBCD Study that optimized achieving the seven scientific objectives from the NIH and minimized the impact of barriers to participation. Thus, a primary consideration of the WG-PRG was to balance assessing the most critical factors using reliable measures, many of which could only be measured at the desired level of granularity with self-reported data, and the burden of the protocol on participating dyads and site infrastructure. Within this framework, the WG-PRG sought to develop a comprehensive, person-centered protocol to collect important informa - tion about the prenatal period in as much detail as possible without negatively impacting data quality and retention. Although there are innumerable environmental influences during the prenatal period that may be associated with unfavorable physical, psychological, and behavioral health outcomes among offspring, the WG-PRG focused on four primary constructs that impact development substantially, which are further detailed in subsequent sections. Maternal physical health Previous pregnancy outcomes are associated with current pregnancy complications and outcomes Chen et al. , 2023; Makhlouf et al. , 2014 , including, but not limited to, previous fetal loss, preterm birth, cesarean delivery, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and gestational diabetes. Furthermore, previous pregnancy experiences have been shown to influence maternal anxiety during the current pregnancy Shapiro et al. Assisted reproductive technology ART has been associated with adverse maternal outcomes, though very little is known about its effect on developmental trajectories during childhood Bay et al. , 2019; Heshmatnia et al. Many other exposures also affect the health of pregnant in- dividuals and fetal development. Preventive exposures include the use of folic acid-containing pre- natal vitamins, which lower the risk of neural tube defects Greenberg et al. , 2011 , and low-dose aspirin for the prevention of preeclampsia Force, 2021. Furthermore, several vaccines are recommended during pregnancy, including influenza, pertussis, respiratory syncytial virus RSV , and COVID-19 if not up to date on the series to protect the birth parent and infant during pregnancy and the early postnatal period Centers for Disease Control and Prevention CDC , n. Other exposures are hypothesized to negatively affect maternal and fetal health.

content_chunk: For example, COVID-19 and other illnesses have been associated with premature birth, offspring who are small for their gestational age, and neurodevelopmental disorders among offspring, among other outcomes Elgueta et al. , 2022; McClymont et al. , 2022; San Martín-Gonz alez et al. Very high maternal fever during pregnancy can be particularly dangerous for the fetus Dior et al. , 2016; Hochler et al. In addition, several sexually transmitted and other infections during pregnancy are associated with adverse outcomes, including major malformations and mental health and neurobehavioral disorders among offspring Jash and Sharma, 2022. Certain chronic conditions are common among women during the reproductive years, and these disease processes can affect fetal devel - opment Ajslev et al. , 2012; Andersen et al. , 2013; Jølving et al. Preexisting or gestational maternal metabolic disorders, such as diabetes and obesity, are known to play a role in offspring health and neurodevelopment Edlow, 2021; Fresch et al. , 2024; Rodolaki et al. Furthermore, delivery and neonatal complications are more frequent among women with these metabolic disorders Fresch et al. Likewise, medications used to treat chronic diseases, including mental health conditions, and infections can affect fetal development. From known teratogens like valproic acid to purported behavioral te- ratogens like acetaminophen, the assessment of prescription and over-the-counter medication use is important for studying offspring health Ornoy, 2009; Ricci et al. Maternal mental health Pregnancy and postpartum are periods of heightened vulnerability for the onset and exacerbation of mental health conditions, a significant public health concern affecting approximately half a million individuals in the US each year Fawcett et al. , 2005; Guintivano et al. Approximately 20 of childbearing individuals report symptoms of a mental health condition, with onset occurring among a third of women during pregnancy and another 40 of women post- partum Fawcett et al. In addition, other maternal mental health conditions, including stress and post-traumatic stress disorder, and mental health disorders among first-degree rela- tives, increase the risk of adverse outcomes among pregnant individuals and their offspring Kingston et al. , 2018; Sanjuan et al. Pregnant individuals with mental health conditions are more likely to experience K. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience 71 2025 101494 adverse birth outcomes, and their infants are at increased risk of developmental delay and behavioral, emotional, and regulatory prob- lems Kingston et al. , 2018; Kingston and Tough, 2014; Monk et al. Furthermore, caretaker mental health during the child s early years of life is a well-documented risk factor for sub-optimal child development Netsi et al. Maternal substance use During pregnancy, the overall prevalence of addictive substance use, including alcohol, cannabis, opioids, and tobacco was at least 10 in the US in 2020 Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Adminis - tration, 2020. Though the prevalence of exposure to tobacco during pregnancy has declined, approximately 7 of pregnant women report using prescription opioids, and the prevalence of exposure to alcohol continues to be at least 10 Bonello et al. , 2023; England et al.

content_chunk: Adverse fetal and child developmental outcomes associated with prenatal exposure to alcohol, tobacco, and stimulants, like cocaine, are well documented, but less is known about the long-term developmental effects of prenatal exposure to opioids or cannabis, alone or in combination with other substances Banderali et al. , 2014; Wouldes and Woodward, 2013. For most of these sub- stances, little is known about their specific influence on brain develop - ment. Furthermore, though protective factors may modify these effects, the timing and mechanism through which adverse effects are mitigated is not well understood Bada et al. , 2012; Bandoli and Chambers, 2023. Pregnancy and birth complications and outcomes Pregnancy and obstetric outcomes influence both postpartum maternal health as well as offspring health throughout the life course. This includes factors, such as cesarean delivery, prematurity, and size for gestational age, are associated with both physical and neuro - developmental outcomes during childhood Bell et al. Protocol Measures to assess the four primary constructs of interest are administered primarily during the prenatal V1 and first post-partum V2 visits Fig. Time-varying parental and or caregiver measures of ongoing interest beyond the neonatal period are assessed during the third V3 and fourth V4 visits. Note that no assessments of adult health and behavior under the purview of the WG-PRG are administered during the fifth, remote visit V5. V1 is an in-person visit, which ideally occurs during the second trimester of pregnancy third trimester enrollment is permitted. Enrollment during the second trimester is preferred as pregnancy loss occurs most often during the first trimester. In addition, enrollment during the second trimester shortens the time elapsed since exposures occurring early in pregnancy, which may result in more accurate data. Second-trimester enrollment also optimizes the likelihood of completing the visit prior to birth. Finally, enrollment of participants during the third trimester could result in systematically over-representing child participants born at term. The second visit V2 of the HBCD protocol occurs within one month of the estimated due date EDD. Information about the domains of interest during the latter part of pregnancy be- tween V1 and delivery and the early postpartum period between de- livery and V2 as well as pregnancy complications and outcomes are collected during V2. Participants are randomly assigned to a one-month window during which V3 and V4 are to be conducted, from relative child participant ages calculated based on EDD, rather than date of birth of three to nine months and nine to fifteen months, respectively. To represent pregnant individuals who receive little to no prenatal care, up to 10 of participants can be recruited within five days of birth if they had four or fewer prenatal care visits. For participants recruited postnatally, the V1 and V2 protocols, including the collection of bio- specimens and assessment of social and environmental determinants, are combined into one, modified postnatal protocol to assess exposures during the entire pregnancy. The measures included in the HBCD Study protocol by the WG-PRG are represented by the Assessments icon in the graphical depiction of the protocol Fig. Each specific measure is listed with the visits during which it is administered Table 1 , and detailed in the following construct-specific subsections. Constructs of interest and measures The measures created, modified, or selected by the WG-PRG to characterize each of the prenatal constructs of interest included in the Fig. Protocol overview for the first five visits of the HEALthy Brain and Child Development HBCD Study. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience 71 2025 101494 HBCD Study protocol are detailed in subsequent, construct-specific sub- sections. Some measures required reports of exposure levels for specific periods during pregnancy. To define gestation, participants are asked for their estimated due date EDD during the screening procedure. The EDD is the anchor used to calculate relative age and define the time periods during which each postnatal study visit should occur, rather than date of birth, which does not account for premature birth. The EDD is also used to identify specific time points during the pregnancy, such as the beginning and end of trimesters. Because recruitment into HBCD study is delayed until the second trimester, most participants have received prenatal care before enrollment and have an ultrasound-dated estimate of the EDD. However, if participants do not know their EDD, they are asked to report their current gestational week of pregnancy. Using the EDD or gestational age GA , the first day of each participant s last menstrual period LMP is calculated. If the participant neither reports the EDD nor the GA, the participant is asked to report LMP. The LMP as well as the start and end dates for each trimester are then populated in questionnaires. EDD is updated in late pregnancy during calls from the research staff at approximately 32 weeks gestation, and all linked gestational milestones are shifted to reflect any updated information. Maternal physical health Measures to characterize certain aspects of the construct maternal physical health are grouped as shown in Table 1and described in the subsequent sub-sections. Obstetric history and current pregnancy. During the prenatal visit, an abbreviated obstetric history is collected to minimize the length of the visit. The WG-PRG chose not to collect detailed information about pregnancy terminations due to recent changes to reproductive health law. , number of pregnancies, is collected, but collection of parity is limited to the number of pregnancies that resulted in a live birth only, i. , no pregnancy outcomes for non-live-born de- liveries are collected. History of any cesarean delivery is collected as well as the date on which the prior pregnancy ended, if applicable, to afford the ability to calculate the latest inter-birth interval for multip - arous participants following delivery.

content_chunk: During V1, participants also report whether the pregnancy was planned, the gestational age at which pregnancy recognition occurred, and whether assisted reproductive technologies were used to conceive the current pregnancy. They also report the gestational age at which prenatal care was initiated, and whether and when prenatal or folic acid- containing vitamins or aspirin prophylactic for preeclampsia were initiated. These latter two exposures are updated at V2. In addition to these self-reported measures, information about the current pregnancy, such as the results of noninvasive prenatal testing, including glucose tolerance tests, and dates of ultrasound, is planned to be obtained from medical records. Pre-pregnancy height and weight. During V1, participants are asked for pre-pregnancy height and weight, from which pre-pregnancy body mass index BMI is calculated. Participants are asked during V1 to report any vac- cines Tdap, Flu, HPV, MMR, Meningitis, Hepatitis A-C, Varicella, Polio, Shingles, Typhoid, Yellow Fever, COVID-19, RSV received after LMP and during which trimester they were administered. This information is updated during V2 for the remainder of pregnancy. COVID-19, STIs, and other infections. Participants are asked if they have had a SARS-COV-2 infection at any time during gestation, the date of the positive test, and whether they had symptoms of COVID-19 during infection. If participants report using over the counter OTC or prescription medications to treat COVID-19, the medications are queried in RxNORM National Library of Medicine, n. during data collection, and participants report the date of initiation, date of cessation, and frequency of use during the reported period. They are then asked if they have had any other illnesses since LMP. Reported illnesses are queried by the research staff using the BioPortal ICD-10 ontology or symptom databases World Health Organization, n. , and participants report when the illness began and when it ended. If the participant reports a fever associated with the illness, the highest temperature and duration of the fever are recorded. The date of initiation, date of cessation, and frequency of use is also recorded for any medications taken for the illness. This information is updated at V2 for the remainder of pregnancy. To ease the burden of collecting information about infections occurring since LMP, a list of infections is provided to participants, including the following sexually transmitted infections STIs : gonor - rhea, chlamydia, herpes, human papillomavirus, and syphilis. Other infections included in the list are cytomegalovirus, group B strep, Hep- atitis A-C, HIV, toxoplasmosis, and urinary tract infection. Participants are asked to report the trimester s in which they had any of the in- fections. Infections not included in the list can be self-reported with other illnesses. In addition to these self-reported measures, test results for sexually transmitted and urinary tract infections; serology results for Hepatitis A- C, HPV, and HIV; and documentation of maternal fever are planned to be obtained from medical records.

Given their potential to be physical or neurodevelopmental teratogens, information about all pre- scription and over the counter OTC medications used during preg- nancy is collected. During V1, participants report all other prescription medications not described in previous subsections of Section 3. 1 that they used during the period from LMP to the day of the visit for any duration. To prompt recall, participants are asked to report use of common medications, including psychotropic medications and medi - cations to treat pain, diabetes, and hypertension, from a list as well as any other unlisted medications. Reported medications are queried in the RxNORM50 database in real time. Participants report the dates of initi- ation and cessation if applicable , frequency of use, and the indication for the medication, which is then queried from the BioPortal ICD-10 ontology and symptom databases World Health Organization, n. content_chunk: During V2, participants are first asked to update the status of pre- scription medications for which current use was reported during V1. They are then asked to report prescription medications initiated after the prenatal visit V1 but before delivery. For reported medications, the same information collected during V1 is also collected during V2. The V2 process for prescription medications is repeated for OTC medications. Healthcare utilization. During V1, participants are asked about their health insurance coverage at the time they became pregnant and if they saw a physician or dentist in the year prior to pregnancy. Partici - pants are also asked if they were seen in an Emergency Department ED or admitted to the hospital since LMP. Those who report an ED or in- patient admission are asked for the primary diagnosis at the visit selected by research personnel from the ICD-10 ontology or symptom database World Health Organization, n. Participants report admis - sion and discharge dates and administration or prescription of medica - tions OTC and prescription for any admissions. Maternal mental health Due to its influence on not only maternal health but also health and developmental outcomes among offspring, both family and personal psychiatric history are assessed. Current maternal mental health is assessed also, focusing on conditions common during pregnancy and the postpartum period Mukherjee et al. , 2016; Van Niel and Payne, 2020. Family and personal psychiatric history. To assess family history of psychiatric disorders, items from the Family History Assessment Module are combined with items from the Personal and Family Health History used in All of Us and included in the V1 assessments All of Us Survey Explorer, n. Alcohol use disorder, autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, bipolar disorder, depression, generalized anxiety disorder, schizo - phrenia, and substance use disorder are all assessed with their respective items from the Personal and Family Health History. However, age at diagnosis and medication used to treat these conditions is not assessed for relatives of the birth parent. To reduce protocol burden on partici - pants from large families, the family history questions are only asked about conditions among the offspring s biological parents and biological grandparents. Prenatal and postpartum depression. The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale EPDS , a sensitive, 10-item screening tool for prenatal and postpartum depression was selected due to its ease of administration and widely accepted use Cox et al. , 1987; Park and Kim, 2023. The EPDS is administered during pregnancy V1 and twice during the year following delivery V2 and V3. Maternal post-traumatic stress and acute stress disorders. To assess the severity of maternal posttraumatic and acute stress symptoms, the nine-item National Stressful Events Survey PTSD Short Scale NSESSS-PTSD and seven-item National Stressful Events Survey Acute Stress Disorder Short Scale NSESSS-Acute Stress Disorder are com- bined into a single assessment for the HBCD Study Kilpatrick et al. , 2011, 2013; LeBeau et al. Six of the items in the NSESSS-Acute Stress Disorder are also included in the NSESSS-PTSD.

content_chunk: These six items are administered only once in combination with the other four unique items for the two scales. The responses to the six overlapping items are used to score each scale individually. This assessment is completed at each of the in-person visits V1 4. Other maternal mental health disorders. To screen more broadly, the DSM-5 Self-Rated Level 1 and Level 2 version 8a Cross-Cutting Symptom Measure Adult was selected Doss and Lowmaster, 2022; Roche et al. This highly sensitive screening tool has two levels when used in community samples. Level 1 includes one to three ques- tions for each of thirteen mental health conditions. When a minimum threshold of level-1 symptoms is reported for anger, mania, anxiety, somatic symptoms, sleep disturbances, and repetitive thoughts, the participant answers several subsequent questions, which ask about additional symptoms associated with each mental health condition. Slight modifications were made due to the use of other measures and the study population. Specifically, the substance use questions were omitted due to the inclusion of other similar measures in the protocol. Level-1 questions for personality functioning are omitted also; instead, all par- ticipants complete the level-2 measures. In addition, the level-2 assess - ment for depression is administered to all participants, regardless of their responses to level 1. Finally, depression and sleep problems are assessed with the Promis 8a; the remaining level-2 domains are assessed using the standard symptom measures included in the Level 2 Cross-Cutting Symptom Measures. This assessment is completed at each of the first four visits V1 4. Maternal substance use A primary aim of HBCD is to investigate the effect of prenatal sub- stance exposure on child development. Within this context, optimal prediction of exposure-related neurodevelopmental risk requires multi- level assessment to capture both between- and within-individual vari- ability in substance use across the prenatal period Bandoli et al. Though biospecimens are also collected to char- acterize prenatal substance exposure, the primary goal of the WG-PRG is to collect detailed information about the use of substances that can only be collected directly from participants. The Timeline Followback TLFB method is the gold standard for collecting self-reported, detailed use information Hjorthøj et al. Due to the stigma associated with substance use, particularly during pregnancy, identifying a non-judgmental approach to collecting these data that mitigated po- tential harm to participants, particularly given the criminalization of prenatal substance use in some states, was prioritized. The burden of reporting detailed information both prior to and during 40 weeks of gestation was also considered. As a result, a two-step process was adopted, using questionnaires during the first step that include a version of the NIDA-modified Alcohol, Smoking, and Substance Involvement Screening Test ASSIST V2. 0 and conducting interviews with partici - pants during the second step, using the TLFB method or self-report entered directly into a web application National Institute on Drug Abuse, n. , 2005; Sobell and Sobell, 2000. content_chunk: During V1, partici - pants are screened for lifetime, pre-pregnancy, and prenatal substance K. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience 71 2025 101494 use and disordered use using a previously validated tool, the NIDA- modified ASSIST National Institute on Drug Abuse, n. , expanded for the HBCD Study from nine to eighteen substances nicotine or to- bacco products, alcohol, cannabis, cannabidiol, synthetic cannabinoids, prescription opioids, heroin or other illicit opioids, methadone, bupre - norphine, benzodiazepines, cocaine, amphetamine-type stimulants, methamphetamine, inhalants, hallucinogens or club drugs, androgenic anabolic steroids, phencyclidine, and kratom. First, participants are asked if they have ever used each of the eighteen substances. For each reported substance, a series of questions are asked about disordered use or use causing problems in their lives. For each substance for which any lifetime use is reported, partici - pants are then asked whether they used the substance in the three months prior to pregnancy, and separately, whether they used the substance during pregnancy. Information about how the participant typically uses each substance is then collected. For tobacco, participants are asked to report the type of product used, such as cigarettes or e- cigarettes. Likewise, participants who use cannabis are asked what types of products they use, such as smoking marijuana flower, vaping, or consuming edibles. If alcohol is reported during this period, the partic - ipant is asked what type of alcohol they consume beer, hard cider, hard seltzer, wine, and spirits. For each type, participants report the average volume of a typical serving or container. US-defined standard drinks are then calculated from the average serving size by dividing the amount reported by 12 ounces for beer, hard cider, and hard seltzer; 5 ounces for wine, and 1. Finally, if participants report opioids, they are asked the type of opioid they use and typical quantities per occasion of use as follows: heroin grams, bags , prescription opioids pills , buprenorphine pills, injectables, films , and methadone mg. At each visit occurring within fifteen months of the EDD V2 V4 , adult participants use a similar version of the ASSIST to report postnatal use of the same 18 substances of interest during the three months prior to each of these three visits. For each reported substance, participants are asked frequency of use, for which the response categories range from once or twice to daily or almost daily. Daily substance use during select weeks immediately prior to and during pregnancy. Participants who report any substance use in the three months before or during pregnancy are interviewed about their use of those substances using the TLFB method. To facilitate efficiency and privacy of data collection, a web application was developed in the R Shiny framework Shiny, n. Research personnel access the applica - tion from an iPad during the interview. Like the original paper-based approach, the application displays a calendar to aid in collecting daily use of substances. The web-based application, however, displays only the windows of interest that are pre-populated based on the EDD collected during screening.

content_chunk: Select weeks of gestation were chosen to capture the often-dynamic use of substances during pregnancy and reduce the burden of reporting use over the entire gestation Bandoli et al. Four periods are represented: pre-pregnancy use; very early prenatal use, likely prior to pregnancy recognition; recent prenatal use at the time of enrollment ; and late pregnancy use just prior to parturition. Specifically, the application displays nine weeks in total: two weeks prior to pregnancy four weeks before LMP through two weeks before LMP , four weeks early in preg- nancy two weeks after LMP through six weeks after LMP , current use at the time of enrollment the week prior to V1 , and two weeks late in pregnancy the last two weeks of gestation, reported during V2. Holi- days occurring during these nine weeks are also pre-populated. During V1, participants are asked about use of each substance re- ported in the ASSIST, disaggregated into product type e. , edible cannabis products , during each of the first seven weeks described above. The number of occasions of use are entered for each day for all products except cigarettes and cigarillos, for which number used are entered per day, and alcohol, for which the number of single servings consumed is entered per day. During V2, the interview using the TLFB method is administered again to collect daily substance use during the last two full weeks of gestation. While the research staff enter use data into the TLFB appli - cation during an interview for most participants, participants enter their own use data into the web application, following a brief training, at sites located in states in which prenatal substance use is reportable by the research staff. Typical substance use by trimester of pregnancy. To minimize participant burden, collection of detailed daily substance use data is limited to select weeks prior to and during gestation, when use is likely to vary. Nevertheless, this approach could result in misclassification of dyads as substance unexposed if infrequent or sporadic use occurs outside the windows of assessment. Thus, participants who report any use of opioids, cannabis, alcohol, nicotine, or stimulants in the three months prior to or during pregnancy are asked additional questions during V2 to assess typical substance-specific use by trimester. For each specific substance e. methadone, buprenorphine, etc. reported, par- ticipants are asked to estimate the number of weeks the substance was used during each trimester and the average number of days of use during the weeks of use for each trimester. Indoor smoke exposure. To differentiate between personal use and passive exposure to indoor smoke among individuals with a positive urine drug screen, participants are asked during V2 if they were exposed during pregnancy to second-hand smoke resulting from cigarettes, marijuana, and methamphetamine. Pregnancy and birth complications and outcomes During V2, participants report any pregnancy complications, including, but not limited to, gestational diabetes; hypertensive disor - ders of pregnancy, including preeclampsia; antiphospholipid syndrome; cervical insufficiency; and placenta previa.

content_chunk: Also, information about the birth is obtained, including whether labor was spontaneous or induced and delivery was vaginal or cesarean the latter with indication. Furthermore, participants report whether they had any of the following delivery complications: forceps-assisted delivery, vacuum-assisted de- livery, chorioamnionitis, presence of meconium, postpartum hemor - rhage requiring transfusion, and breech presentation. Finally, they report the length of stay of the birth hospitalization. In addition to these self-reported measures, an expanded list of pregnancy and birth complications as well as additional information about labor and delivery such as antenatal administration of antibiotics and steroids are planned to be obtained from medical records. Administration Most of these data are collected and managed using REDCap elec- tronic data capture tools Harris et al. The electronic question - naires are administered during in-person visits on a study iPad. These instruments are designed for participants to complete independently due to the sensitive nature of many of the questions and to minimize the length of the visit. While all questions have to be completed, all ques- tions in the WG-PRG measures include the response options Don t know and Decline to answer. For certain assessments, participants are asked to hand the iPad back to research personnel, who administer more complex measures such as the questions about medication use that rely on on- tologies. Research personnel can administer all the questionnaires for participants that need assistance or prefer not to complete any of the measures themselves. For V2, links to questionnaires that capture most of the information collected are sent to the adult participant one week prior to the in-person portion of V2. Questionnaires that are incomplete at the beginning of the in-person portion of V2 are then administered during the visit in addition to other surveys that can be administered K. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience 71 2025 101494 only during an in-person visit Table 1. In addition to the questionnaires, research personnel also conduct in- person interviews about substance use at V1 and V2 using the timeline follow back TLFB method, detailed in Section 3. Due to the interpretation of Alabama s chemical endangerment laws by some prosecutors, the consortium opted to blind the research team in Alabama to measures of substance use. Therefore, those portions of the protocol that typically involve research personnel are all self-administered at those sites. Instructions for completing the assessments were developed that include brief video instructions for the TLFB. To minimize participant burden with respect to visit length and varying degrees of health literacy among participants, the HBCD study consents participants to acquire health records, such as the medical re- cord from the birth hospitalization, to complement self-reported maternal and child health data. When possible, information is extrac - ted from electronic health records automatically; otherwise, specific information is planned to be manually abstracted from medical records by trained research personnel. content_chunk: Thus, to ensure adequare power to examine the effect of prenatal substance exposure on child development, pregnant individuals who use substances are oversampled to reach the consortium enrollment goal of 25 of the study population. To operationalize this objective and ensure an adequate range of exposure to detect effects, the WG-PRG developed criteria for minimum thresholds of opioid, alcohol, cannabis, and nicotine tobacco use by which to classify dyads as substance-exposed to track enrollment goals Table 2. These criteria were determined by expert opinion of WG members for each substance and approved by the HBCD Steering Committee. Alcohol thresholds are based on National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism criteria for what exceeds low-risk drinking Willenbring et al. , 2009; National In- stitutes of Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, n. Whether each dyad meets the minimum criteria to be classified as substance exposed for tracking enrollment is based on participant- reported use during pregnancy through the TLFB, results of toxicology carried out on biospecimens collected during or shortly after pregnancy Sullivan et al. , 2024 , and self-reported or documented in the medical record diagnoses of child participants during the neonatal period with substance-related syndromes Neonatal Opioid Withdrawal Syndrome and Fetal Alcohol Syndrome. These criteria are used solely to ensure sampling of the study population is enhanced for opioid and other substance use of interest during pregnancy. The protocol for assessing the extent to which study participants 1 represent the US population of individuals who recently gave birth and 2 use substances during pregnancy is detailed elsewhere Si et al. Importantly, in- dividuals with substance use below these criteria are also enrolled. Researchers using HBCD Study data can use the raw and calculated data to be released publicly as described in Section 4to define substance use based on the aims of their research. Piloting The first three visits of the HBCD Study protocol V1 3 were piloted at each of 27 sites prior to the launch of the main study. Sites were required to enroll at least three participants in the age range for each of these visits, totaling a minimum of nine pilot dyads per site. As a result of the information obtained during this pilot phase, the response options Don t know and Decline to answer were added to all questions. Other changes to the measures because of the pilot study included streamlining questions related to SARS-CoV-2 infection and COVID-19 vaccination to reduce participant burden. An indication for medication use was added, and hard cider and hard seltzers were added to the ASSIST question - naire. Finally, substance use data collected at sites at which participants self-administered the web application using the TLFB method were compared to substance use data collected at sites at which the research staff conducted interviews with participants using the TLFB method and entered the responses into the web application on their behalf. The data collected using the two approaches were comparable.

content_chunk: In addition, the consortium adheres to key principles of a trauma- informed approach, which include providing a family-centered phys- ical environment, training research personnel to interact with vulner - able populations effectively, and linking participants with unmet needs to community resources. Finally, to expand recruitment and retention of participants reflec - tive of the US population, participants who speak Spanish are eligible to participate in the HBCD Study. Participant-facing documents and data collection instruments were translated into Spanish by an external vendor and verified by a committee of native Spanish speakers in the consortium. The majority of sites employ Spanish-speaking staff mem- bers Anunziata et al. Conclusions Exposure to adverse conditions in utero is linked to atypical varia - tions in brain development that are associated with a variety of physical, psychological, and behavioral health sequelae that extend beyond the childhood years. Adverse environments are ubiquitous, including pre- natal and postnatal exposure to substances, socioeconomic deprivation, structural racism and other forms of exclusion, stress, maltreatment, food insecurity, and poor access to adequate health care. The complex interplay among genes and the environments children experience, particularly during early life, have historically presented methodologic challenges to mechanistic clarity in developmental research. Combined with the contributions of other workgroups to the protocol, assessment of prenatal exposures in the HBCD study will result in an unparalleled resource for the scientific community, resulting in an unprecedented opportunity to advance understanding of brain and child development. Findings resulting from this nationwide, multi-year investment have the potential to optimize early prevention among the most vulnerable families and shape public policy in ways that promote equitable in- vestment in the future. Masseye, Sharlene Newmanf, Vidya Rajagopalang, Lynne M. Smithh, Anna Zilverstandi, Gretchen Bandolij, The HBCD Pregnancy Exposures, Including Substances Workgroup aUniversity of Florida, PO Box 100231, Gainesville, FL 32610-0231, USA bChildren s Hospital of Philadelphia, University of Pennsylvania, 734 Schuylkill Ave, Room 19363, Philadelphia, PA 19146, USA cOklahoma State University, 116 Psychology Building, Stillwater, OK 74074, USA dEmory University School of Medicine, 12 Executive Park Drive, Atlanta, GA 30329, USA eMassachusetts General Hosptial, Harvard Medical School, 55 Fruit Street, Boston, MA 02114, USA fUniversity of Alabama, NE Medical Building, Box 870328, Tuscaloosa, AL 35487, USA gChildren s Hospital Los Angeles, Keck School of Medicine, University of Southern California, 4650 Sunset Blvd, Los Angeles, CA 90703, USA hHarbor-UCLA Medical Center, 1124 West Carson Street, Box 17, Torrance, CA 90502, USA iUniversity of Minnesota, 717 Delaware Street, Minneapolis, MN 55414, USA jUniversity of California San Diego, 9500 Gilman Drive, MC 0828, La Jolla, CA 92093, USA Keywords: Brain Child development HBCD Maternal health Pregnancy Prenatal exposure delayed effects Substance-related disordersABSTRACT The Healthy Brain and Child Development HBCD Study, a multi-site, prospective, longitudinal cohort study, will examine human brain, cognitive, behavioral, social, and emotional development beginning prenatally and planned through early childhood. Prenatal exposures, including substances of abuse, impact fetal development and have effects across the life course. During the development of the HBCD Study, the Pregnancy Exposures, Including Substances Workgroup WG-PRG was charged with characterizing maternal health and behavior during pregnancy into the childhood years. Maternal physical and mental health, including substance use, and pregnancy and birth complications and outcomes were prioritized. Pregnancy, chronic and acute health con- ditions, family mental health, and healthcare utilization were assessed using existing and novel measures. Maternal mental health was assessed with the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale, select items in the DSM-5 Self-Rated Level-1 and 2 Cross-Cutting Symptom Measures, and the National Stressful Events Survey-PTSD Short Scale. Finally, participants reported lifetime, recent, and current use of substances using a modified- ASSIST during pregnancy and postpartum. Quantities and frequencies of reported substances were collected for select periods prior to and during pregnancy through an interview or web application using the timeline- followback method. HBCD will advance our understanding of the impact of the intrauterine environment on early development. Introduction The Healthy Brain and Child Development Study HBCD https : hbcdstudy. org is the largest study of brain development from birth into middle childhood in the United States US. Launched in 2023, the HBCD study is enrolling from 27 sites and plans to follow a na- tionally representative sample of over 7000 pregnant individuals and their offspring beginning in the second trimester of pregnancy through the first decade of life.

Located in every region of the US, study sites map available at hbcdstudy. org recruitment-sites enroll participants from catchment areas that collectively represent the US population of individuals aged 15 50 years who have recently given birth. To ensure the study pop- ulation reflects the population of childbearing individuals nationally, the consortium developed site-specific enrollment goals based on the characteristics of this population, including race, Hispanic ethnicity, educational attainment, household income, and the urbanicity and area deprivation index for the location of residence. In addition, because use of certain substances during pregnancy is relatively rare, the HBCD Study over-samples participants who have or continue to use alcohol, cannabis, nicotine, or opioids during the current pregnancy 25 of the overall sample to ensure sufficient power to investigate the impact of prenatal exposure to opioids and other substances on later brain development. The rationale for this innovative study, its goals and the overall approach taken to develop the protocol is described in detail elsewhere Nelson et al. , 2024 ; Volkow et al. Briefly, the HBCD protocol was designed by a collection of Workgroups WGs , each comprising intramural scientists from the NIH and extramural scientists from the coordinating centers and study sites with expertise in specific domains. Each WG worked independently to ensure its respective domain was well specified and collectively to ensure its domain was incorporated cohesively into the protocol with the other domains. Investigators serving on multiple workgroups with interrelated domains served as liaisons between the WGs to minimize redundancy. This paper focuses on the portion of the protocol developed by the Pregnancy Exposures, Including Substances Workgroup WG-PRG for the first four visits of the HBCD Study, which span pregnancy and the first fifteen months following the estimated due date.

content_chunk: The specific focus of the WG-PRG was to characterize a range of protective and adverse prenatal influences on neurodevelopment, while balancing measure quality with participant burden. Within the domain of pregnancy exposures, the constructs of interest include 1 maternal physical health, 2 maternal mental health, 3 maternal substance use, and 4 pregnancy and birth complications and outcomes. This paper describes the scientific rationale for assessing each of these constructs, and the measures selected to assess them during the first four study visits. Not all pregnant individuals identify as mothers; the term maternal is used only to distinguish the birth parent enrolled during pregnancy from other parents or caregivers of the child participant. Domain of interest An overarching goal of the consortium was to develop a protocol for the HBCD Study that optimized achieving the seven scientific objectives from the NIH and minimized the impact of barriers to participation. Thus, a primary consideration of the WG-PRG was to balance assessing the most critical factors using reliable measures, many of which could only be measured at the desired level of granularity with self-reported data, and the burden of the protocol on participating dyads and site infrastructure. Within this framework, the WG-PRG sought to develop a comprehensive, person-centered protocol to collect important informa - tion about the prenatal period in as much detail as possible without negatively impacting data quality and retention. Although there are innumerable environmental influences during the prenatal period that may be associated with unfavorable physical, psychological, and behavioral health outcomes among offspring, the WG-PRG focused on four primary constructs that impact development substantially, which are further detailed in subsequent sections. Maternal physical health Previous pregnancy outcomes are associated with current pregnancy complications and outcomes Chen et al. , 2023; Makhlouf et al. , 2014 , including, but not limited to, previous fetal loss, preterm birth, cesarean delivery, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and gestational diabetes. Furthermore, previous pregnancy experiences have been shown to influence maternal anxiety during the current pregnancy Shapiro et al. Assisted reproductive technology ART has been associated with adverse maternal outcomes, though very little is known about its effect on developmental trajectories during childhood Bay et al. , 2019; Heshmatnia et al. Many other exposures also affect the health of pregnant in- dividuals and fetal development. Preventive exposures include the use of folic acid-containing pre- natal vitamins, which lower the risk of neural tube defects Greenberg et al. , 2011 , and low-dose aspirin for the prevention of preeclampsia Force, 2021. Furthermore, several vaccines are recommended during pregnancy, including influenza, pertussis, respiratory syncytial virus RSV , and COVID-19 if not up to date on the series to protect the birth parent and infant during pregnancy and the early postnatal period Centers for Disease Control and Prevention CDC , n. Other exposures are hypothesized to negatively affect maternal and fetal health.

content_chunk: For example, COVID-19 and other illnesses have been associated with premature birth, offspring who are small for their gestational age, and neurodevelopmental disorders among offspring, among other outcomes Elgueta et al. , 2022; McClymont et al. , 2022; San Martín-Gonz alez et al. Very high maternal fever during pregnancy can be particularly dangerous for the fetus Dior et al. , 2016; Hochler et al. In addition, several sexually transmitted and other infections during pregnancy are associated with adverse outcomes, including major malformations and mental health and neurobehavioral disorders among offspring Jash and Sharma, 2022. Certain chronic conditions are common among women during the reproductive years, and these disease processes can affect fetal devel - opment Ajslev et al. , 2012; Andersen et al. , 2013; Jølving et al. Preexisting or gestational maternal metabolic disorders, such as diabetes and obesity, are known to play a role in offspring health and neurodevelopment Edlow, 2021; Fresch et al. , 2024; Rodolaki et al. Furthermore, delivery and neonatal complications are more frequent among women with these metabolic disorders Fresch et al. Likewise, medications used to treat chronic diseases, including mental health conditions, and infections can affect fetal development. From known teratogens like valproic acid to purported behavioral te- ratogens like acetaminophen, the assessment of prescription and over-the-counter medication use is important for studying offspring health Ornoy, 2009; Ricci et al. Maternal mental health Pregnancy and postpartum are periods of heightened vulnerability for the onset and exacerbation of mental health conditions, a significant public health concern affecting approximately half a million individuals in the US each year Fawcett et al. , 2005; Guintivano et al. Approximately 20 of childbearing individuals report symptoms of a mental health condition, with onset occurring among a third of women during pregnancy and another 40 of women post- partum Fawcett et al. In addition, other maternal mental health conditions, including stress and post-traumatic stress disorder, and mental health disorders among first-degree rela- tives, increase the risk of adverse outcomes among pregnant individuals and their offspring Kingston et al. , 2018; Sanjuan et al. Pregnant individuals with mental health conditions are more likely to experience K. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience 71 2025 101494 adverse birth outcomes, and their infants are at increased risk of developmental delay and behavioral, emotional, and regulatory prob- lems Kingston et al. , 2018; Kingston and Tough, 2014; Monk et al. Furthermore, caretaker mental health during the child s early years of life is a well-documented risk factor for sub-optimal child development Netsi et al. Maternal substance use During pregnancy, the overall prevalence of addictive substance use, including alcohol, cannabis, opioids, and tobacco was at least 10 in the US in 2020 Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Adminis - tration, 2020. Though the prevalence of exposure to tobacco during pregnancy has declined, approximately 7 of pregnant women report using prescription opioids, and the prevalence of exposure to alcohol continues to be at least 10 Bonello et al. , 2023; England et al.

content_chunk: Adverse fetal and child developmental outcomes associated with prenatal exposure to alcohol, tobacco, and stimulants, like cocaine, are well documented, but less is known about the long-term developmental effects of prenatal exposure to opioids or cannabis, alone or in combination with other substances Banderali et al. , 2014; Wouldes and Woodward, 2013. For most of these sub- stances, little is known about their specific influence on brain develop - ment. Furthermore, though protective factors may modify these effects, the timing and mechanism through which adverse effects are mitigated is not well understood Bada et al. , 2012; Bandoli and Chambers, 2023. Pregnancy and birth complications and outcomes Pregnancy and obstetric outcomes influence both postpartum maternal health as well as offspring health throughout the life course. This includes factors, such as cesarean delivery, prematurity, and size for gestational age, are associated with both physical and neuro - developmental outcomes during childhood Bell et al. Protocol Measures to assess the four primary constructs of interest are administered primarily during the prenatal V1 and first post-partum V2 visits Fig. Time-varying parental and or caregiver measures of ongoing interest beyond the neonatal period are assessed during the third V3 and fourth V4 visits. Note that no assessments of adult health and behavior under the purview of the WG-PRG are administered during the fifth, remote visit V5. V1 is an in-person visit, which ideally occurs during the second trimester of pregnancy third trimester enrollment is permitted. Enrollment during the second trimester is preferred as pregnancy loss occurs most often during the first trimester. In addition, enrollment during the second trimester shortens the time elapsed since exposures occurring early in pregnancy, which may result in more accurate data. Second-trimester enrollment also optimizes the likelihood of completing the visit prior to birth. Finally, enrollment of participants during the third trimester could result in systematically over-representing child participants born at term. The second visit V2 of the HBCD protocol occurs within one month of the estimated due date EDD. Information about the domains of interest during the latter part of pregnancy be- tween V1 and delivery and the early postpartum period between de- livery and V2 as well as pregnancy complications and outcomes are collected during V2. Participants are randomly assigned to a one-month window during which V3 and V4 are to be conducted, from relative child participant ages calculated based on EDD, rather than date of birth of three to nine months and nine to fifteen months, respectively. To represent pregnant individuals who receive little to no prenatal care, up to 10 of participants can be recruited within five days of birth if they had four or fewer prenatal care visits. For participants recruited postnatally, the V1 and V2 protocols, including the collection of bio- specimens and assessment of social and environmental determinants, are combined into one, modified postnatal protocol to assess exposures during the entire pregnancy. The measures included in the HBCD Study protocol by the WG-PRG are represented by the Assessments icon in the graphical depiction of the protocol Fig. Each specific measure is listed with the visits during which it is administered Table 1 , and detailed in the following construct-specific subsections. Constructs of interest and measures The measures created, modified, or selected by the WG-PRG to characterize each of the prenatal constructs of interest included in the Fig. Protocol overview for the first five visits of the HEALthy Brain and Child Development HBCD Study. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience 71 2025 101494 HBCD Study protocol are detailed in subsequent, construct-specific sub- sections. Some measures required reports of exposure levels for specific periods during pregnancy. To define gestation, participants are asked for their estimated due date EDD during the screening procedure. The EDD is the anchor used to calculate relative age and define the time periods during which each postnatal study visit should occur, rather than date of birth, which does not account for premature birth. The EDD is also used to identify specific time points during the pregnancy, such as the beginning and end of trimesters. Because recruitment into HBCD study is delayed until the second trimester, most participants have received prenatal care before enrollment and have an ultrasound-dated estimate of the EDD. However, if participants do not know their EDD, they are asked to report their current gestational week of pregnancy. Using the EDD or gestational age GA , the first day of each participant s last menstrual period LMP is calculated. If the participant neither reports the EDD nor the GA, the participant is asked to report LMP. The LMP as well as the start and end dates for each trimester are then populated in questionnaires. EDD is updated in late pregnancy during calls from the research staff at approximately 32 weeks gestation, and all linked gestational milestones are shifted to reflect any updated information. Maternal physical health Measures to characterize certain aspects of the construct maternal physical health are grouped as shown in Table 1and described in the subsequent sub-sections. Obstetric history and current pregnancy. During the prenatal visit, an abbreviated obstetric history is collected to minimize the length of the visit. The WG-PRG chose not to collect detailed information about pregnancy terminations due to recent changes to reproductive health law. , number of pregnancies, is collected, but collection of parity is limited to the number of pregnancies that resulted in a live birth only, i. , no pregnancy outcomes for non-live-born de- liveries are collected. History of any cesarean delivery is collected as well as the date on which the prior pregnancy ended, if applicable, to afford the ability to calculate the latest inter-birth interval for multip - arous participants following delivery.

content_chunk: During V1, participants also report whether the pregnancy was planned, the gestational age at which pregnancy recognition occurred, and whether assisted reproductive technologies were used to conceive the current pregnancy. They also report the gestational age at which prenatal care was initiated, and whether and when prenatal or folic acid- containing vitamins or aspirin prophylactic for preeclampsia were initiated. These latter two exposures are updated at V2. In addition to these self-reported measures, information about the current pregnancy, such as the results of noninvasive prenatal testing, including glucose tolerance tests, and dates of ultrasound, is planned to be obtained from medical records. Pre-pregnancy height and weight. During V1, participants are asked for pre-pregnancy height and weight, from which pre-pregnancy body mass index BMI is calculated. Participants are asked during V1 to report any vac- cines Tdap, Flu, HPV, MMR, Meningitis, Hepatitis A-C, Varicella, Polio, Shingles, Typhoid, Yellow Fever, COVID-19, RSV received after LMP and during which trimester they were administered. This information is updated during V2 for the remainder of pregnancy. COVID-19, STIs, and other infections. Participants are asked if they have had a SARS-COV-2 infection at any time during gestation, the date of the positive test, and whether they had symptoms of COVID-19 during infection. If participants report using over the counter OTC or prescription medications to treat COVID-19, the medications are queried in RxNORM National Library of Medicine, n. during data collection, and participants report the date of initiation, date of cessation, and frequency of use during the reported period. They are then asked if they have had any other illnesses since LMP. Reported illnesses are queried by the research staff using the BioPortal ICD-10 ontology or symptom databases World Health Organization, n. , and participants report when the illness began and when it ended. If the participant reports a fever associated with the illness, the highest temperature and duration of the fever are recorded. The date of initiation, date of cessation, and frequency of use is also recorded for any medications taken for the illness. This information is updated at V2 for the remainder of pregnancy. To ease the burden of collecting information about infections occurring since LMP, a list of infections is provided to participants, including the following sexually transmitted infections STIs : gonor - rhea, chlamydia, herpes, human papillomavirus, and syphilis. Other infections included in the list are cytomegalovirus, group B strep, Hep- atitis A-C, HIV, toxoplasmosis, and urinary tract infection. Participants are asked to report the trimester s in which they had any of the in- fections. Infections not included in the list can be self-reported with other illnesses. In addition to these self-reported measures, test results for sexually transmitted and urinary tract infections; serology results for Hepatitis A- C, HPV, and HIV; and documentation of maternal fever are planned to be obtained from medical records.

content_chunk: During V2, participants are first asked to update the status of pre- scription medications for which current use was reported during V1. They are then asked to report prescription medications initiated after the prenatal visit V1 but before delivery. For reported medications, the same information collected during V1 is also collected during V2. The V2 process for prescription medications is repeated for OTC medications. Healthcare utilization. During V1, participants are asked about their health insurance coverage at the time they became pregnant and if they saw a physician or dentist in the year prior to pregnancy. Partici - pants are also asked if they were seen in an Emergency Department ED or admitted to the hospital since LMP. Those who report an ED or in- patient admission are asked for the primary diagnosis at the visit selected by research personnel from the ICD-10 ontology or symptom database World Health Organization, n. Participants report admis - sion and discharge dates and administration or prescription of medica - tions OTC and prescription for any admissions. Maternal mental health Due to its influence on not only maternal health but also health and developmental outcomes among offspring, both family and personal psychiatric history are assessed. Current maternal mental health is assessed also, focusing on conditions common during pregnancy and the postpartum period Mukherjee et al. , 2016; Van Niel and Payne, 2020. Family and personal psychiatric history. To assess family history of psychiatric disorders, items from the Family History Assessment Module are combined with items from the Personal and Family Health History used in All of Us and included in the V1 assessments All of Us Survey Explorer, n. Alcohol use disorder, autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, bipolar disorder, depression, generalized anxiety disorder, schizo - phrenia, and substance use disorder are all assessed with their respective items from the Personal and Family Health History. However, age at diagnosis and medication used to treat these conditions is not assessed for relatives of the birth parent. To reduce protocol burden on partici - pants from large families, the family history questions are only asked about conditions among the offspring s biological parents and biological grandparents. Prenatal and postpartum depression. The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale EPDS , a sensitive, 10-item screening tool for prenatal and postpartum depression was selected due to its ease of administration and widely accepted use Cox et al. , 1987; Park and Kim, 2023. The EPDS is administered during pregnancy V1 and twice during the year following delivery V2 and V3. Maternal post-traumatic stress and acute stress disorders. To assess the severity of maternal posttraumatic and acute stress symptoms, the nine-item National Stressful Events Survey PTSD Short Scale NSESSS-PTSD and seven-item National Stressful Events Survey Acute Stress Disorder Short Scale NSESSS-Acute Stress Disorder are com- bined into a single assessment for the HBCD Study Kilpatrick et al. , 2011, 2013; LeBeau et al. Six of the items in the NSESSS-Acute Stress Disorder are also included in the NSESSS-PTSD.

content_chunk: These six items are administered only once in combination with the other four unique items for the two scales. The responses to the six overlapping items are used to score each scale individually. This assessment is completed at each of the in-person visits V1 4. Other maternal mental health disorders. To screen more broadly, the DSM-5 Self-Rated Level 1 and Level 2 version 8a Cross-Cutting Symptom Measure Adult was selected Doss and Lowmaster, 2022; Roche et al. This highly sensitive screening tool has two levels when used in community samples. Level 1 includes one to three ques- tions for each of thirteen mental health conditions. When a minimum threshold of level-1 symptoms is reported for anger, mania, anxiety, somatic symptoms, sleep disturbances, and repetitive thoughts, the participant answers several subsequent questions, which ask about additional symptoms associated with each mental health condition. Slight modifications were made due to the use of other measures and the study population. Specifically, the substance use questions were omitted due to the inclusion of other similar measures in the protocol. Level-1 questions for personality functioning are omitted also; instead, all par- ticipants complete the level-2 measures. In addition, the level-2 assess - ment for depression is administered to all participants, regardless of their responses to level 1. Finally, depression and sleep problems are assessed with the Promis 8a; the remaining level-2 domains are assessed using the standard symptom measures included in the Level 2 Cross-Cutting Symptom Measures. This assessment is completed at each of the first four visits V1 4. Maternal substance use A primary aim of HBCD is to investigate the effect of prenatal sub- stance exposure on child development. Within this context, optimal prediction of exposure-related neurodevelopmental risk requires multi- level assessment to capture both between- and within-individual vari- ability in substance use across the prenatal period Bandoli et al. Though biospecimens are also collected to char- acterize prenatal substance exposure, the primary goal of the WG-PRG is to collect detailed information about the use of substances that can only be collected directly from participants. The Timeline Followback TLFB method is the gold standard for collecting self-reported, detailed use information Hjorthøj et al. Due to the stigma associated with substance use, particularly during pregnancy, identifying a non-judgmental approach to collecting these data that mitigated po- tential harm to participants, particularly given the criminalization of prenatal substance use in some states, was prioritized. The burden of reporting detailed information both prior to and during 40 weeks of gestation was also considered. As a result, a two-step process was adopted, using questionnaires during the first step that include a version of the NIDA-modified Alcohol, Smoking, and Substance Involvement Screening Test ASSIST V2. 0 and conducting interviews with partici - pants during the second step, using the TLFB method or self-report entered directly into a web application National Institute on Drug Abuse, n. , 2005; Sobell and Sobell, 2000.
