content_chunk: During V1, partici - pants are screened for lifetime, pre-pregnancy, and prenatal substance K. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience 71 2025 101494 use and disordered use using a previously validated tool, the NIDA- modified ASSIST National Institute on Drug Abuse, n. , expanded for the HBCD Study from nine to eighteen substances nicotine or to- bacco products, alcohol, cannabis, cannabidiol, synthetic cannabinoids, prescription opioids, heroin or other illicit opioids, methadone, bupre - norphine, benzodiazepines, cocaine, amphetamine-type stimulants, methamphetamine, inhalants, hallucinogens or club drugs, androgenic anabolic steroids, phencyclidine, and kratom. First, participants are asked if they have ever used each of the eighteen substances. For each reported substance, a series of questions are asked about disordered use or use causing problems in their lives. For each substance for which any lifetime use is reported, partici - pants are then asked whether they used the substance in the three months prior to pregnancy, and separately, whether they used the substance during pregnancy. Information about how the participant typically uses each substance is then collected. For tobacco, participants are asked to report the type of product used, such as cigarettes or e- cigarettes. Likewise, participants who use cannabis are asked what types of products they use, such as smoking marijuana flower, vaping, or consuming edibles. If alcohol is reported during this period, the partic - ipant is asked what type of alcohol they consume beer, hard cider, hard seltzer, wine, and spirits. For each type, participants report the average volume of a typical serving or container. US-defined standard drinks are then calculated from the average serving size by dividing the amount reported by 12 ounces for beer, hard cider, and hard seltzer; 5 ounces for wine, and 1. Finally, if participants report opioids, they are asked the type of opioid they use and typical quantities per occasion of use as follows: heroin grams, bags , prescription opioids pills , buprenorphine pills, injectables, films , and methadone mg. At each visit occurring within fifteen months of the EDD V2 V4 , adult participants use a similar version of the ASSIST to report postnatal use of the same 18 substances of interest during the three months prior to each of these three visits. For each reported substance, participants are asked frequency of use, for which the response categories range from once or twice to daily or almost daily. Daily substance use during select weeks immediately prior to and during pregnancy. Participants who report any substance use in the three months before or during pregnancy are interviewed about their use of those substances using the TLFB method. To facilitate efficiency and privacy of data collection, a web application was developed in the R Shiny framework Shiny, n. Research personnel access the applica - tion from an iPad during the interview. Like the original paper-based approach, the application displays a calendar to aid in collecting daily use of substances. The web-based application, however, displays only the windows of interest that are pre-populated based on the EDD collected during screening.

content_chunk: Select weeks of gestation were chosen to capture the often-dynamic use of substances during pregnancy and reduce the burden of reporting use over the entire gestation Bandoli et al. Four periods are represented: pre-pregnancy use; very early prenatal use, likely prior to pregnancy recognition; recent prenatal use at the time of enrollment ; and late pregnancy use just prior to parturition. Specifically, the application displays nine weeks in total: two weeks prior to pregnancy four weeks before LMP through two weeks before LMP , four weeks early in preg- nancy two weeks after LMP through six weeks after LMP , current use at the time of enrollment the week prior to V1 , and two weeks late in pregnancy the last two weeks of gestation, reported during V2. Holi- days occurring during these nine weeks are also pre-populated. During V1, participants are asked about use of each substance re- ported in the ASSIST, disaggregated into product type e. , edible cannabis products , during each of the first seven weeks described above. The number of occasions of use are entered for each day for all products except cigarettes and cigarillos, for which number used are entered per day, and alcohol, for which the number of single servings consumed is entered per day. During V2, the interview using the TLFB method is administered again to collect daily substance use during the last two full weeks of gestation. While the research staff enter use data into the TLFB appli - cation during an interview for most participants, participants enter their own use data into the web application, following a brief training, at sites located in states in which prenatal substance use is reportable by the research staff. Typical substance use by trimester of pregnancy. To minimize participant burden, collection of detailed daily substance use data is limited to select weeks prior to and during gestation, when use is likely to vary. Nevertheless, this approach could result in misclassification of dyads as substance unexposed if infrequent or sporadic use occurs outside the windows of assessment. Thus, participants who report any use of opioids, cannabis, alcohol, nicotine, or stimulants in the three months prior to or during pregnancy are asked additional questions during V2 to assess typical substance-specific use by trimester. For each specific substance e. methadone, buprenorphine, etc. reported, par- ticipants are asked to estimate the number of weeks the substance was used during each trimester and the average number of days of use during the weeks of use for each trimester. Indoor smoke exposure. To differentiate between personal use and passive exposure to indoor smoke among individuals with a positive urine drug screen, participants are asked during V2 if they were exposed during pregnancy to second-hand smoke resulting from cigarettes, marijuana, and methamphetamine. Pregnancy and birth complications and outcomes During V2, participants report any pregnancy complications, including, but not limited to, gestational diabetes; hypertensive disor - ders of pregnancy, including preeclampsia; antiphospholipid syndrome; cervical insufficiency; and placenta previa.

content_chunk: Also, information about the birth is obtained, including whether labor was spontaneous or induced and delivery was vaginal or cesarean the latter with indication. Furthermore, participants report whether they had any of the following delivery complications: forceps-assisted delivery, vacuum-assisted de- livery, chorioamnionitis, presence of meconium, postpartum hemor - rhage requiring transfusion, and breech presentation. Finally, they report the length of stay of the birth hospitalization. In addition to these self-reported measures, an expanded list of pregnancy and birth complications as well as additional information about labor and delivery such as antenatal administration of antibiotics and steroids are planned to be obtained from medical records. Administration Most of these data are collected and managed using REDCap elec- tronic data capture tools Harris et al. The electronic question - naires are administered during in-person visits on a study iPad. These instruments are designed for participants to complete independently due to the sensitive nature of many of the questions and to minimize the length of the visit. While all questions have to be completed, all ques- tions in the WG-PRG measures include the response options Don t know and Decline to answer. For certain assessments, participants are asked to hand the iPad back to research personnel, who administer more complex measures such as the questions about medication use that rely on on- tologies. Research personnel can administer all the questionnaires for participants that need assistance or prefer not to complete any of the measures themselves. For V2, links to questionnaires that capture most of the information collected are sent to the adult participant one week prior to the in-person portion of V2. Questionnaires that are incomplete at the beginning of the in-person portion of V2 are then administered during the visit in addition to other surveys that can be administered K. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience 71 2025 101494 only during an in-person visit Table 1. In addition to the questionnaires, research personnel also conduct in- person interviews about substance use at V1 and V2 using the timeline follow back TLFB method, detailed in Section 3. Due to the interpretation of Alabama s chemical endangerment laws by some prosecutors, the consortium opted to blind the research team in Alabama to measures of substance use. Therefore, those portions of the protocol that typically involve research personnel are all self-administered at those sites. Instructions for completing the assessments were developed that include brief video instructions for the TLFB. To minimize participant burden with respect to visit length and varying degrees of health literacy among participants, the HBCD study consents participants to acquire health records, such as the medical re- cord from the birth hospitalization, to complement self-reported maternal and child health data. When possible, information is extrac - ted from electronic health records automatically; otherwise, specific information is planned to be manually abstracted from medical records by trained research personnel. Enrollment goals related to substance use Use of specific substances of interest during pregnancy is relatively rare.

content_chunk: Thus, to ensure adequare power to examine the effect of prenatal substance exposure on child development, pregnant individuals who use substances are oversampled to reach the consortium enrollment goal of 25 of the study population. To operationalize this objective and ensure an adequate range of exposure to detect effects, the WG-PRG developed criteria for minimum thresholds of opioid, alcohol, cannabis, and nicotine tobacco use by which to classify dyads as substance-exposed to track enrollment goals Table 2. These criteria were determined by expert opinion of WG members for each substance and approved by the HBCD Steering Committee. Alcohol thresholds are based on National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism criteria for what exceeds low-risk drinking Willenbring et al. , 2009; National In- stitutes of Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, n. Whether each dyad meets the minimum criteria to be classified as substance exposed for tracking enrollment is based on participant- reported use during pregnancy through the TLFB, results of toxicology carried out on biospecimens collected during or shortly after pregnancy Sullivan et al. , 2024 , and self-reported or documented in the medical record diagnoses of child participants during the neonatal period with substance-related syndromes Neonatal Opioid Withdrawal Syndrome and Fetal Alcohol Syndrome. These criteria are used solely to ensure sampling of the study population is enhanced for opioid and other substance use of interest during pregnancy. Sites were required to enroll at least three participants in the age range for each of these visits, totaling a minimum of nine pilot dyads per site. As a result of the information obtained during this pilot phase, the response options Don t know and Decline to answer were added to all questions. Conclusions Exposure to adverse conditions in utero is linked to atypical varia - tions in brain development that are associated with a variety of physical, psychological, and behavioral health sequelae that extend beyond the childhood years. Adverse environments are ubiquitous, including pre- natal and postnatal exposure to substances, socioeconomic deprivation, structural racism and other forms of exclusion, stress, maltreatment, food insecurity, and poor access to adequate health care. The complex interplay among genes and the environments children experience, particularly during early life, have historically presented methodologic challenges to mechanistic clarity in developmental research. Combined with the contributions of other workgroups to the protocol, assessment of prenatal exposures in the HBCD study will result in an unparalleled resource for the scientific community, resulting in an unprecedented opportunity to advance understanding of brain and child development. Maternal-fetal attachment and maternal prenatal depression have been identified as factors influencing maternal lifestyle during pregnancy. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 224 pregnant women in their third trimester, attending an antenatal appointment at a community health center in Surakarta, Indonesia, from July to September 2019. Introduction Lifestyle during pregnancy appears as a key factor associated with health and disease in pregnant women. To achieve a high level of health during pregnancy, psychosocial and demographic aspects should be considered as key factors. 1Several studies have found that a healthier behavior during pregnancy was related to several factors such as age, income, religion, parity, and education. 2 4Alternative variables that were negatively correlated with a healthy nutrition were trait anxiety, marital dissatisfaction β 0. 001 , social support β 0. 1 see Table 1 Table 1 Depressive and anxiety disorders are the most frequent prenatal psychiatric illnesses, affecting 15 29 of women; low- and middle- income countries LMICs have more prenatal mental problems, poor health practice, and lack of research identifying maternal-fetal attach - ment than high-income countries. 5Prenatal depression can harm new- borns and families, particularly other children during their early years, can impair parental-infant bonding6,7and is associated with low health outcomes during pregnancy. 8 A number of studies have investigated the link between prenatal depression and maternal-fetal attachment. A comprehensive review spanning 45 papers across America, Europe, Asia, and Australia found a negative association between prenatal attachment and symptoms of prenatal depression. 9Additional studies have explored how postnatal depressive symptoms can be related with low levels of prenatal attachment. Maternal attachment plays a vital role in both maternal and infant well-being, involving a pattern of interaction and communication be- tween a mother and her unborn child. Establishing and nurturing this connection before and after childbirth is crucial for cognitive and physical development of both the mother and the infant.

Discussion This study examined the association between maternal-fetal attach - ment, maternal prenatal depression, and a healthy lifestyle among pregnant women. The findings revealed that education, religion, employment, income, parity, maternal depression, and maternal-fetal attachment MFA were linked to adopting a health-promoting life- style. In Surakarta, pregnant women showed varied health-promoting lifestyle scores. Surakarta, an urban area in Java, has numerous health facilities accessible to pregnant women, ensuring they meet the government-recommended minimum of four prenatal visits. Despite this, studies indicate that Indonesian pregnant women often have nutrient intakes below the recommended levels, highlighting the need for promoting healthier behaviors through well-trained healthcare providers. Some characteristics of the study group differed from the overall population of Indonesia. For instance, most participants were house - wives, while many Indonesian women work outside the home. Addi- tionally, the women in this study had at least a high school education. Education is crucial for developing a health-promoting lifestyle. This study aligns with previous research in the Netherlands, showing that higher education levels correlate with better health literacy, which re- duces risky behaviors and promotes healthier choices. 22Therefore, encouraging higher education for women remains essential. Bivariate analysis in this study also showed that religious affiliation significantly influenced health-promoting behavior. Muslim women had lower health-promoting lifestyle scores compared to women of other religions. Given that most Indonesians are Muslim, it is important for health professionals, educators, religious leaders, and the government to promote a healthy lifestyle within the Muslim community, emphasizing that caring for one s health is a duty in Islam. 23 In terms of employment, results showed that employed women had higher health behavior scores compared to housewives. Previous study said that staying at home has been linked to worse physical and mental health due to fewer financial and social resources. 24Income and employment status affect health-seeking behavior, particularly for pregnant adolescents.

content_chunk: 25Thus, more effort is needed to educate and encourage housewives and low-income women to empower themselves to have such a healthy lifestyle, especially during pregnancy. Moreover, government income subsidies for low-income women could improve overall health status. 26Regarding parity, primiparas exhibited healthier practices than multiparas, possibly due to stronger family support. Both groups need support, but multiparas face additional responsibilities and less societal support. Therefore, education and support from family and healthcare providers are crucial for multiparas. This study found that most women were not depressed, although their mean score was higher compared to some countries. However, depression screening in Indonesia, primarily in Community Health Centers, where most pregnant women receive prenatal check-ups, is not widespread. Routine screening for psychological problems in early pregnancy is necessary to address this gap. Regarding maternal-fetal attachment MFA , the study revealed a relatively high mean score among women. Previous systematic review shows that prenatal depressive symptoms were found to be negatively associated with prenatal attachment. 9Furthermore, lower levels of prenatal attachment were related to higher postnatal depressive symp - toms. Maternal-fetal attachment has been linked to a lower risk of postpartum depression. 27However, compared to women in other Asian countries,28the MFA score among women in Surakarta, Indonesia, was lower. Improving MFA scores could decrease depression rates, promote healthy lifestyles, and enhance the well-being of both mothers and infants. Hierarchical multiple linear regression analysis revealed that maternal-fetal attachment and maternal depression significantly pre- dicted the health-promoting lifestyle of pregnant women. Depression negatively impacted health behavior, while attachment positively influenced it. This aligns with previous findings suggesting that emotional disturbances like depression hinder self-care and health behavior adoption. 1Consequently, pregnant women experiencing depression may face challenges in adopting healthier behaviors. Moreover, maternal-fetal attachment was found to positively influ- ence health practices in previous research. 29The bond with the fetus may drive mothers to prioritize health responsibility, leading them to seek information from healthcare providers and attend pregnancy classes. This study observed a correlation between health responsibility and maternal fetal-attachment, suggesting that pregnant women may demonstrate attachment by actively seeking health information and assuming responsibility for their own and their baby s well-being. Understanding pregnant women s beliefs about healthy lifestyles during pregnancy, their prioritization of fetal health, and their maternal- fetal attachment is crucial. Strong maternal attachment prompts women to adopt healthier behaviors to safeguard their baby s well-being. These findings call for several recommendations. Firstly, depression un- dermines health behavior, underscoring the importance of addressing depression among pregnant women. Yet, stigma surrounding mental health treatment in Indonesia poses a challenge. 30Thus, raising awareness about mental health during pregnancy can destigmatize seeking help, enabling depressed individuals to access support and improve their lifestyle. Secondly, enhancing maternal-fetal attachment is vital. Midwives can play a key role by providing high-quality ante- natal care, offering prenatal classes that foster attachment, emotional support, and activities like gentle yoga. 31Integrating healthy lifestyle programs with educational initiatives can further engage mothers support groups.

content_chunk: 32Thirdly, midwives must pay special attention to vulnerable groups, such as pregnant women with low education and income or multiple children. Enhancing midwives skills to educate and support pregnant women and their families is imperative for promoting healthier behaviors across all socioeconomic backgrounds. This study provides evidence that maternal depression and maternal- fetal attachment directly affect health behaviours of pregnant women. It provides a point of comparison for researchers working with different populations to verify this effect. Moreover, this data can be used to develop strategies to improve maternal mental health of pregnant women to prevent severe mental health problems, for example, by using the EPDS to screen for maternal depression during antenatal checks-up. Study limitations This study has limitations, as participants were primarily Javanese, making the findings less generalizable to Indonesia s multicultural population. Different ethnicities may have varying cultural traditions affecting pregnancy health behaviors. However, this study provides new insights, supporting previous research and encouraging further studies on depression, maternal-fetal attachment, and health-promoting life- style behavior. Clinical and research implications Understanding the factors influencing health-promoting behaviors among pregnant women provides valuable insights for clinical practice and public health initiatives. The findings of this study highlight the significant roles of maternal-fetal attachment and maternal depression in shaping a healthy maternal lifestyle. Clinically, routine screening for maternal depression should be in- tegrated into antenatal care using tools such as the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale EPDS. Early detection and management of depressive symptoms not only improve maternal well-being but also facilitate the R. Clinical Epidemiology and Global Health 31 2025 101904 adoption of healthier behaviors during pregnancy. Midwives and healthcare providers should be equipped with skills to assess and address psychological challenges, fostering better outcomes for mothers and their babies. The promotion of maternal-fetal attachment through prenatal classes and structured interventions, such as mindfulness exercises, yoga, or guided bonding activities, can enhance maternal health responsibility. Such initiatives can be included in antenatal care programs to strengthen emotional connections between mothers and their unborn children. Conclusion The findings highlight the role of maternal depression and maternal- fetal attachment in promoting a healthy behavior among pregnant women. Certain groups, especially low-income women, unemployed, less educated, and those with previous children are at a high risk of unhealthy lifestyles. Interventions should address these demographic challenges, ensuring antenatal care materials are accessible and affordable to everybody. Healthcare providers and families must recognize the impact of depression during pregnancy and support healthier behaviors. Despite the potential impact of UPF intake during pregnancy on maternal and childhealth, studies in this area are limited. Therefore, this narrative comprehensive review aimed to identify associations between UPF consumption, categorized by the NOVA system, during pregnancy and maternal and child health outcomes over the past ﬁve years 2019 e2024. Methods: Following PRISMA-ScR criteria 2018 , MedLine PubMed, Scopus, and Embase databases were searched for articles on maternal and child health outcomes associated with UPF consumption catego- rized by the NOVA system during pregnancy, out of 767 studies identi ﬁed, 22 were eligible. Results: Overall, high UPF consumption during pregnancy was positively associated with various adverse maternal-child outcomes, including gestational diabetes mellitus, gestational weight gain, poor glycemic control, negative nutrition biomarkers, in ﬂammatory markers, and hypertensive disorders during pregnancy. It also negatively impacted child growth and development, and was associated with adipositygain, potential adverse mental disorders, indicators of poor nutrition, and poor overall diet quality. Conclusions: Despite the limited data, high consumption of UPF during pregnancy adversely affected the health outcomes of both mothers and children, impacting nutrition indicators and diet quality. Furtherstudies on this topic are needed. Introduction Food processing has become essential in modern diets due to the rapid global population growth, ensuring food preservation, safety, and improved nutritional quality over time 1. The evolu- tion of food processing and agro-industrial systems 2 led to the development of a comprehensive classi ﬁcation system known asthe NOVA system. Over the past ﬁfteen years, the NOVA classi ﬁ- cation system was created to categorize foods based on the extent and purpose of food processing, thus classifying food products into four groups based on the number of processed ingredients: I unprocessed or minimally processed foods, II processed culinary ingredients, III processed foods, and IV ultra-processed foods UPF 3.

These ultra-processed products contain just a small proportion of unprocessed foods, if any, re ﬂecting a high level of food processing 4. As a result, they are typically rich in sugars, oils, fats, sodium, calories, and food additives, while having low amounts of ﬁber. This combination Corresponding author. Although food processing's purpose is to ensure food safety, palatability, and shelf-life, high demand for low-cost, easy-to-cook, or ready-to-eat food items, has led to other natural or arti ﬁcial ingredients and industrial techniques being used to achieve the purpose 4,5. Recent studies have linked UPF with low-quality diets, high- energy diets, nutritional de ﬁciencies, chronic diseases i. : obesity, cancer, diabetes mellitus, overall cardiovascular diseases, etc. , depression, and premature death 6e13. Over the last three decades, there has been a noticeable shift in dietary patterns globally. UPF purchases have surged while the consumption of unprocessed or minimally processed foods has declined 14,15 , underscoring a global convergence towards a more highly processed diet 16,17 , especially in developing countries where they were not initially marketed, which has led to over- exposure to risk factors derived from these products worldwide 18. These shifts in dietary patterns are particularly concerning during pregnancy, due to women's physiological changes that de- mand greater consumption of macronutrients and micronutrientsfor proper fetal growth and development 19e22. Maternal nutrition during this period signi ﬁcantly in ﬂuences both the mother and child's short- and long-term health outcomes 23,24. Studies have noted a signi ﬁcant proportion of energy intake from UPF among pregnant women, raising concerns about its po- tential negative impact on maternal and child health 25,26. Therefore, adequate nutritional quality during pregnancy is crucial to prevent perinatal outcomes, such as maternal anemia, pre- eclampsia, and fetal development complications 27e31. Understanding and addressing UPF consumption during preg- nancy are vital steps in improving maternal and neonatal health outcomes. Focusing on nutritional quality can mitigate potential risks associated with UPF and contribute to healthier pregnancy outcomes overall 3,16,29. Current literature lacks studies on the application of the NOVA system in classifying food concerning gestational nutrition and its repercussions on maternal and child health 32e53. This research gap underscores the necessity for comprehensive studies addressing these crucial gaps.

content_chunk: Our study aims to investigate maternal and child health outcomes associated with UPF con- sumption categorized by the NOVA system during pregnancy dur- ing the previous ﬁve years. Our goal is to comprehensively examine and provide insights for developing guidelines for pregnant women and embrace further research into UPF consumption during preg-nancy and its impact on maternal and child health. Materials methods This comprehensive narrative review adheres to the guidelines outlined in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews PRISMA-ScR 54. The search was conducted up to March 2024 across MedLine PUBMED, SCOPUS, and EMBASE databases. The search strategyinvolved key terms such as ultra-processed foods , NOVA , diet during pregnancy , maternal health , fetal development , pregnancy outcomes , and birth outcomes , combined using Boolean operators AND and OR, resulting in the search string: ultra-processed foods Mesh AND NOVA Mesh AND diet during pregnancy Mesh AND maternal health Mesh AND pregnancy outcomes Mesh AND birth outcomes Mesh. The PICO framework used in this study was de ﬁned as follows: Participants P : Mother-child pairs exposed to UPF during preg- nancy; Intervention I : Consumption of UPF during pregnancy, deﬁned by the NOVA classi ﬁcation system; Comparison C : Notapplicable as there is no speci ﬁc comparison group; Outcome O : Maternal Health Outcomes: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus, Meta- bolic Disorders, Metabolic Health Markers In ﬂammatory Markers, Micronutrient Status, and Child Health Outcomes: Fetal Develop- ment, Birth Outcomes, Neurodevelopmental Outcomes, and Po- tential Congenital Anomalies. Studies were considered eligible if: I Pregnant and or postpartum women and or Children aged 0 e10 years; II They reported health outcomes associated with UPF consumption in the speci ﬁed population using the NOVA classi ﬁ- cation system; III Study designs included Observational, Cohort, Cross-sectional, Longitudinal, Narrative Reviews, Systematic Re- views, and Meta-analyses; IV Publications were in Spanish and English, and V The publication period ranged from 2019 to 2024. Initially, after the removal of duplicates, 554 records were identi ﬁed from the three different databases. After applying the eligibility criteria, 170 records were sought for retrieval out of which, 13 were not able to be retrieved. Additionally, 6 records were identi ﬁed from citations, sought for retrieval and assessed for eligibility. All eligible retrieved articles, 157 identi ﬁed from databases and 6 identi ﬁed from citations, underwent independent evaluation by two researchers. Based on their titles and abstracts, 102 reports identi ﬁed from databases were excluded. The Cohen's Kappa Co- efﬁcient for the agreement of the researchers in this step was 0. Fifty- ﬁve full-text reports identi ﬁed from databases and 6 identi- ﬁed from citations were subsequently assessed. Based on the full- text, 38 reports identi ﬁed from databases and 1 identi ﬁed from citations were excluded. The Cohen's Kappa Coef ﬁcient for the agreement of the researchers in this step eligibility based on title and abstract was 0.

content_chunk: Two studies 44,50 indicated that UPF consumption negatively affects the nutritional quality of diets, which in turn may impact neonatal health outcomes. Similarly, another two 52,53 reported that the quality of maternal diet, in ﬂuenced by UPF consumption, can adversely affect neonatal health and cognitive development. For Dietary Habits, an increased frequency of maternal UPF consumption in the antenatal period was negatively associated with adverse fetal outcomes 45. While another study highlighted a concerning rise in UPF intake among pregnant women, however older and more educated women and those with healthy behaviors showed lower UPF intake in pregnancy 48. In summary, 9 9 studies concluded that higher UPF consump- tion during pregnancy was linked to reduced intake of essential nutrients, resulting in a less favorable nutrient pro ﬁle that could affect both maternal and offspring health 35,36,39,42e44, 46,50,51. Likewise, 10 10 studies concluded that diet quality was reduced due to increased UPF intake, which may impact maternal and neonatal health and development 36,38e40,42,44, 46,50,52,53. Lastly, 2 2 studies highlighted a concerning rise in UPF intake among women 32,48. Discussion The escalating consumption of UPF 14e17 has raised concerns due to its strong association with low diet quality, leading to an elevated risk of chronic diseases and all-cause mortality amongadult populations 6e13. Recent research, including four pivotal studies integrated into this analysis, underscores these concerns and highlights speci ﬁc health impacts. Zupo's narrative review 53 underscores how a diet rich in UPF can adversely affect a child's cognitive development, emphasizing the importance of early nutrition. Oliveira's systematic review 51 provides comprehen- sive insights into the negative health consequences of UPF con- sumption during critical life stages such as pregnancy, lactation, and infancy. Additionally, two meta-analyses by Paula et al. 52 shed light on the positive association between maternal UPF-rich diet consumption during pregnancy and the increased risk of developing gestational diabetes mellitus and preeclampsia. 50 , further contribute to this understanding by demon- strating the detrimental effects of increased UPF consumption on the nutritional quality of diets. Incorporating these recent and robust studies alongside other selected research is crucial in establishing a foundational understanding based on scienti ﬁc and valid evidence, guiding future directions in maternal and child health research. Maternal health outcomes Our analysis reveals compelling evidence linking higher UPF consumption to adverse maternal health outcomes such as GDM, GWG issues, adverse glycemic control, alterations in in ﬂammatory markers, and increased oxidative stress levels. The complications associated with GDM extend across maternal, fetal, neonatal, and even childhood and adulthood health domains. Understanding and effectively managing GDM during pregnancy is paramount to mitigate risks 55. Although some studies did not ﬁnd a clear association between UPF consumption and GDM risk, a sig- niﬁcant 48 increase in GDM odds was reported in the meta-analysis 52 for higher UPF intake during pregnancy. On top of that, a cohort study suggested that pre-gestational UPF consumption, particularly in women aged 30 years or older, could pose a risk for GDM 32,51.

content_chunk: However, another cohort 41 did not ﬁnd a signi ﬁcant link, likely due to limitations in sample size and the dif ﬁculty in accurately catego- rizing UPFs using current assessment tools. Mixed ﬁndings regarding a direct association were shown, especially in older women. The limitations in sample size and tools for assessment could explain the varying results across the different studies. Nevertheless, managingUPF intake during pregnancy, especially for older women, remains crucial in reducing the risks associated with GDM. Glycemic control during pregnancy is crucial for managing GDM and reducing associated complications. The selected studies have shown that increased UPF intake during pregnancy, especially in the third trimester 51 , is associated with adverse glycemic control outcomes. Silva's study 33 found that for every 1 kcal increase from UPF in the third trimester, there was a 0. 007 increase in HbA1c and a 0. 14 mg dL rise in 1-h postprandial glucose. This in- dicates a signi ﬁcant impact on glycemic control. Therefore, the association between UPF consumption and GDM risk underscores the importance of dietary choices in managing maternal glycemic health during pregnancy. Studies on GWG and UPF consumption during pregnancy have produced varied and interesting ﬁndings. A cohort study 33 i n d i - cated that for every 1 kcal increase in UPF calorie intake during the third trimester, there was an associated 0. 11 kg increase in total GWG, alongside a notable percentage of participants experiencing inade- quate weight gain. Cummings 37 reported 31 higher odds of excessive GWG linked to increased UPF intake. 42,51 found associations between higher UPF energy consumption and inadequate GWG, with Oliveira et al. also noting high weight gain in the third trimester among UPF consumers. However, Yisahak et al. 41,52 d i dn o t ﬁnd signiﬁcant associations between UPF-rich diets during pregnancyand GWG. These con ﬂicting results suggest a need for further investiga- tion into the speci ﬁc mechanisms linking UPF consumption and GWG during pregnancy, especially considering that excessive GWG is associated with adverse outcomes such as cesarean delivery, large- for-gestational-age newborns, and postpartum weight retention, which can contribute to obesity in later life. Monitoring this trend is crucial for maternal and child health outcomes 52. In a previous large observational prospective study, higher consumption of UPF was associated with increased risks of car- diovascular events 6. However, ﬁndings regarding UPF intake and HDP are mixed. While one study 41 did not ﬁnd clinical signi ﬁ- cance in UPF intake and HDP, another study 50 highlighted a clear association between elevated UPF consumption and HDP. Similarly, although three cohort studies did not ﬁnd signi ﬁcant links between UPF-rich diets and hypertension during pregnancy, four cohort studies reported a 28 higher risk of preeclampsia associated with UPF intake 52. These contradictory ﬁndings emphasize theM. Rocha-Velasco Clinical Nutrition ESPEN 65 2025 288 e304 necessity for further research to understand the speci ﬁc mecha- nisms and impacts of UPF intake on hypertensive disorders in pregnancy.

content_chunk: The demonstrated increased risk of preeclampsia un- derlines the importance of implementing dietary interventions to mitigate potential adverse health outcomes. Increased oxidative stress is a signi ﬁcant factor in reproductive complications like infertility, miscarriage, pre-eclampsia, fetal growth restriction, and preterm labor 56. Studies have shown that UPF intake during pregnancy may exacerbate oxidative stress, indicated by lower total antioxidant capacity levels and higher malondialdehyde levels 35. Moreover, increased UPF consump- tion was associated with elevated tHcy levels, indicating potential metabolic disturbances 49. Keeping CRP levels within a normal range during pregnancy is crucial as elevated CRP levels can indicate in ﬂammation or infection and can adversely affect maternal and fetal health 57. UPF intake during pregnancy has been associated with elevated CRP levels, indicating increased in ﬂammation 37,38 , with another study noting a weak positive association between UPF consumption and CRP levels 38. These ﬁndings underscore the importance of dietary choices during pregnancy, as higher consumption of ultra-processedfoods may contribute to systemic in ﬂammation, potentially increasing the risk of adverse maternal and fetal outcomes. Moni- toring CRP levels alongside dietary habits can be valuable in assessing and managing in ﬂammation-related risks during preg- nancy, promoting better maternal and fetal health outcomes. The impact of UPF intake on nutrition biomarkers is notable, with increases observed in certain nutrients like vitamin E, creati- nine, potassium, and sodium, alongside decreases in carotenoids, vitamin A, molybdenum, and selenium 38. These changes emphasize the importance of monitoring nutrition biomarkers during pregnancy, as higher UPF consumption can lead to imbal- ances in essential nutrients critical for maternal and fetal health. For instance, reduced serum alpha-tocopherol vitamin E levels asso- ciated with UPF diets may heighten the risk of inadequate vitamin E content in breast milk, potentially affecting infant health 51. Therefore, monitoring UPF intake's impact on nutrition biomarkers during pregnancy is crucial because of the disruption of essential nutrient balances, affecting maternal, fetal, and infant health. Child health outcomes There were several health outcomes in children related to maternal UPF consumption. These changes in maternal dietary patterns pose risks to maternal health and have implications for fetal development and child health outcomes, Initial studies 42,52 found no signi ﬁcant association between maternal UPF intake and infant low birth weight. However, A cross- sectional study 47 suggested that higher UPF consumption increased the risk of insuf ﬁcient birth weight. Subsequent adjust- ments revealed complexities, likely in ﬂuenced by various factors such as sociodemographic and gestational variables. This un- derscores the multifactorial nature of infant anthropometry and highlights the challenge of establishing a direct association withUPF intake. Focusing on neurodevelopment, one study 34 highlighted a potential adverse association between maternal UPF intake during pregnancy and verbal functioning in early childhood, where higher UPF consumption during the third trimester correlated with lower verbal function in children aged 4 to 5.

content_chunk: Additionally, it was observedthat infants exposed to higher UPF diets displayed lower scores in both cognitive and psychomotor development, concluding that high UPF consumption during pregnancy may adversely affect a child's neurodevelopment and cognitive function, crucial across various stages of infant development 53. Embryonic growth studies reveal potential concerns with maternal UPF intake during pregnancy. Associations between PEI- UPF and reduced embryonic growth trajectories, including smaller CRL and EV were highlighted 40 , which are measures of embryonic brain development, reinforcing the association with neurodevelopment reported 34. Lourenco's study 45 un- derscores adverse effects on late pregnancy, such as decreased head circumference HC and femur length FL percentiles. In terms of sexual development 42 , higher UPF consumption was linked to shorter male infant AGD, indicating broader impacts on fetal development beyond physical growth. Evidence indicates that adiposity and excess weight are asso- ciated with an increased risk of related comorbidities in adulthood, leading to decreased life expectancy, loss of productivity, and increased costs to the health system 17. 51 , re- ported a positive association between adiposity measurements and high UPF consumption, attributing UPF intake to weight gain due to its higher energy density than whole foods. 25 , support this link by showing that higher maternal UPF intake was associated with increased adiposity in neonates. These ﬁndings highlight the importance of dietary choices during pregnancy tomitigate risks associated with adiposity gain and related health outcomes in both mothers and infants. Maternal UPF consumption during pregnancy may increase ADHD symptoms in children 51 , and this may also increase the risk of emotional and behavioral symptoms in children. Addition- ally, Zupo et al. 53 found a weak positive relationship between prenatal exposure to UPF and offspring ADHD, emphasizing the need for further investigation into the impact of dietary choices on neurodevelopment and mental health in children. Dietary intake, diet quality, and dietary habits Birhaine et al. 28 emphasize the nutritional vulnerability of pregnant and lactating women, infants, and young children, high- lighting the critical need for adequate nutrient intake during these stages to prevent adverse outcomes such as stillbirths and early neonatal deaths due to maternal anemia and related micronutrient deﬁciencies. Adding to the above, the evidence consistently shows that higher consumption of UPF during pregnancy leads to reduced intake of essential nutrients critical for maternal and fetal health, such as proteins, ﬁber, zinc, potassium, magnesium, and various vitamins such as A, C, D, B12, and niacin, contributing to nutritional imbalances 36,39,44,46. Additionally, the evidence underscores the reduced iron and folate intake, critical for all pregnancy stages 42,43. These studies also highlight a concerning rise in total fat and saturated fat, contributing to an imbalanced diet 50,51. Maternal high-fat diets during pregnancy can lead to adverse metabolic effects in both the mother and fetus, increasing the risk of metabolic disorders in offspring later in life 58.

content_chunk: These ﬁndings underscore the urgent need for interventions targeting nutritional education and dietary interventions to ensure optimal health out-comes during pregnancy and early childhood. Increased consumption of UPF during pregnancy is associated with low essential nutrient intake, leading to compromised diet quality. Studies 38,40,42 highlight this link, showing alterations in protein, iron, magnesium, and folate levels due to UPF consumption 39,46. This negative impact on diet quality is further supported by the inverse correlation between UPF intake and overall diet quality 36. Consequently, UPF consumption displaces bene ﬁcial foods crucial for health 47. For example, UPF consumption has been shown to be inversely related to the Mediterranean dietary pattern 59 , which has healthful effects on pregnant women and offspring 60. Moreover, for Dietary Habits, an increased frequency of maternal UPF consumption in the antenatal period was negativelyM. Rocha-Velasco Clinical Nutrition ESPEN 65 2025 288 e304 associated with adverse fetal outcomes 45. While, another study highlighted a concerning rise in UPF intake among pregnant women, however older and more educated women and those with healthy behaviors showed lower UPF intake in pregnancy 48. Implementing targeted interventions to improve nutritional edu- cation, promote healthier dietary habits, and reduce UPF intake among pregnant women is paramount to safeguarding maternal and child health during pregnancy and early childhood. Limitations encountered include the need for more data and heterogeneity of exposure, leading to challenges in reliability and analysis due to variability in assessment techniques. Addressing these limitations requires employing validated assessment tools compatible with the NOVA system and involving trained nutri- tionists or dietitians to assess dietary intake effectively and reduce potential biases associated with self-reporting, a limitation observed in most studies included in this review. Many studies analyze diet rich in UPF without NOVA classi ﬁcation, and these results may compromise the robustness of author's analysis and discussion. Larger sample sizes and robust methodological quality are imperative to strengthen the reliability and generalizability of ﬁndings in future research efforts. Plausible mechanisms of action of UPF Although mechanistic research on how UPF exert their actions is still in its infancy and de ﬁnitive proof of the speci ﬁcm e c h a n i s m s by which UPF may affect health outcomes and diet are largely unknown, some hypotheses do exist. Further research is required to better comprehend the aspects of UPF that correlate them with poor health outcomes and premature mortality 61,62. Current evidence suggests that UPFs differ from unprocessed and mini- mally processed foods in several key areas, which may elucidate their potential links to adverse health consequences. These vari- ations encompass inferior nutrient compositions, the replacement of non-ultra-processed foods in the diet, and modi ﬁcations to the physical characteristics of food items due to extensive ultra- processing.

content_chunk: Emerging data indicate that characteristics related to UPF, such as alterations in food matrices and textures, potential contaminants from packaging materials and processing, the presence of food additives and other industrial ingredients, and poor nutrient pro- ﬁles, may have synergistic or compounded effects. These effects could manifest through established or plausible physiological mechanisms 61,63e66. The complex interconnected biological mechanisms through which UPF negatively impact health encompass various pathways. These mechanisms involve changes in microbiome-related func- tions, in ﬂammatory responses, and disruptions in digestive and metabolic processes, all of which collectively lead to non- communicable diseases such as obesity, cardiovascular disease, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. UPF generally contain a low level of nutrients while being rich in additives, preservatives, and arti ﬁcial components. Nutrient- deﬁcient dietary patterns have been associated with the preva- lence and onset of chronic diseases via multiple pathways, including in ﬂammatory processes 63,64,66. Diets that are high in UPF are particularly linked to indicators of subpar diet quality. These diets tend to contain elevated amounts of added sugars, saturated fats, and sodium, exhibit greater energy density, and are characterized by reduced levels of ﬁber, protein, and essential micronutrients 5,67. UPF tend to replace more nutritious options in diets, including fruits, vegetables, legumes, nuts, and seeds. This substitution leads to a decrease in the consumption of bene ﬁcial bioactive compounds found in these foods, such as polyphenols and phytoestrogens like enterodiol 68,69. One signi ﬁcant way in which ultra-processed foods UPF may inﬂuence health is through their high caloric density, which frequently results in excessive calorie consumption without suf ﬁ- cient feelings of fullness. This phenomenon contributes to the rising rates of weight gain and obesity observed in contemporary dietary patterns. Research has demonstrated a strong causal link between diets rich in ultra-processed foods and an increase in energy intake, with ﬁndings indicating an average excess of approximately 500 kcal 2000 kJ per day and a weight gain of about 0. 9 kg during periods of consuming ultra-processed diets 70. Additionally, other studies have revealed that employing the NOVA food classi ﬁcation system for nutritional guidance, in conjunction with physical ac- tivity, can effectively mitigate excessive weight gain among preg- nant women with elevated body mass index 71. The factors that contribute to the excessive consumption asso- ciated with diets high in ultra-processed foods UPF appear to be linked to the type of energy source, particularly distinguishing between solid foods and beverages 70. Furthermore, the higher energy density, rapid consumption rates, and heightened palat- ability of UPF are considered signi ﬁcant elements that affect this phenomenon 72. UPF often inhibit the normal signals of satiety due to their elevated energy density and low ﬁber content, which can lead to overeating and subsequent weight gain 73. Moreover, the altered structure of UPF impacts nutrient absorption and the sensation of fullness, resulting in increased caloric intake and a potential rise in insulin 74,75.

content_chunk: UPF often include re ﬁned carbohydrates that are quickly digested, leading to heightened feelings of hunger and a greater likelihood of overeating. Additionally, the elevated sugar levels found in many UPF can trigger swift increases in blood glucose, which may foster insulin resistance and elevate the risk of obesity and metabolic disorders. The intake of UPF is linked to heightened inﬂammation and oxidative stress, which can contribute to the development of chronic diseases 75,76. Furthermore, the inclu- sion of various additives and preservatives not only improves ﬂavor and texture but may also disrupt metabolic functions and affect appetite regulation, thereby complicating the connection between these foods and health outcomes. The negative health effects linked to ultra-processed foods UPF cannot be solely attributed to their nutrient composition and en- ergy density; rather, they are also in ﬂuenced by the physical and chemical characteristics resulting from industrial processing tech- niques, ingredients, and by-products. Firstly, the modi ﬁcations in the food matrix that occur during extensive processing, referred to as dietary reconstitution, can impact digestion, nutrient absorption, and the sensation of fullness 77. Secondly, recent studies in humans have identi ﬁed associations between the consumption of additives dsuch as non-sugar sweeteners, emulsi ﬁers, colorants, and nitrates nitrites dand adverse health effects 78e83. A recent review of experimental studies indicated that ultra-processed weight loss products, which may appear to have balanced nutrient pro ﬁles but include various additives, including non-sugar sweeteners, could negatively affect the gut microbiome. This microbiome is believed to play a signi ﬁcant role in numerous dis- eases and related in ﬂammatory processes 84. Furthermore, the World Health Organization has recently cautioned against thecontinued use of sugar substitutes for weight management or non- communicable diseases, stating in its latest report that non-sugar sweeteners may increase the risk of cardiometabolic diseases and mortality 85. UPF can adversely affect the gut microbiome, leading to meta- bolic dysregulation, in ﬂammation, and conditions such as NAFLD 74. The incorporation of food additives, emulsi ﬁers, and arti ﬁcial sweeteners in UPF may enhance gut permeability and activate in- ﬂammatory pathways, thereby exacerbating the onset of chronicM. Rocha-Velasco Clinical Nutrition ESPEN 65 2025 288 e304 diseases. Additionally, UPF can disturb the gut microbiome, resulting in dysbiosis, which is associated with obesity and various metabolic disorders 86. Additionally, UPF are linked to the presence of carcinogenic substances generated during food processing, potentially increasing the risk of cancer 87. UPF may also include harmful additives and contaminants that could facilitate carcinogenesis, especially concerning colorectal cancer 76. In addition, the In- ternational Agency for Research on Cancer has recently classi ﬁed the non-sugar sweetener aspartame as possibly carcinogenic to humans group 2 B , citing limited evidence in human studies 88. An expanding array of research indicates that exposure to various combinations of additives may result in cocktail effects, which could have more signi ﬁcant health implications than expo- sure to individual additives 89.

content_chunk: The extensive industrial processing of food can lead to the for- mation of potentially harmful compounds that have been associ- ated with an increased risk of chronic in ﬂammatory diseases. These compounds include acrolein, acrylamide, advanced glycation end products, furans, heterocyclic amines, industrial trans-fatty acids, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons 61,90. Finally, UPF may contain health-related contaminants that leach from packaging materials, such as bisphenols, microplastics, mineral oils, and phthalates 61. Together, these factors underscore the considerable health risks linked to the consumption of UPF. There is an urgent need for further mechanistic research on UPF to pinpoint the speci ﬁc char- acteristics that contribute to health detriment, with an emphasis on developing effective reformulation strategies to reduce their adverse impacts on human health. Conclusion Our study delved into maternal and child health outcomes linked to UPF consumption categorized by the NOVA system during pregnancy in recent years. Despite encountering limited data, the main ﬁndings suggest that UPF consumption impacts various do- mains, including maternal health indicators like GDM, GWG, gly- cemic control, in ﬂammatory markers, nutrition biomarkers, oxidative stress levels, and HDP, as well as child health factors such as embryonic and infant growth, neurodevelopment, adiposity gain, and adverse mental disorders. Additionally, it sheds light on nutrient intake and diet quality. The involvement of a multidisciplinary team and validated tools compatible with the NOVA system are crucial for consolidating evidence on food processing's impact on health outcomes. Moni- toring pregnancy diets and promoting healthy dietary habits among pregnant women and their children is essential to ensure optimal health outcomes. content_chunk: Available online at www. com Review Pregnancy complications and later-life maternal cardiovascular health: mechanistic insights from animal models Amanda A de Oliveira1,2, Floor Spaans1,2, Murilo E Graton1,2, Christy-Lynn M Cooke1,2and Sandra T Davidge1,2,3 Cardiovascular disease CVD is the leading cause of death globally in both men and women. Sex differences exist in the onset, progression, and outcomes of CVD, with sex-specific factors such as pregnancy-related conditions likely contributing to these disparities. Preeclampsia PE and gestational diabetes mellitus GDM are two of the most common medical complications of pregnancy, affecting approximately 3 5 and 5 18 , respectively. Women with a history of PE or GDM are at a higher risk of developing CVD later in life. Still, the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood. This review presents an overview of the mechanisms underlying the development of PE and GDM, and discusses pathophysiological pathways revealed through animal models that could contribute to long- term maternal cardiovascular dysfunction. Introduction Despite global declines in cardiovascular mortality, car- diovascular disease CVD remains the leading cause of death worldwide in both men and women 1. Cardiovascular mortality rates declined between 1979 and 2011 in the United States; however, the rate of decline was slower among younger adults 55 years , particularly for women 2. A subsequent study of trends from 2000 to 2014 also reported a deceleration in cardi - ovascular mortality after 2011, with a more pronounced slowdown among women 1. Thus, understanding the mechanisms under - lying worsening risk factor profiles in women is essential to reducing future cardiovascular mortality. Sex-specific CVD risk factors affecting pregnant individuals have been identified. Pregnancy is increasingly recognized as a physiological stress test, as the demands it places on the body can unmask underlying predispositions to disease that might otherwise not become apparent until much later in life 4,5. Moreover, failure to adequately adapt to the physiological demands of pregnancy predisposes women to complications, and those who experience a complicated pregnancy are at a higher risk of developing later-life CVD 6. Preeclampsia PE and gestational diabetes mellitus GDM are amongst the most common medical complica - tions of pregnancy, with reported incidence rates of 3 5 and 5 18 , respectively 7 9.

content_chunk: Women with a history of PE have a fourfold increased risk of heart failure and a twofold increased risk of coronary heart disease and stroke 10. Si- milarly, those with prior GDM face a 2. 3-fold higher risk of future cardiovascular events 11. Importantly, in both cases, these adverse cardiovascular outcomes tend to occur within a decade after delivery 10,11. Considering that the mean age at first birth in most high-income countries is 30 years, these data underscore the need for early cardiovascular risk assessment and intervention in a substantial population of women before the age of 40. Since 2011, the American Heart Association has recommended incorporating preg- nancy complications, such as PE and GDM, into cardio - vascular risk assessments for women 12. Still, it was reported that 40 of women do not attend postpartum appointments in the United States 13. Moreover, despite the compelling epidemiological evidence that PE and GDM have long-term implications for maternal cardiovas - cular health, the underlying mechanisms are not fully un- derstood. This review presents an overview of the mechanisms underlying the development of PE and GDM, and www. com Current Opinion in Physiology 2025, 46:100870 discusses pathophysiological pathways revealed through animal models that could contribute to long-term ma- ternal cardiovascular dysfunction. Preeclampsia and later-life maternal cardiovascular health PE is a leading cause of maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality, as well as a risk factor for later-life maternal CVD 9,14. The condition is characterized by new- onset hypertension after mid-gestation, accompanied by signs of end-organ damage such as proteinuria, throm - bocytopenia, renal insufficiency, impaired liver function, pulmonary edema, neurological symptoms, placental insufficiency, and or fetal growth restriction 14. In PE, there is widespread maternal endothelial dysfunction and a vasoconstrictive phenotype that is characterized by an imbalance between pro-relaxing factors e. reduced nitric oxide NO , prostacyclin, and endothelium-de - rived hyperpolarization-mediated responses and pro- contractile factors e. increased thromboxane A₂, en- dothelin-1, angiotensin II, and oxidative stress 15 , ultimately leading to the clinical manifestations of PE 9,14. Intriguingly, PE s clinical signs tend to resolve after delivery of the fetoplacental unit, which is, to date, the only cure for PE. This cure often leads to devas - tating pregnancy outcomes and does not protect the pregnant individuals against long-term maternal cardio - vascular dysfunction 6. There are two theories to ex- plain the increased cardiovascular risk among women with a history of PE: i PE unmasks pre-existing car- diovascular conditions in those with subclinical risk factors before conception, and ii PE itself leads to persistent cardiovascular dysfunction 4. While there is evidence supporting both theories and, they are not mutually exclusive 4 , the underlying mechanisms are unclear. Mechanistic insights into disrupted pathways in women with a history of PE have been recently summarized by Yang and collaborators 16.

content_chunk: However, it should be noted that many human clinical studies cannot determine whether the impaired maternal cardiovascular function observed later in life is due to a pre-existing condition, the direct impact of PE, or a combination of both. Such a distinction can often only be made in preclinical studies. However, because rodents do not spontaneously develop PE, the condition is typically induced in mice term 19. 5 days and rats term 22 days using surgical, pharmaco - logical, immunological, environmental, or genetic ma- nipulation reviewed in refs. Several studies have examined the cardiovascular effects of PE during preg- nancy and the early postpartum period 17,18 , but few have assessed long-term at least four weeks postpartum in mice and rats, which equals 2. 5 human years 19,20 maternal cardiovascular outcomes. The key findings from these studies are summarized below: PE induced by sFlt-1 overexpression: Infusion of soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 sFlt-1 , a splice variant of the vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-1 gene, in CD-1 mice on gestational day GD 8 in- duces a PE-like phenotype including high blood pressure and fetal growth restriction 21 without long-term effects on blood pressure and cardiac renal function at 8 weeks postpartum 22 , or blood pres- sure and vascular reactivity in the mesenteric arteries at 24-32 weeks postpartum 23. However, at 8 weeks postpartum, exposure to unilateral carotid artery in- jury revealed that PE-exposed CD-1 mice have en- hanced vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation and vessel fibrosis, indicating that vessels exposed to PE retain a phenotype of enhanced vascular response to injury despite the resolution of PE-signs postpartum 22. Proteomic analysis of maternal plasma at 24 weeks postpartum revealed that the most abundant proteins in CD-1 mice exposed to high levels of sFlt- 1 are the ones associated with vascular disease, atherosclerosis, and atherosclerotic lesions 24. Moreover, infusion of sFlt-1 in C57Bl 6 mice also induces PE-like signs such as high blood pressure and glomerular endotheliosis, and a history of PE was sufficient to drive hyperresponsiveness to hyperten - sive stimuli i. 4 high salt diet or angiotensin II infusion at 8 weeks postpartum 25. These animals also had increased aortic stiffness and microvascular vasoconstriction 25. Mechanistically, these post- partum alterations were absent in mice lacking the mineralocorticoid receptor in smooth muscle cells 25. Similarly, low-density lipoprotein LDL receptor knockout mice infused with sFlt-1 on GD 9 develop a PE-like phenotype with high blood pressure and glo- merular endotheliosis, with blood pressure normalizing postpartum 26. Further exposure to a high-fat diet for 8 weeks postpartum revealed that prior exposure to a PE pregnancy does not affect atherosclerosis plaque size or plaque lipid necrotic core content, but did result in increased aortic arch plaque inflammation. There were high levels of plaque CD45 leukocytes, which were associated with increased aortic levels of CCL22 and fetuin A, and decreased levels of IGFBP6 and CCL21 26.

content_chunk: As plaque inflammation is a surrogate marker of plaque instability 27 , this may contribute to the increased risk of myocardial infarction and stroke in those who had PE. PE induced by placental ischemia: The reduced uter- oplacental perfusion RUPP model Sprague Dawley rats, surgery on GD 14 presents a PE-like phenotype with high blood pressure and a reduced glomerular filtration rate 28. At 4 weeks postpartum, these changes in pregnancy resulted in increased vasocon - striction responses to phenylephrine in mesenteric arteries due to an underlying loss of basal NO mod - ulation, which was improved at 12 weeks postpartum 29. Endothelium-dependent vasodilation was also 2Recent Advancements in Women s Heart Health www. com Current Opinion in Physiology 2025, 46:100870 reduced in mesenteric arteries at 4 and 12 weeks postpartum due to reduced NO bioavailability 29. Moreover, at 8 weeks postpartum, the glomerular filtration rate and cardiac ejection fraction were re- duced in RUPP animals compared to controls without changes in kidney and heart structure, respectively 30. At 10 weeks postpartum, RUPP animals also presented with a reduced stroke volume together with reduced cardiac complex IV protein abundance and activity, suggesting impaired cardiac mitochon - drial activity 31. And all of these changes could be prevented by blockade of angiotensin II type 1 re- ceptor AT1 agonistic autoantibodies, indicating that immune dysregulation during pregnancy plays a role in the long-term maternal impact of RUPP pregnan - cies 31. Signs of cerebral inflammation increased levels of tumor necrosis factor-α and interleukin IL - 6 without changes in IL-10 and IL-4 , cerebral oxi- dative stress due to high levels of H2O2 , and astro - cyte activation were also observed in RUPP rats 6 weeks postpartum 32. This proinflammatory phe- notype persists at 8 weeks postpartum and likely contributes to posterior cortical inflammation in- creased levels of IL-17, IL-1α, IL-1β, leptin, and MIP2 and cerebral edema via reduced occludin le- vels 33. Interestingly, while studies using the RUPP rat model consistently demonstrate impaired cardio - vascular outcomes later in life, findings on postpartum blood pressure are inconsistent. Some studies report no changes in blood pressure between 4 to 12 weeks postpartum 29,30 , whereas others observe sustained hypertension at 6 and 10 weeks postpartum 31,32. PE induced by excessive hypercholesterolemia in pregnancy: A high cholesterol diet HCD from GD 6 to 20 in- duces classical PE-like signs in Sprague Dawley rats reviewed by de Oliveira and colleagues 34. 12 weeks postpartum , HCD rats have normal blood pressure and vascular function in me- senteric and coronary arteries 35. However, carotid artery vasoconstriction responses to phenylephrine were increased due to a loss of basal NO modulation, and endothelium-dependent vasodilation was re- duced due to prostaglandin H synthase 2 activation 35.

content_chunk: Carotid artery stiffness was also increased in HCD postpartum rats, along with reduced elastin density, and associated with a loss of myogenic tone 35 , which may contribute to the increased suscept - ibility to stroke observed in women with a history of PE. Similarly, C57Bl 6 mice fed an HCD in late ge- station presented with persistent endothelial dys- function in aortas, with reduced levels of phosphorylated endothelial NO synthase and super - oxide dismutase-1, and increased levels of inducible NO synthase, superoxide, and peroxynitrite 36. There was also an increased susceptibility of HCD vessels to exposure to oxidized LDL 36. Moreover, exposure to an HCD in pregnancy that continued postpartum was associated with high blood pressure, hippocampal artery dysfunction due to hypertrophic remodeling and impaired reactivity to various agents , and impaired long-term memory without changes in spatial memory at 20 weeks postpartum in rats 37. This model also leads to an increased ischemic stroke severity larger infarct size and edema linked to sys- temic oxidative and nitrative stress both at the end of gestation 38 and at 16 to 36 weeks postpartum 39. PE induced by L-NAME infusion: Infusion of L-NAME pan-NO synthase inhibitor, 50 mg kg day from GD 7. 5 in C57Bl 6 mice induces a PE-like phe- notype that includes high blood pressure, impaired fetal and placental growth, and high circulating levels of sFlt-1. However, after delivery, mice that received L-NAME have no discernible changes in measured cardiovascular indices at 4 weeks postpartum 40. Interestingly, at 10 weeks postpartum, mesenteric artery vasoconstriction responses to phenylephrine, kidney Mmp9:Timp1, and heart Tnf mRNA levels were increased in these mice 40. In a conflicting study, another group reported increased vasocon - striction responses to phenylephrine in mesenteric arteries at 5 weeks postpartum, but not at 10 weeks postpartum, and this was associated with no changes in various markers of kidney and heart function 41. PE induced by genetic manipulations: Female rats transfected with the human angiotensinogen gene TGR hAogen L1623 develop a PE-like phenotype high blood pressure and albuminuria during preg - nancy when mated with male rats harboring the human renin gene TGR hRen L10J 42. While hypertension resolves within 1 week postpartum, these rats present cardiac hypertrophy, reduced ejection fraction, increased plasma BNP, substantial interstitial and perivascular fibrosis, and capillary rar- efaction at 4 weeks postpartum 42. Similarly, over- expression of the storkhead box 1A isoform of the Stox1 gene in mice induces classical PE-like signs, and these signs resolve postpartum 43. However, at 32 weeks postpartum, Stox1 mice present cardiac hypertrophy, fibrosis, altered cardiac function upon dobutamine stress, and changes in the endothelial transcriptome favoring an inflammatory profile 43. It has also been reported that female C57Bl 6J mice bred with complement component C1q-deficient male mice present classical PE-like symptoms due to impaired placentation, a process that is mainly influ - enced by paternal genes 44.

content_chunk: At 28 weeks post- partum, these mice have reduced endothelium- dependent vasodilation in mesenteric arteries and increased vasoconstriction responses to pheny - lephrine, but the underlying mechanisms were not investigated 44. PE induced by immune system activation: Wistar rats in- jected with AT1 agonistic autoantibodies on GD 13 and 14 present classical PE-like signs, and this Maternal health after a complicated pregnancy de Oliveira et al. com Current Opinion in Physiology 2025, 46:100870 phenotype is associated with long-term changes in left ventricular morphology hypertrophy, interstitial fibrosis, and mitochondria swelling and function, in- cluding a delayed recovery to an ischemic insult, 16 weeks postpartum 45. Similarly, infusion of lipopo - lysaccharide to induce an inflammatory response in Wistar rats on GD 13. 5 induces classical PE- like symptoms, and is associated with left ventricular hypertrophy and dyslipidemia, plus high levels of markers of cardiac hypertrophy at 16 weeks post- partum 46. In summary, exposure to a pregnancy complicated by PE, regardless of the animal model used and in- dependent of pre-existing factors, impairs later-life maternal cardiovascular function Table 1. The under - lying mechanisms vary depending on the experimental model and the timing of outcome assessments. Overall, studies report impaired left ventricular function char- acterized by hypertrophy, fibrosis, inflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Vascular endothelial dys- function in both small and large arteries is also observed, driven by reduced NO bioavailability and oxidative stress, as well as increased arterial stiffness. Notably, many studies reveal that subclinical cardiovascular dys- function often becomes evident only after a secondary insult, highlighting the heightened susceptibility of the maternal cardiovascular system following PE. Gestational diabetes mellitus and later-life maternal cardiovascular health GDM, defined as hyperglycemia first recognized during the second or third trimester of pregnancy, affects 1 in 6 live births 7,8. In normal pregnancies, placental hor- mones induce insulin resistance, while also stimulating insulin secretion and pancreatic β-cell expansion to avoid excessive increases in maternal hyperglycemia 7,8. Conversely, in those who develop GDM, there is a failure or delayed response of the pancreatic β-cells to compensate for maternal insulin resistance due to var- ious risk factors such as obesity, physical inactivity, hy- pertension, low HDL, polycystic ovarian syndrome, and abnormal glucose metabolism, as well as genetic pre- disposition 7,8. Thus, the American Diabetes Asso - ciation and other international societies advocate for a one-step screening approach for GDM using a two-hour 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 24 28 weeks of ge- station 7,8. A diagnosis is made if at least one of these measurements meets or exceeds established thresholds 7. GDM is associated with adverse pregnancy out- comes, including PE, fetal macrosomia, and neonatal hypoglycemia 8. Beyond pregnancy, GDM has long- term implications for maternal cardiovascular health, including a 2. 3-fold higher risk of future cardiovascular events 11 , as well as an increased risk of developing cardiovascular risk factors such as type 2 diabetes 47 and metabolic dysfunction associated steatotic liver disease MASLD 48. There is, however, a paucity of data for the mechanisms linking GDM to long-term maternal cardiovascular outcomes Figure 2. Preclinical models of GDM can be created by surgical or chemical interventions, or by dietary or genetic mod - ifications 49. However, there is a stark paucity of data directly assessing the impact of GDM on later-life i. 4 weeks postpartum maternal cardiovascular health using animal models, as most studies focused on preg - nancy outcomes and offspring health 49,50. Verma and colleagues have demonstrated that female rats specifi - cally expressing human amylin in pancreatic β-cells have glucose intolerance during pregnancy and signs of car- diac hypertrophy, of which the latter persists until at least 8 weeks postpartum 51. This cardiac hypertrophy was induced via activation of calcineurin nuclear factor of activated T cells NFAT signaling due to higher diastolic calcium levels 51. In a more recent study, Badmus and colleagues, using a mouse model of re- versible GDM induced by the insulin receptor antago - nist S961, showed that these mice develop cardiac dysfunction accompanied by cardiac hypertrophy, en- dothelial dysfunction linked to reduced NO bioavail - ability, and arterial stiffness associated with fibrosis at 10 weeks postpartum 52. As GDM is a significant risk factor for type 2 diabetes 47 , a recent study has as- sessed metabolomic and lipidomic profiles in a lean rat model of GDM at 2 weeks postpartum 53.

However, there remains a paucity of studies investigating the underlying me- chanisms that drive this increased risk, knowledge that is essential for developing effective interventions to miti- gate the long-term maternal impact of these pregnancy complications. Thomas, PhD; Jeannette R. Ickovics, PhD OBJECTIVE: To systematically review the literature on associations between climate drivers and health outcomes among pregnant people. This review ﬁlls a gap by synthesizing evidence for a clinician audience. DATA SOURCES: Systematic scoping review of articles published in PubMed and clinicaltrials. gov from January 2010 through December 2023. STUDY ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: Empirical studies published in English-language peer-reviewed journals, assessing associations between select climate drivers and adverse maternal and birth outcomes. The review included studies examining heat, storms, sea level rise, ﬂooding, drought, wild ﬁres, and other climate-related factors. Health outcomes included preterm birth, low birthweight, small for gestational age, gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia eclampsia, miscarriage stillbirth and maternal mortality. STUDY APPRAISAL AND SYNTHESIS METHODS: The scoping review protocol was registered with the International Platform of Registered Systematic Review and Meta-analysis Protocols INPLASY202410004, January 3, 2024 and conducted in accordance with the Pre-ferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis PRISMA. Data were extracted by 2 authors; quality and risk of bias wasassessed independently. RESULTS: Total of 966 references were screened; 16. 35 k 158 met inclusion criteria. The majority of studies 146 158; 92. 4 docu- mented statistically signi ﬁcant and clinically meaningful associations between climate drivers and adverse perinatal health outcomes, including risk of preterm birth, low birthweight, and stillbirth as well as preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, miscarriage, and maternal death. Among themost durable ﬁndings: extreme heat exposure in early and late pregnancy were associated with increased risk of preterm birth and stillbirth. Driven in part by large often population-based studies and objective outcomes from surveillance data or medical record reviews, studies in this scoping review were evaluated as high quality scoring 7-9 on the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Risk of bias was generally low. CONCLUSIONS: Climate drivers are consistently associated with adverse health outcomes for pregnant people. Continuing education for clinicians, and clinician-patient communications should be expanded to address risks of climate change and extreme weather exposure, espe-cially risks of extreme heat in late-pregnancy. Results from this review should inform multilevel interventions to address adverse health effects o f climate during pregnancy as well as practice advisories, protocols, checklists, and clinical guidelines in obstetrics.
