content_chunk: The effect of maternal pre-pregnancy body mass index on hypertensive disorders of pregnancy HDP : a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of cohort studies involving 50 million pregnancies Yiquan Xiong,a,b,cJingwen Chen,a,b,cYue Wu,dPeng Zhao,a,b,cMingyu Liao,a,b,cJin Guo,a,b,cChunrong Liu,a,b,cMengyuan Zheng ,a,b,cYan Ren,a,b,c Kang Zou,a,b,cXin Sun,a,b,c, and Jing Tana,b,c, aGeneral Practice Medical Center , Chinese Evidence-based Medicine Center , West China Hospital, Sichuan University , Chengdu, 610041, China bNMPA Key Laboratory for Real World Data Research and Evaluation in Hainan, Chengdu, 610041, China cSichuan Center of Technology Innovation for Real World Data, Chengdu, 610041, China dSchool of Public Health, Zhejiang Chinese Medical University , Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, 310053, China Summary Background Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy is a prevalent pregnancy complication worldwide, and the dose- response association between maternal pre-pregnancy body mass index BMI and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy has not been precisely studied. The aim of this study was to assess dose-response association between maternal pre-pregnancy BMI and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, including pregnancy induced hypertension, preeclampsia and eclampsia. Methods This dose-response meta-analysis searched four electronic databases Pubmed, Web of science, OVID Embase and OVID Medline for relevant publications up to October, 2023. Cohort studies evaluated the association between pre-pregnancy or early pregnancy maternal BMI and pregnancy induced hypertension, preeclampsia, eclampsia and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy were included. Non-linear or linear dose- response association was modeled. Unadjusted and adjusted effects were pooled separately, and four subgroups, meta-regression, five sensitivity analyses were conducted. Study protocol was registered on the PROSPERO CRD42022290318. Findings 157 cohort studies involving 51,813,975 pregnancies were finally included. Of 157 studies, multiple outcomes were reported: 58 on pregnancy induced hypertension, 92 on preeclampsia, 6 on eclampsia, and 84 on hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, have assessed the association with pre-pregnancy BMI. A significant linear dose-response relationship was identified between BMI and pregnancy induced hypertension with a crude relative risk cRR of BMI per 5-unit increase of 1. 73 95 confidence intervals CI : 1. 81 , and an adjusted odds ratio aOR per 5-unit increase of 1. Similar dose-response relationship was observed between BMI and preeclampsia cRR: 1. 80 , eclampsia cRR: 1. 53 and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy cRR: 1. Subgroup analyses revealed that the pooled risk of BMI for pregnancy induced hypertension, preeclampsia, eclampsia, and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy was likely higher in Asian pregnant women compared to those in American and European regions. Sensitivity analyses results were mainly consistent with the primary results. Interpretation This meta-analysis demonstrated a clear and significant dose-response relationship between increasing maternal pre-pregnancy BMI and elevated risks of pregnancy induced hypertension, preeclampsia, eclampsia, and overall hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, underscoring the clinical importance of maintaining a healthy BMI prior to conception. Pre-pregnancy BMI may be an important focus for preconception counseling and subsequent pre-pregnancy weight management for both clinicians and women. Keywords: Preeclampsia; Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy; Body mass index; Obesity; Dose-response relationship; Systematic review Introduction Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy HDP , mainly including pregnancy induced hypertension PIH , pre - eclampsia, eclampsia and HELLP syndrome, is a prev - alent pregnancy complication and constitute one of the leading causes of maternal and perinatal mortality and morbidity worldwide. 1,2 It is estimated that preeclamp - sia complicates 2 8 of pregnancies globally and causes at least 46,000 maternal deaths annually. 3,4 It has been reported that HDP was associated with higher risk of intrauterine growth restriction, preterm birth, post - partum hemorrhage, and even for future cardiovascular health of pregnant women. 5 8 Despite the high disease burden of HDP, no therapeutic interventions have been identified that effectively modify the progression of the disease,5 reflecting that identification of the underlying risk factors for HDP and early prevention are critical to HDP management. It has been documented that variety factors were associated with higher risk of HDP, such as advance maternal age, nulliparity, preeclampsia in a previous pregnancy, autoimmune disease and maternal obesity. 5,7,8 Of these, maternal obesity is one of the strongest risk factors for HDP, and also is one of the most cost-effective interventional factors for HDP prevention. 1,2,5,9 The prevalence of maternal overweight and obesity was increasing in the recent decades worldwide, particular in developing and developed countries. 10,11 Previous studies have explored the association be - tween maternal abnormal pre-pregnancy body mass index BMI i. , underweight, overweight, and obesity and adverse obstetric outcomes, including gestational diabetes GDM , HDP, early pregnancy loss, preterm birth and stillbirth. 11 18 For instance, there was a non- linear dose-response relationship between maternal BMI before or in early pregnancy and adverse fetal Research in context Evidence before this study Previous studies have suggested that maternal pre- pregnancy overweight or obesity significantly increases the risk of pregnancy induced hypertension PIH , and preeclampsia. However , the dose-response relationship between maternal pre-pregnancy body mass index BMI and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy HDP , including PIH, preeclampsia, and eclampsia, has not been precisely studied. We conducted a systematic search of PubMed for relevant studies through March 10, 2025, using the terms: body mass index , obesity , pregnancy induced hypertension , preeclampsia , eclampsia , hypertensive disorders of pregnancy , with no language restriction. The results of search showed that hundreds of cohort studies or case- control studies, and several meta-analyses have evaluated the association between different categories of maternal pre- pregnancy bodyweight i. , underweight, overweight, and obesity and HDP.

However , the dose- response relationship between maternal pre-pregnancy BMI and eclampsia, HDP , and this relationship in other regions e. , Asia , was poorly understood. Added value of this study By including 157 studies involving more than 50 million pregnancies, this study comprehensively addressed the dose- response relationship between maternal pre-pregnancy BMI and PIH, preeclampsia, eclampsia and HDP , and accurately revealed the risk of increasing maternal pre-pregnancy BMI per 5 kg m2. A significant dose-response relationship was identified between maternal pre-pregnancy BMI and PIH adjusted odds ratio aOR per 5 kg m2 of 1. 90 , preeclampsia aOR of 1. 80 , eclampsia aOR of 1. In addition, the risk of maternal pre-pregnancy BMI for PIH, preeclampsia, eclampsia, and HDP was likely higher in Asian pregnant women compared to those in American and European regions. Implications of all the available evidence Given the significantly negative dose-response relationship between excess maternal pre-pregnancy BMI and PIH, preeclampsia, eclampsia and HDP , the findings in this study support that pre-pregnancy BMI may be an important focus for preconception counseling and subsequent weight management for both women and clinicians. com Vol 86 August, 2025 outcomes i. , stillbirth, and infant death. 19 A meta- analysis showed that compared to normal weight, maternal pre-pregnancy obesity was associated with higher risk for HDP with odd ratio OR of 2. 17 Similarly, an individual participant data IPD meta-analysis showed that maternal pre- pregnancy overweight or obesity significantly increased the risk of PIH and preeclampsia. 15 However, most of the previous meta-analysis used a categorical approach to investigate the association between maternal bodyweight i. , underweight, over - weight, and obesity and HDP. 13,14,16 18 Because the cut- off values for abnormal bodyweight varied worldwide and across published studies, it was understandably imprecise to use only a comparison of different body - weight groups e. normal body weight to determine the impact on HDP. Therefore, dose- response analysis is an alternative approach that could accurately assess the impact of maternal body weight,20,21 and provide more guidance for weight management during the pre-pregnancy period. Unfor - tunately, the dose-response impact of maternal body - weight on HDP has not been precisely studied,15,17 and remains to be determined. Therefore, we conducted this systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis to evaluate the dose-response association between maternal pre-pregnancy BMI and HDP, including PIH, preeclampsia and eclampsia. In addition, the following studies were also excluded: 1 those that did not report the original number of events and total participants in each BMI group; 2 those that did not include a normal body weight group; 3 those included less than 100 participants; 4 case-control studies, conference abstracts, case reports, opinions, editorials, or review articles. Literature search Pubmed, Web of science, OVID Embase and OVID Medline were initially searched for relevant studies from inception to November 10, 2021, and updated to October 13, 2023. A pre-designed search strategy Appendix S1 , which combined MeSHs and free-text terms, was used to identify relevant studies. The MeSHs terms included body mass index, overweight, obesity, thinness, hypertension pregnancy-induced, pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, HELLP syndrome. And the free-text terms included BMI, underweight, thin, obese, obesity, bodyweight, preeclampsia, pre-eclampsia, HELLP syndrome, gestational hypertension, pregnancy-induced hypertension, and pregnancy induced hypertension. The search was restricted to human studies. Reference lists of included articles and relative systematic reviews were also manually checked for additional relevant studies. Study process According to the inclusion criteria, two investigators JWC and YW trained in research methods indepen - dently screened the titles, abstracts, and then full texts for eligibility. content_chunk: According to World Health Organization WHO standards,23 pregnant women were divided into underweight BMI 18. 5 kg m2 , normal weight BMI: 18. 99 kg m2 , overweight BMI: 25 29. 99 kg m2 and obesity BMI 30 kg m2. In this study, consid - ering different definitions of normal weight in original studies, a deviation of 1. 5 kg m2 in the classification of normal weight was accepted. To conducted dose-response analysis, we extracted mean or median BMI of each body weight category reported in the original study as dose of BMI. For studies that did not report these data, the dose of BMI for each body weight category was calculated as fol - lows21 ,24: 1 for closed category of body weight group, midpoint of lower and upper bound was calculated as the dose of BMI e. 99 divided by 2 ; 2 for open-ended category of body weight group, width of the adjacent interval was used to calculate a lower or upper bound in the lowest or highest group, and then the midpoint was calculated. 19 Definition of outcomes According to the criteria of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists ACOG guidelines,1 PIH was defined as systolic blood pressure of 140 mm Hg or more, or diastolic blood pressure of 90 mm Hg or more, on two occasions at least 4 h apart after 20 gestational weeks in a pregnant woman with a previously normal blood pressure. Preeclampsia was defined as PIH accompanied by the presence of pro - teinuria. 1 Proteinuria was identified as having 300 mg or more per 24 h urine collection, or protein creatinine ratio of 0. 3 or more in a random urine specimen or dipstick reading of 2 if a quantitative measurement is unavailable. 1 Eclampsia was identified as occurrence of seizures and unconsciousness in a pregnant woman with preeclampsia. In this study, the definition of HDP predominantly includes PIH, preeclampsia and eclampsia, which do not include HELLP syndrome, chronic hypertension, and chronic hypertension with superimposed preeclampsia. Moreover, given that the definition of HPD was not consistent across the orig - inal study, the combination of PIH and preeclampsia, and the combination of PIH, preeclampsia, and eclampsia, are considered as HDP in this study. Risk of bias assessment The risk of bias of included cohort studies was assessed by using the Newcastle Ottawa Scale NOS. 25 ,26 This scale includes three key domains for cohort studies: selection of study groups representativeness and ascertainment of cohorts , comparability of groups, and assessment of outcomes including adequacy of follow- up. All included studies were graded on an ordinal scoring scale with a maximum score of nine. Higher score represented better quality of study and lower risk of bias. When a study was awarded a score of 7 or more, 5 or 6, or 5, it was considered a low, moderate, or high risk of bias, respectively.

content_chunk: Statistical analysis In this study, dose-response analysis was conducted to evaluate the association between maternal pre- pregnancy BMI and PIH, preeclampsia, eclampsia and HDP, respectively. The dose-response association non-linear or linear was assessed by random effect meta-analysis performed in two stages. We first esti - mated study-specific slope lines, and then estimated an overall average slope for all included studies, which combined the previous study-specific slope. 27 We employed restricted cubic splines RCS with three knots at the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles of the BMI distribution, in line with established approaches from previous studies,28 ,29 to evaluate linear or non-linear associations. A P value for non-linearity Pn was assessed by testing the null hypothesis that the coeffi - cient of the second spline in RCS was equal to zero. 05 was considered as statistical non-linear dose- response association, otherwise, a linear dose-response association was considered. For non-linear dose- response analyses, RCS was applied by treating BMI as a continuous variable, and a reference point 21. 75 kg m2, the midpoint of the normal bodyweight category 18. 99 kg m2 was set, with its risk fixed at 1. 0, to facilitate interpretation of relative risks across BMI values. For comparison, we also modeled a linear rela - tionship when the test for non-linearity was statistically significant. 19 ,30 The linear dose-response association was estimated by using generalized least-squares GLS method,27 ,31 and the risk of BMI for outcomes was presented as each 5-unit increase in BMI. Between- study heterogeneity was determined by the clinical features, the Cochran Chi-square test and I2 statistic. 32 When I2 50 was defined as significant heteroge - neity. For each outcome, we separately estimate the dose-response association using unadjusted data crude RR cRR and adjusted data aOR. For an individual study, if the number of outcomes was zero in one of the BMI groups, we added 0. 5 to both zero and non-zero groups. These studies that only reported two cate - gories of BMI, were excluded in the primary analyses. Four subgroup analyses were performed: 1 study design prospective vs. retrospective ; 2 multiple gestation singleton vs. unspecified singleton and or multiparas ; 3 geographic location Americas vs. Europe ; and 4 timing of maternal weight measurement pre-pregnancy vs. The statistical difference of the effects be - tween subgroups was tested by means of interaction test. For geographic location subgroup analysis, since the number of studies included in each pooled analysis Articles 4 www. com Vol 86 August, 2025 was less than five, we did not perform dose-response analysis of these studies conducted in Africa or Oce - ania. For timing of maternal weight measurement subgroup analysis, these studies that reported the time of maternal weight measurement during pre- pregnancy or first trimester were classified in first trimester group.

For those studies that did not report an overall effect i. , aOR between BMI and outcomes, but had sub - group analysis results available e. , maternal age 35 and 35 years, early-onset or late-onset preeclampsia , we combined the subgroup specific estimates using a fixed-effects model to generate an overall estimate. 19 ,34 For those studies that did not use normal weight group as reference category to calculate aOR, we recal - culated risk estimates assuming the normal weight group as reference using the method described by Hamling et al. 35 Since limited studies reported the as- sociation between BMI and eclampsia, subgroup and sensitivity analysis were not performed. content_chunk: A significant dose-response association was observed between maternal BMI and all four outcomes, with cRR per 5-unit increase in maternal BMI based on unadjusted data ranged from 1. 73, and aOR based on adjusted data ranged from 1. Several prior meta-analyses have examined the as- sociation between maternal pre-pregnancy BMI and PIH or preeclampsia. 13 18 For example, a meta-analysis published in 2015 showed a significant association be - tween maternal underweight, overweight, and obesity with PIH 5 studies, pooled OR: 0. 61, respectively and preeclampsia 8 studies, pooled OR: 0. 87, respectively in low- and middle- income countries. 13 In 2020, another update meta- analysis has assessed the association between maternal overweight 13 studies, pooled aOR: 1. 71 , and obesity 19 studies, pooled aOR: 2. 48 with preeclamp - sia. 16 These studies have consistently concluded that maternal pre-pregnancy underweight is associated with a lower risk of PIH or preeclampsia, while overweight or obesity is associated with a higher risk. However, due to the limited studies published, the relationship be - tween BMI and eclampsia, HDP remains to be fully elucidated. Moreover, the dose-response association has not been precisely studied. 15,17,18In 2019, an IPD meta-analysis, encompassed 39 cohorts involving 267,270 births, reported the dose- response risk of BMI per 1 kg m2 for PIH aOR: 1. 12 and preeclampsia aOR: 1. 15 However, the scope of that study was limited to data from the American, European, and Oceania regions. Pregnant women in other regions e. , Asia , who exhibit different somatotypes, obesity risk factors, and different recommendations for weight gain during pregnancy,196,197 were not included in that study. By including studies conducted in 6 geographical re- gions and over 40 countries, our study showed the risk aOR of BMI per 1 kg m2 was 1. 14, 30 studies involving 1,634,738 pregnancies for PIH, and 1. 12, 43 studies involving 2,158,040 pregnancies for preeclampsia. Probably due to the low incidence and would require for large sample size, only a few studies evaluated the association between maternal BMI and eclampsia. 39,40,80,141,142,195 Including more than 30 million pregnancies from 2009 to 2018 in the USA, Dongarwar et al. found that maternal underweight was associated with a lower risk of eclampsia aOR: 0. 91 , whereas overweight aOR: 1. 58 and obesity aOR: 2. 50 were associated with a higher risk. 195 By combing all available studies, our results suggested a linear dose- response relationship between maternal BMI and eclampsia cRR for each 5-unit increase in BMI: 1. 53; aOR for each 5-unit increase in BMI: 1. Furthermore, the dose-response relationship be - tween maternal pre-pregnancy BMI and HDP is not fully understood. reported a dose- response relationship between maternal BMI during the first trimester and HDP, with an OR for each 5-unit increase in BMI of 2.

content_chunk: 17 Never - theless, the reliability of the results is challenging to ascertain due to the inadequate literature review only 10 studies with 12,757 participants were included and the absence of methodological descriptions of the dose- response relationship calculations. 17 By incorporating more exhaustive studies and a greater sample size 42 studies with 9,723,366 participants , our study demon - strated a linear dose-response relationship between maternal pre-pregnancy BMI and HDP, with an aOR for each 5-unit increase in BMI of 1. In this study, subgroup analyses showed that the risk of BMI per 5-unit increase for PIH was higher in Asia aOR: 2. 12 than that in Europe aOR: 1. 80 and Americas aOR: 1. Similar region-specific differ - ences were also observed for preeclampsia and overall HDP Figs. 3 and 4 , indicating a modifying effect of geographic location. Although the precise mecha - nisms remain unclear, several factors may contribute to these geographic disparities, including genetic Articles 10 www. com Vol 86 August, 2025 predisposition, racial ethnic differences in suscepti - bility, dietary patterns, socioeconomic status, and healthcare access. For example, prior studies have re- ported that race or ethnicity is independently associ - ated with increased risks of HDP, GDM, and stillbirth. 198 200 Our findings suggest that Asian pop - ulations may particularly benefit from targeted in- terventions such as stricter pre-pregnancy weight management and enhanced clinical monitoring of blood pressure and proteinuria. Further research is essential to clarify these mechanisms and optimize region-specific preventive strategies for HDP. Our results indicated statistical evidence of non- linear relationships between pre-pregnancy BMI and the risks of preeclampsia unadjusted and adjusted analyses and HDP unadjusted analysis. Nevertheless, visual examination revealed largely linear relationships Fig. 2c and d , with a consistent gradual increase in risk across higher BMI levels, and without distinct thresholds or curvilinear patterns such as U-shaped or inverted U-shaped curves, as previously observed in associations with outcomes like preterm birth,201 or fetal death. 19 Despite the statistical non-linearity identified, our findings reinforce the clinical interpretation that higher maternal BMI is consistently associated with increased risk of PIH, preeclampsia, eclampsia, and overall HDP. Maternal pre-pregnancy BMI has been identified as a potential biomarker for a variety of pregnancy complications, as well as for maternal and infant pregnancy outcomes, and even long-term infant outcomes. 8,11 13,202 204 It has been reported that 23. 9 of any pregnancy complication e. , gestational hyper - tension, GDM, preterm birth, small size for gestational age, large size for gestational age were attributable to maternal overweight and obesity. 15 Meanwhile, a lot of studies have showed maternal pre-pregnancy BMI was associated with childhood obesity, type 1 diabetes, psychiatric disorders, and cardio-metabolic outcomes. 202 206 Considering the substantial negative effects of maternal pre-pregnancy overweight and obesity, several clinical guidelines recommend weight loss before conception.

content_chunk: 207 However, evidence from a pragmatic randomized controlled trials RCT indicated that behavioral weight-loss interventions prior to preg - nancy reduced spontaneous pregnancy loss but did not significantly affect risks of HDP, GDM, cesarean de - livery, or preterm birth. 208 Likewise, a meta-analysis of RCTs evaluating lifestyle and or medication-based weight-loss interventions in women planning preg - nancy showed increased pregnancy rates but no sig - nificant impact on live births or miscarriage rates. 209 Thus, the effectiveness of pre-pregnancy weight-loss interventions for reducing adverse maternal-fetal outcomes warrants further investigation. In addition to the extant evidence, we elucidated the dose-response association between maternal pre- pregnancy BMI and HDP, assessing the risk of each BMI unit change and underscoring the clinical impor - tance of maintaining a healthy BMI prior to conception. In cases of pre-pregnancy overweight or obesity, weight control during pregnancy is particularly challenging, and this has been shown to further aggravate adverse obstetric outcomes. 15 Previous study indicated that maternal pre-pregnancy excess bodyweight was more strongly associated with adverse maternal and infant outcomes than excess gestational weight gain. 210 The findings in this study support that pre-pregnancy BMI may be an important focus for preconception coun - seling and subsequent pre-pregnancy weight manage - ment both for women and clinicians. Our findings also support the recommendation of weight loss before conception in several guidelines. 207 However, future studies employing composite outcomes encompassing multiple adverse pregnancy events e. , eclampsia, preterm birth, and maternal near-miss are essential to determine a balanced, evidence-based optimal pre- pregnancy BMI for clinical recommendations. Furthermore, the stronger negative impact of maternal BMI observed in Asian populations suggests that healthcare policies in Asia should prioritize stricter preconception weight management. Pregnant women in this region, particularly those with overweight or obesity, may benefit from intensified pre-pregnancy lifestyle interventions and closer antenatal monitoring of blood pressure and proteinuria. This study has three main strengths. First, to our knowledge, this was the most comprehensive dose- response meta-analysis examining the relationship be - tween maternal pre-pregnancy BMI and gestational hypertension. In addition to PIH and preeclampsia, we also obtained significant dose-response relationships between maternal BMI and eclampsia and HDP, which have received less attention in previous studies. Second, we conducted detailed and comprehensive data anal - ysis, encompassing the utilization of unadjusted and adjusted effects pooled separately, two-stage and one- stage dose-response model, linear and non-linear dose-response model, and multiple categories of sub - group and sensitivity analyses, which demonstrated the reliability of the findings. Third, by including 157 cohort studies conducted in 6 geographical regions and over 40 countries, our findings suggested that the as- sociation between maternal BMI and hypertensive dis - orders of pregnancy was modified by geographical location. This study also had four major limitations. First, pre-pregnancy weight in some included studies was self-reported, while in others, first-trimester maternal weight measurements were used as proxies for pre- pregnancy weight. Both approaches could introduce misclassification bias, potentially resulting in slight inaccuracies in pre-pregnancy BMI.

content_chunk: However, sub - group analyses and meta-regression indicated that this Articles www. com Vol 86 August, 2025 11 potential misclassification had only a minimal effect on the observed association between maternal pre- pregnancy BMI and HDP. Second, there was signifi - cant heterogeneity in pooled analyses of observational studies. Although we conducted several subgroup ana - lyses and meta-regression to explore the sources of heterogeneity and used a random-effects model, this heterogeneity was not fully explained. A variety of other factors may introduce significant heterogeneity, such as participant characteristics e. , race ethnicity , outcome definitions e. , early-onset and late-onset preeclampsia , and parity i. , nulliparity or multi - parity , which require further exploration. Third, vari - ability in adjustment factors across included studies may affect pooled estimates. Not all studies consistently adjusted for potential confounding factors such as maternal age, parity, or comorbidities, introducing heterogeneity. Future meta-analyses incorporating standardized adjustment protocols or individual participant data are needed to improve harmonization and reduce confounding. Fourth, our literature search was conducted up to October, 2023, so more recently published studies were not included in the analysis, which may have a slight influence on the current findings. We conducted a quick search of four elec - tronic databases Pubmed, Web of science, OVID Embase and OVID Medline up to July 12, 2025, using the same search strategy in Appendix S1. Compared to the literature search at October 13, 2023, we identified 1808 additional potentially relevant studies. Using the same ratio of final eligible studies to potentially relevant studies 0. 012, 157 13,185, Supplementary Fig. S1 , we estimate that there are approximately 22 eligible studies among the additional potentially relevant studies. However, considering that this study included 157 cohort studies involving a large sample size of 51,813,975 pregnancies and demonstrated robust find - ings through multiple categories of subgroup and sensitivity analyses, the inclusion of newly published studies is unlikely to substantially alter the overall conclusions. In conclusion, based on more than 50 million pregnancies, significant dose-response relationships were identified between maternal pre-pregnancy BMI and PIH, preeclampsia, eclampsia and HDP. Maternal pre-pregnancy underweight was associated with a lower risk, whereas overweight and obesity were associated with a higher risk of PIH, preeclampsia, eclampsia and HDP. For women who are overweight or obese, given the risk for pregnancy complications and adverse pregnancy outcomes, appropriate weight loss in- terventions should be considered prior to conception. Maternal physical activity during preg- nancy promotes fetal lung development and the newborn s lung function; thus, it could lower asthma risk andaid in asthma prevention. The objective of this study is to determine whether maternal physical activity duringpregnancy is associated with asthma development in the child. Methods: The study population included 963 mother-infant pairs from the prospective Kuopio Birth Cohort study. Data on maternal physical activity during pregnancy, confounding factors, and children s asthma at 5 to 7 years of age were obtained from the Kuopio University Hospital birth registry and questionnaires. Findings: Maternal physical activity during pregnancy, when practiced three or more times per week, was associated with a reduced risk of asthma in the child, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0. 54 95 conﬁdenceinterval 0. The association was stable across a comprehensive set of adjustments, including length of gestation, mode of delivery, and maternal health indicators e. , asthma, smoking,pre-pregnancy body mass index and weight gain during pregnancy, infections, medication, healthy diet,stress , as well as various family environment variables. Conclusions: Maternal physical activity during pregnancy may be associated with marked protection of asthma in childhood and should be studied further as an applicable measure for asthma prevention. CONTEXT AND SIGNIFICANCE Maternal living habits during pregnancy signiﬁcantly impact a child s health and could offer methods to prevent diseases like asthma, which has limited prevention strategies. Maternalexercise provides numerous beneﬁts for both mother and child, including improved newborn lung function. investigated the link between maternal exercise and childhood asthma risk. Their results re- vealed that exercising three or more times per week nearly halved the risk of asthma in children compared to less-frequent exercise. These ﬁndings suggest that promoting maternal exercise during pregnancy could bea valuable strategy in reducing childhood asthma risk. Med 6, 100514, February 14, 2025 ª2024 The Author s. 1 This is an open access article under the CC BY license. ll Asthma is a complex disease that causes a signiﬁcant health burden affecting nearly 10 of the global population. 1In addi- tion to genetic inheritance,2the risk of asthma in offspring may be elevated by various maternal factors, such as prenatal anti- biotic treatments,3smoking,4and overweight. 5Due to the multi- tude of potential causal factors,6the current approach to asthma management revolves around symptom treatment7rather than prevention. The prenatal period encompasses a critical developmental window for the future health of the child, including the risk of asthma development. 8,9Maternal physical activity during preg- nancy has numerous beneﬁcial effects on both the progressionof pregnancy and the well-being of the child. Engaging in prena- tal exercise can decrease maternal gestational weight gain, lowers the risk of cesarean delivery,11and protects against gestational diabetes,12macrosomia,13and preeclampsia. 14 Several of these health parameters related to prenatal exercise can impact childhood health and contribute to the development of asthma. 15 18In a recent study, maternal inactivity during the ﬁrst half of pregnancy was linked to decreased lung function in the newborn,19which is a risk factor for the development of asthma. 20However, whether maternal physical activity during pregnancy is associated with the risk of asthma in childhood is unknown. The World Health Organization WHO and the US Department of Health and Human Services recommend that pregnant women exercise for a minimum of 150 min week, divided over at least 3 days. 21,22These recommendations are generally insuf- ﬁciently met. 23For example, in a Norwegian study, fewer than half 46 of the mothers exercised regularly R3 times per week prior to pregnancy, and as the pregnancy progressed, only 20 of the mothers exercised regularly by the lasttrimester. 24Similar results have been found among Canadian women; only 23 of pregnant women and 34 of non-pregnant women reach the Canadian exercise recommendations. 25 We hypothesize that in addition to reducing the risk of compli- cations during pregnancy and delivery and promoting the well- being of both the mother and the fetus, engaging in physical ac-tivity while pregnant may reduce the risk of offspring asthma. Ouraim here was to test this hypothesis.

No linear dose-response relationship was observed, which aligns with previous ﬁndings between maternal exercise andoffspring lung function. 19We utilized data on physical activity during pregnancy ob- tained from both an open-ended and cate-gorically structured question in two sepa- rate questionnaires ﬁlled out at different points during pregnancy. The answers tothese questions showed a signiﬁcant cor-relation, produced similar effect sizes in relation to asthma both with and without imputing the missing data, and thus mutu-ally validated each other. Within our data- set, we did not observe statistically sig- niﬁcant associations between maternalexercise prior to pregnancy and asthma development in the child. Furthermore, in sensitivity analyses, maternal exercisewas associated with protection from the persistent but not transient early wheezing phenotype and was clearer among atopic infants as indicated bypositive inhalant allergen-speciﬁc IgE levels. To the best of our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst study demon- strating a protective association between maternal physical ac- tivity during pregnancy and later development of childhoodasthma. The protective potential of maternal exercise against asthma development in the child is, however, convergently sup- ported by previous studies. In a study of Norwegian and Swedishchildren, maternal physical inactivity during the ﬁrst half of preg- nancy was linked to reduced lung function in the child at 3 months of age, 19and reduced lung function early in life is asso- ciated with an increased risk of childhood asthma. 20In our study, the strongest protective association against asthma was seen with the exercise frequency of three times per week, and further engagement did not enhance this association. Accord-ingly, based on the late-pregnancy questionnaire, maternal exer- cise of three or more times per week for a minimum duration of 20 min without interruption, experiencing at least slight short-ness of breath and sweating, was associated with decreased asthma risk in the child.

content_chunk: Similarly, in the study of Norwegian and Swedish infants, lung function was improved if the moth-ers had engaged in moderate- to high-intensity exercise of Med 6, 100514, February 14, 2025 5Articlell moderate frequency 120 min week as compared to mothers engaging in no or solely low-intensity exercise. More exercise than this impaired rather than improved the respiratory parameters. 19 The potential mechanisms between maternal physical activity and a lower risk of asthma development in the child remain to be determined. The beneﬁcial inﬂuence on fetal lung function devel-opment through the augmentation of fetal breathing movements seems feasible, 29,30although the evidence regarding this rela- tionship is inconsistent and warrants further research. 31If the biological mechanism of the protective association is the augmentation of fetal breathing movements, then the results would likely be applicable to other populations, although this re-mains to be conﬁrmed. Another plausible explanation could bethat maternal physical activity correlates with overall maternal health, healthy lifestyle habits of the family, including the child af- ter birth, or other obvious confounders such as maternal BMI. However, we were able to test against this hypothesis and demonstrate that the association was independent of a great va- riety of potential confounders, including healthy nutrition, medi-cation, infections and stress during pregnancy, BMI and weight gain during pregnancy, socioeconomic status, breastfeeding, smoking, the child s own attendance at sports practices, orparental asthma. Similarly, several variables associated withthe family and the living environment such as number of previous deliveries, pet ownership, or residential type had no inﬂuence on the results. Risk of preterm labor could also inﬂuence maternalphysical activity and be associated with asthma. 32However, neither gestational weight nor duration of gestation at birth affected the association, excluding the possible confoundingby preterm delivery fears. Confounding by genetic predisposi- tion seems also unlikely since adjustment with maternal or paternal asthma had no inﬂuence on the protective association. Maternal stress, gestational weight gain, and the child s birth weight are factors that could both be affected by maternal phys- ical activity and affect the child s asthma risk. 15,33 37They could, therefore, be potential mediators of the association, but notably,no mediation effect was seen. Maternal low-grade inﬂammation during pregnancy could similarly be a mediator, but we did not have biomarkers of low-grade inﬂammation determined, andthus, we could not properly address this. However, low-gradeinﬂammation has been shown to correlate with factors such as maternal weight gain, healthy nutrition, smoking, socioeconomic status, and caesarean section, 38and none of these inﬂuenced the association between maternal exercise during pregnancy and the child s asthma. The inﬂuence of maternal physical activ- ity on fetal immunological development is nonetheless anotherplausible mechanism that should be addressed in further studies. In our sensitivity analyses, the association between maternal physical activity and asthma was somewhat stronger,with the presence of at least moderate levels 0. 7 kU L of inha-lation allergen-speciﬁc IgE in serum at 5 years of age, but no direct association was seen between maternal exercise and allergic sensitization in children.

content_chunk: Accordingly, the sensitivity ana-lyses also indicated that maternal exercise during pregnancy inﬂuenced only persistent but not transient wheezing phenotype; the latter is often associated with respiratory infections and theformer with atopic predisposition. 39The sample sizes in these sensitivity analyses were limited, and whether maternal physical activity during pregnancy has differential effects on allergic vs. non-allergic asthma remains to be conﬁrmed by future studies. Our study suggests that maternal exercise at least three times per week may reduce the risk of asthma in children. This adds tothe present knowledge on the positive overall impact of prenatalexercise on child health, 40and aligns with the WHO recommen- dation of 150 min of maternal exercise distributed throughout the week during pregnancy. 22Thus, in addition to preventing preg- nancy and delivery complications and improving maternal and fetal health, advocating adherence to these guidelines could also promote reduced prevalence of asthma in children. Largerstudies in different countries with objective measurements of maternal physical activity during pregnancy e. , with an accel- erometer and interventions are called for to clarify the relation-ship of exercise mode, intensity, and frequencies on childasthma risk, as well as the causal relationship. Limitations of the study The strengths of this study include the longitudinal, population-based design; control over the comprehensive list of potential confounders; and information on maternal physical activity from two sources for the same individuals. However, there aresome limitations in the present study. One potential limitation is the possibility of interpreting differently what type of activity and duration constitutes a physical activity session in the birthregistry data. However, that question was followed by anopen-ended question that asked participants to describe the ac- tivity. The majority of answers reﬂected intentional physical ac- tivity such as jogging, muscle strengthening, and group exerciseclasses or working out at home, with estimated Metabolic Equiv- alent Task scores ranging from 3 to 10. 41Furthermore, the re- sponses to the birth registry exercise frequency question were Figure 2. Ana-lyses against asthma yielded highly comparable results utilizing either source. Our sensitivity analyses did not indicate a marked difference in the signiﬁcance of exercise frequency at differenttrimesters. In addition, sensitivity analyses showed no effect of exercise on transient wheezing but did indicate clearer effects on persistent wheezing and asthma associated with inhalantallergen sensitization. However, our study was not designed to properly answer these questions, and they should therefore be addressed in future studies. The study sample size was modest,but the signiﬁcant ﬁndings with the binary variables on maternalphysical activity, maternal and paternal asthma, and offspring gender and the risk of asthma in children support sufﬁcient sta- tistical power.

content_chunk: 10 Med 6, 100514, February 14, 2025Articlell STAR METHODS Study population and design The study population included 963 mother-child pairs from the Kuopio Birth Cohort KuBiCo , which is described in detail in the articleby Huuskonen et al. 42The KuBiCo study was designed to investigate the impact of prenatal exposures on the health of mothers and their children in Eastern Finland region among mothers giving birth in the Kuopio University Hospital KUH. All pregnant women expected to deliver in the KUH are invited to participate the study without exclusion criteria. The inclusion criteria for the current studypopulation were singleton pregnancy, birth between 2012 and 2017, available information on exercise during pregnancy and child s asthma status at 5, 6 or 7 years of age Figure 1. As described below and in Table S1 , data on outcome variables, physical activity, and potential confounders and covariates were derived from KUH birth registry, questionnaire on environmental factors ﬁlled in early-pregnancy, late-pregnancy questionnaire, and Food Frequency Questionnaire FFQ ﬁlled in during the last trimester of the preg- nancy, and from yearly follow-up questionnaires on child health from 1 to 7 years of age. The KUH birth registry is a computerized database compiled by the KUH Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology. It includes data from an electronic questionnaire on themothers lifestyle habits, pregnancy parameters, and environmental factors. The KuBiCo study and its follow-ups have beenapproved in 2011 by the Research Ethics Committee of Hospital District of Central Finland, in Jyva skyla 18U 2011. An informed consent of the participation to the KuBiCo study was ﬁlled in by mothers during their ﬁrst visit at the maternity clinic. Gender of the mother giving birth was not collected, and the term woman or women is used to refer to adult participant giving birth. Using the term woman or women is not intended to exclude participants who do not identify as cisgender women. The child s gender was analyzed binarily, based on the biological sex assigned at birth by a healthcare professional. The information on ancestry, race, or ethnicity of the study participants was not speciﬁed, since the study participants were recruited during their routine visit in theFinnish healthcare system s universally accessible prenatal care. In principle, all pregnant individuals are monitored by the public healthcare system regardless of ancestry, race, or ethnicity, and therefore these factors are not speciﬁed. Asthma and IgE-levels in the child and maternal physical activity The primary health outcome of the study was childhood asthma, which was deﬁned as doctor diagnosis ever reported in the 5-, 6-, or7-year KuBiCo follow-up questionnaire. In sensitivity analyses we also utilized as secondary health outcomes transient and persistent wheezing. Transient wheezing was deﬁned as parent-reported wheezing from 1 to 4 years without doctor diagnosis of asthma from 5 to 7 years. Persistent wheezing was deﬁned as parent-reported wheezing from 1 to 4 years with doctor diagnosis of asthma from 5 to7 years.

Statistical analyses on health outcomes All statistical analyses were performed using SAS Enterprise Guide 8. The association between maternal physical activity and asthma in the child was studied with logistic regression models PROC LOGISTIC statement. Thesemodels were adjusted as per a priori decision for maternal asthma, smoking, and pre-pregnancy BMI, based on their established link with the risk on child s asthma 28,43,44and the potential correlation with maternal exercise. We utilized the largest possible study pop- ulation in all analyses without approximation of missing data on variables used for adjustments. Mothers pre-pregnancy BMI wascalculated by taking the ratio of weight in kilograms to the square of height in meters, using average weight and height scores derivedfrom the KUH birth registry and late-pregnancy questionnaire. Maternal active smoking prior to pregnancy was chosen to indicate maternal smoking as it had stronger predisposing association with asthma than active or passive smoking during pregnancy in this study, perhaps due to underreporting of smoking during pregnancy. The risk of childhood asthma associated with maternal activesmoking before pregnancy was OR 1. In contrast, the risk associated with maternal active or passive smoking during pregnancy was OR 0. Adjusted analyses were controlled for maternal pre-pregnancy BMI and maternal asthma. BMI was categorized in three groups: under- BMI 18. 5 BMI 25 , and overweight BMI R25 , with thresholds deﬁned by WHO. 45In addition to the a priori selected adjustments, the confounding effect of several other variables on the association be- tween maternal physical activity during pregnancy and asthma in the child were tested using the change-in-estimate criterion with10 cutoff. The tested variables included maternal age at delivery and infections, stress, nutrition and use of medication during preg- nancy, gestational age, mode of delivery, breastfeeding, and child s birth weight and sex as well as variables related to the lifestyle and family environment such as child attendance to supervised sports, pet ownership, and residential area. Please see Table S1 for the complete list, description, and origin of the tested variables. Child s birth weight was tested trichotomized based on low birthweight 2500 g 46and high birth weight 4000 g. 47Gestational weight gain, deﬁned as the difference between pre-delivery weight and pre-pregnancy weight, was normalized relative to maternal pre-pregnancy BMI. 48Causal mediation analysis was used to assess whether the association between maternal physical activity during pregnancy and asthma in the child was mediated by birth weight,maternal stress, or weight gain during pregnancy PROC CAUSALMED statement. content_chunk: Protocol Integ ration of a Patient-Centered mHealth Intervention Suppor t-Moms Into Routine Antenatal Care to Impro ve Mater nal Health Among Pregnant Women in Southw ester n Uganda: Protocol for a Randomiz ed Controlled Trial Esther Cath yln Atukunda1, PhD; Godfre y Rwambuka Mugyen yi1, MD; Jessica E Haberer2, MD, MS; Mark J Siedner2, MPH, MD; Angella Musiimenta1, PhD; Josephine N Najjuma1, MSN; Celestino Obua1, PhD; Lynn T Matthe ws3, MD 1Mbarara University of Science and Technology , Mbarara, Uganda 2Department of Medicine and Center for Global Health, Harv ard Medical School, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, United States 3Division of Infectious Diseases, School of Medicine, University of Alabama at Birmingham, Birmingham, AL, United States Corr esponding Author: Esther Cath yln Atukunda, PhD Mbarara University of Science and Technology P. O Box 1410 Mbarara Uganda Phone: 256 702949832 Email: Abstr act Backgr ound: Mobile health mHealth interv entions that leverage social support SS can impro ve partner involvement and pregnanc y experiences and promote antenatal care ANC attendance and skilled births. In our previous studies, we used behavioral frame works to develop a user-centered mHealth-based, audio SMS text messaging app to support pregnant individuals to use maternity care services in rural Uganda Support-Moms app. In our pilot study , we observ ed high interv ention uptak e, acceptability , and feasibility , as well as increased ANC attendance and skilled births. Objecti ve: With the promising pilot data, we propose a type 1 hybrid implementation-ef fectiveness trial to test if this novel patient-centered automated and customized mHealth-based SS interv ention is effective and cost-ef fective enough to warrant future large-scale implementation into Uganda s routine maternity care. Methods: We will physically recruit 824 pregnant women at 20 weeks of gestation living in Mbarara and Mitooma districts, southwestern Uganda, and randomize them 1:1 to recei ve standard of care or the Support-Moms app, with at least 2 of their identif ied social supporters. Our primary outcome will be the proportion of skilled births. Secondary outcomes will include number of ANC visits strong , strong institution-based delivery, mode of infant delivery, preterm birth, birth weight, SS, obstetric complications, and deaths maternal, fetal, and newborn. We will assess other implementation, service, and client outcomes through study records, the mHealth platform, and questionnaires with all women in the interv ention, their social supporters, health care providers HCPs , and managers from participating facilities. We will conduct face-to-f ace in-depth exit intervie ws with 30 purposi vely selected interv ention participants and 15 facility HCPs and managers to explore implementation strate gies for scale-up. Annual maternity resource allocations, costs, number of ANC visits, and deliveries will be assessed from facility records up to 36 months after implementation. We will estimate incremental cost-ef fectiveness ratios concerning cost per additional HCP-led delivery, per death averted, and per quality-adjusted life year gained as cost-ef fectiveness measures. Results: This study was funded in September 2023.

Conclusions: We are testing the feasibility , acceptability , and cost-ef fectiveness of implementing Support-Moms into routine maternity care from individual and facility perspecti ves. Over 99 of infant deaths also occur in LMICs 2,3. Persistently high maternal mortality ratios MMRs in LMICs are partly attrib uted to challenges accessing care, with undiagnosed or poorly managed pregnanc y-related complications from direct or indirect causes 1. Recurrence risks of fatal episodes increase exponentially among women who survi ve previous fatal episodes unless preventive measures for early detection and monitoring throughout the perinatal period are adopted 2,4-6. Antenatal care ANC prevents perinatal and maternal morbidity and mortality by early detection and treatment of prenatal complications and identifying women at high risk to ensure delivery in skilled settings 7-11. ANC supports women, their families, and communities to navigate challenges at a critical time during pregnanc y; debunks misconceptions; increases information transfer; and can motivate women to seek facility delivery and care 9. The World Health Organization WHO and other authorities have called for urgent evaluation of adaptable and conte xt-specif ic health solutions to promote ANC uptak e and maternity services to reduce maternal and early childhood mortality and morbidity 9,11-14. Identifying and scaling up interv entions that impro ve access to and the use of available health care in pregnanc y and childbirth has the potential to prevent 823,000 stillbirths, 1,145,000 neonatal deaths, and 166,000 maternal deaths annually in the 75 highest-b urden countries 2,4-6.

content_chunk: Despite expanded capacity to increase the number of skilled birth attendants at community facilities, Ugandan women still have low rates of ANC use and skilled births, resulting in one of the highest MMR 189 100,000 and perinatal mortality rates 34 deaths 1000 births in the world 15. Women s lack of information, social support SS , financial independence for emotional and economic provisions, decision-making autonomy regarding childbirth, birth preparedness, and percei ved need for maternity care services are important challenges to using available maternity services in these settings 1,16-19. One analysis showed that women at risk of unskilled home births needed relevant and conte xt-specif ic strate gies to encourage ANC attendance and skilled delivery 20. The high cost of MMR highlights the need for adaptable interv entions that boost ANC and maternity services use to reduce MMR and early childhood deaths 12. SS is an important pillar of health promotion that has been directly linked to health care seeking behavior, infant care practices among mothers, and HIV care in sub-Saharan Africa SSA 21-25. SS can mitig ate structural and physical barriers to health care access at individual and societal levels, including facilitating self-ef ficacy to complete positi ve health behaviors 26-28. Spouses, relati ves, and friends have been the sources of SS among individuals living with HIV in SSA 23-25. Community health workers CHWs can provide or promote additional SS during pregnanc y, leading to better health outcomes 29,30. Village health teams VHTs , which comprise community members identif ied by their community who are trained on major health programs, impro ve timely care seeking for facility delivery 31-35. VHTs have historically focused on the treatment of infectious diseases, such as malaria, pneumonia, and tuberculosis 35. Their role as an additional resource for peripartum women has not been harnessed. Therefore, social netw ork involvement not only addresses individual but also family- and societal- or community-le vel barriers to care in a setting with modest availability of health centers HCs providing needed services 17,25,36-38. Mobile health mHealth interv entions can be practical, effective, and scalable tools to impro ve maternal health care delivery and outcomes. Many SMS text messaging and other mHealth interv entions can help individuals internalize risks and potential impact of various medical conditions as well as the needs and benef its of health services 11,13. mHealth approaches can empo wer individuals to seek help, address specif ic health concerns, strengthen informed decision-making, and impro ve outcomes in the perinatal period 14,39. Scheduled SMS reminders and telephone voice messaging approaches can enable people to increase control over their health by impro ving knowledge transfer , learning, and comprehension. These gains may impro ve the percei ved need to use available services, especially when interv entions are well directed and executed to provide accurate and relevant information on the promoted behavior 11,13,14,25,39-42.

content_chunk: Several studies have found that mobile phone based messages can be motivational as a source of individual or family SS 43 , cues to action 44 , or to challenge societal negative beliefs 45. Mobile phone interv entions have also been shown to increase ANC attendance 46,47 , institutional delivery 48,49 and vaccination rates such as tetanus toxoid 11,49. mHealth interv entions that specif ically bolster SS can impro ve pregnanc y experiences by decreasing anxiety and depression 50-53 and increasing perinatal bonding 52 and communication within social netw orks 53. These benef its are mediated by promoting existing family structure and social netw orks, which in turn foster financial and emotional coping mechanisms to enable women to overcome socioeconomic and JMIR Res Protoc 2025 vol. or g 2025 1 e67049 page number not for citation purposes Atukunda et al JMIR RESEARCH PROTOCOLS XSL FO RenderX physical barriers to care, such as food insecurity , transportation, and provision of delegated service to overcome competing priorities 25,53-55. Community and social netw ork engagements toward mobilization of resources to enable health care access are practical, scalable, and sustainable approaches toward participatory health care financing and use 56. Although SMS alone is a convenient and lower cost approach to support health care interv entions with higher delivery success, the provision of multiple messaging options, such as voice messages and social netw orks involvement, has been crucial to extend reach beyond the individual literate personal phone owners in SSA 57,58. Health awareness and motivating health care use are key elements of developing effective behavior change interv entions 59. However, mHealth interv entions are not always effective in impro ving health care and use. Whereas the failure of impact has been attrib uted to a mismatch between the function, adaptability , and need for mHealth interv entions in some settings 11,14 , end-user designs that use iterati ve approaches in app development can impro ve health care service use 60. In a formati ve study , we observ ed that knowledge gaps influenced women s past and future decisions to not attend ANC and pursue unskilled home births 17,20. Women were also largely dependent on their signif icant others for economic provisions, which, together with the existing gender and traditional norms, limited women s ability and freedom to make family or health decisions to seek skilled care. Therefore, we developed an mHealth-based SS interv ention the Support-Moms interv ention using the health care use model by Andersen 61 that incorporates predisposing-, enabling-, and need-based factors to impro ve interv ention uptak e and service use. We then considered the frame work by Bendix en et al 62 to personalize the information and tailor the system for our targeted end users. Our novel mHealth app was developed as part of a career development award NIH-K43TW011004. This app or interv ention was compatible with local regular mobile phone types, providing varying text and audio delivery mediums for individuals who were literate and who were not.

content_chunk: In a randomized 3-arm pilot study N 120 pregnant women who had not presented for ANC by their second trimester were equally randomized to recei ve 1 standard of care, which is the routine ANC information given at the maternity centers control ; 2 scheduled SMS audio messages from the final messaging prototype scheduled messaging SM ; and 3 SM, plus social supporter engagement through SMS SS 63. We observ ed high interv ention acceptability and feasibility , with 80 of women recei ving 85 of intended messages within 1 hour. Over 95 of women found the app easy to use and compatible with their existing messaging programs; they also reported that the messages were useful and engaging and would strongly recommend the interv ention to others. Nearly all women in the SS arm 39 40, 98 had a skilled delivery compared to 78 31 40 and 70 28 40 of the women in the SM and control groups, respecti vely. All women whose social supporters were engaged on the app SS arm: 40 40, 100 attended 4 ANC visits, compared to 83 33 40 and 50 20 40 of the women in the SM and control groups, respecti vely. Fewer women 8 40, 20 in the SS arm missedany visits due to the lack of transportation compared to 58 23 40 and 68 27 40 of the women in the SM and control groups, respecti vely. In addition, fewer maternal or fetal complications 3 40, 8 were reported in the SS arm compared to 13 5 40 and 25 10 40 complications in the SM and control groups, respecti vely. Using the Duke-Uni versity of North Carolina UNC Functional Social Support scale 64 , women in the SS arm reported impro ved SS median 3. 8 in the SM and control arms, respecti vely score ranges from 1 to 4, and 4 indicates high levels of SS. In qualitati ve intervie ws, all women described the interv ention as useful, actionable, and easy to use; tailored health information helped them to learn, internalize, and comprehend ANC and skilled delivery benef its, strengthening their informed decision-making as they were reportedly able to easily share and discuss information with their signif icant others, who in turn committed to providing them the needed support to prepare and seek help. Women also expressed that the involvement of their signif icant others within a friendly , trusted, and familiar environment helped them to mobilize needed support during pregnanc y. Involving both health care providers HCPs and end users in characterizing, developing, and formulating the mHealth interv ention allowed its tailoring to their preferences.

content_chunk: Given the success in our pilot work where 78 93 120 of the women used feature phones and promising preliminary efficacy data presented earlier 36,63 , the next logical step was to assess the effectiveness, implementation, and scalability of such multiple messaging strate gies to impro ve care access in SSA, where the conte xtual factors that drive successful interv entions differ, but the public health impact of such interv entions is likely to be the greatest 65. Objecti ves We now propose a type 1 hybrid implementation-ef fectiveness trial to evaluate and implement this interv ention into routine care. We will test the effectiveness of the interv ention in a randomized controlled trial aim 1. We will apply the implementation outcomes frame work by Proctor et al 66 to evaluate implementation, service, and client outcomes and conduct in-depth intervie ws with users and key stakeholders to conte xtualize or clarify these outcomes as well as explore implementation strate gies for future scale-up using the Consolidated Frame work for Implementation Research CFIR; aim 2. We will then assess the costs and cost-ef fectiveness of implementing the Support-Moms interv ention into routine care aim 3. We hypothesize that implementing Support-Moms will be an effective and cost-ef fective strate gy to impro ve maternity service use. Methods Study Overview We propose to evaluate the effectiveness and implementation of the Support-Moms app into routine care. We hypothesize that Support-Moms will impro ve maternity service use and reduce the MMR when integrated into routine care. We will test the effectiveness of the Support-Moms interv ention in a randomized controlled design aim 1 ; evaluate interv ention JMIR Res Protoc 2025 vol. or g 2025 1 e67049 page number not for citation purposes Atukunda et al JMIR RESEARCH PROTOCOLS XSL FO RenderX implementation using the implementation outcomes frame work by Proctor et al 66 , as outlined in Figure 1 aim 2 ; and then refine implementation strate gies for future scale-up using the CFIR, as outlined in subsequent sections 67. We will assess the cost and cost-ef fectiveness of implementing this interv ention into routine care and its implication for sustainability aim 3. These outcomes will serve as indicators of implementation success or necessary preconditions for attaining desired service outcomes for women in rural, resource-limited settings. This will enable us to identify practical, conte xt-specif ic, and actionable strate gies for achie ving optimal implementation effectiveness at a low cost. The interv ention strate gies weredeveloped in our pilot work together with facility HCPs. In the cost-ef fectiveness analysis, if Support-Moms and standard of care are found to have equivalent effectiveness, we will conduct a cost-minimization analysis where only the cost of Support-Moms per participant will be estimated and reported no incremental cost-ef fectiveness ratios ICERs will be calculated. This alternati ve approach would remain informati ve to the polic y makers and stakeholders in maternity service use.

content_chunk: Notably , simultaneous assessment is warranted given the 1 strong preliminary evidence, 2 relati vely low investment needed for costing, and 3 overall efficienc y of our proposed type 1 hybrid effectiveness-implementation trial approach. Modif ied conceptual frame work by Proctor et al 66 for implementation and evaluation. Study Setting Uganda s public health system is organized into 7 tiers with national and regional referral hospitals, general district hospitals, and 4 levels of community HCs. Staffing and available services vary across the 4 levels; HC3 carry out vaginal deliveries, whereas HC1 and HC2 serve as low-resource referral units. HC4s and hospitals conduct normal and cesarean deliveries and have ambulances and blood transfusion services 68. Private HCPs operate in parallel to the public health system to provide maternal health care. Mbarara District is located approximately 270 km southwest of the capital, Kampala 69. Mbarara District hosts a regional referral hospital that serves the southwestern region Mitooma district inclusi ve ; most deliveries are high risk 70. Mitooma District borders Congo and is situated approximately 370 km southwest of the capital 71. These 2sites were selected for this research based on their geographic, sociocultural, and institutional diversity and high maternal mortality and morbidity data Table 1presents more details. Both districts have publicly funded and operated facilities with an active maternity care unit. Participants may be seen at any of the maternity sites in these 2 districts or other neighboring districts Table 1 , with recruitment and follow-up organized through CHWs. This consideration, plus the diversity of the settings and the study population, has potential for generalizability to similar settings. The local economy of these 2 districts is also largely based on subsistence agriculture, with both food and water insecurity being common 72,73 ; ANC attendance of 4 visits is still at 58 , and the skilled facility delivery rate is approximately 70. content_chunk: Consenting participants will be randomized 1:1 at enrollment to standard of care Ministry of Health MOH guidelines based routine care and information giving, n 412, 50 versus the Support-Moms interv ention group n 412, 50. We will identify , screen, and enroll people through the existing CHWs or VHT structure from areas within a 10 km radius of all publicly funded maternity centers across Mbarara and Mitooma districts, who have not yet presented for ANC by the beginning of their second trimester. We will power the study to test the superiority of the Support-Moms interv ention for our primary effectiveness outcome: HCP-led skilled birth delivery. Secondary outcomes will include 1 number of ANC visits, 2 institution-based delivery, 3 SS, 4 mode of infant delivery, 5 all deaths maternal, fetal, and newborn , 6 preterm birth, 7 birth weight, 8 breastfeeding, 9 completion of postnatal care, and 10 complications of pregnanc y and childbirth eg, obstructed labor , ruptured uterus, need for neonatal or maternal resuscitation or assisted ventilation, severe preeclampsia or eclampsia, postpartum hemorrhage, maternal or newborn sepsis, and other infections. Recruitment and Enrollment of Study Participants We will include individuals who 1 are in the first trimester of pregnanc y and have not yet presented for ANC, 2 reside in the catchment area of a study HC, 3 are emancipated minors and adults aged 18 years, 4 report access to a cell phone with reception in their home, 5 are able to identify at least 2 social supporters living within the study districts, and 6 are able to provide consent. Notably in our pilot study , 95 of screenedindividuals had access to a cell phone, and all were able to identify at least 2 social supporters living within their communities 63. We will track the exclusion rates to inform generalizability. CHWs will notify study research assistants RAs about potentially eligible participants, who will then contact and seek written informed consent and assent for emancipated minors ie, those aged 18 years and pregnant before enrollment into the study. Participants will be asked to identify 2 individuals from their existing SS netw ork with whom they have had stable, long-term relationships and belie ve they would be available to help them during the pregnanc y and study follow-up period. Eligible social supporters will include spouses, relati ves, CHWs, and friends 23-25 aged 18 years; who are aware that the study participant is pregnant; and who own a cell phone for personal use with reported reliable reception. Potential social supporters will be excluded from the study if they are unable to use SMS or are unwilling to receive SMS notifications, as this was identif ied as a barrier in the pilot study. In the pilot study , one of the eligible social supporters identif ied by women included a spouse 75 , friend 38 , sibling 10 , parent 53 , and a CHW 25 , and we expect a similar distrib ution in the trial.

content_chunk: There will be no gender exclusion criteria for social supporters. We will emphasize the selection of an existing partner , who is aware of the pregnanc y, as one of the social supporters. This was not a problem in our pilot study , as most women were able to suggest a partner as a potential social supporter , alongside a friend, sibling, parent, or CHW. A few partners were excluded because they did not own a cell phone for personal use 5 40, 13 or were not aware of the pregnanc y 5 40, 13. All other eligible social supporters that were identif ied by participants in the social supporter arm 80 80, 100 were successfully enrolled and completed study procedures. RAs will contact social supporters from the interv ention arm within 2 weeks of the enrollment of pregnant women to confirm an active relationship at the time of their JMIR Res Protoc 2025 vol. or g 2025 1 e67049 page number not for citation purposes Atukunda et al JMIR RESEARCH PROTOCOLS XSL FO RenderX enrollment. Eligible social supporters will be offered an explanation of the study procedures and an opportunity to participate in informed consent. The study nurse will inform consenting social supporters about the objecti ves of ANC and skilled delivery as well as danger signs during pregnanc y using standard MOH and WHO guidelines 9,74. Randomization Before the study initiation, the study statistician will generate a randomization table, inaccessible by other study team members, and lock it and store it in the REDCap Research Electronic Data Capture; Vanderbilt University study database. Participants will be stratif ied according to district and HC level and randomly assigned to either interv ention or control arms in a ratio of 1:1 in blocks of 10. RAs will be informed of the arm assignment by the REDCap module after consent and at the time of enrollment. Study participants in the control group will recei ve MOH guidelines based routine care and information giving. The interv ention group will recei ve the interv ention described in the next section. Inter vention Delivery and Components The final messaging prototype that includes tailored SMS and audio health information described earlier will be delivered by the Support-Moms app developed through a partnership with iStreams-Ug anda, an app development compan y based in Mbarara that developed the app, and with an existing mHealth platform 75. The unique multimedia design allows women to be registered on the platform and be track ed throughout pregnanc y and the postpartum period. Enrolled women recei ve automated and scheduled SMS text messages, reminders, and notifications about upcoming appointments as well as informational voice messages in their preferred language. The app includes a data collection platform and stores information submitted in real time directly from the participant s phone, thus allowing managers to access up-to-date data on process measures eg, automated SMS text messages sent and accessed as well as interv ention delivery and health outcomes.

content_chunk: Fixed SMS data are stored in a secure cloud, which is Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act HIPAA compliant. iStreams-Ug anda works in partnership with Africa s Talking, a platform that facilitates access to a telco infrastructure that uses automated SMS, voice, airtime, and other applicationprogramming interf aces mechanisms tested and successfully used during our pilot study. This automated technology for SMS 23,25 and calls 36,63 has also been used for other studies in Uganda. Both SMS and audio messages will be delivered at participants preferred time and day of the week for free to optimize interv ention delivery. A weekly SMS reminder on the impending ANC appointment and expected date of delivery at their preferred time and day of the week, plus a day before the scheduled ANC visit, will be sent to study participants. Social supporters will recei ve weekly SMS notifications to motivate the pregnant women participants to be present for scheduled ANC visits during the pregnanc y as well as for delivery. Notif ications to the 2 preidentif ied social supporters will provide information about the upcoming ANC visits and delivery due date during the study follow-up period. ANC appointment dates will automatically be generated based on the provided LNMP and MOH guidelines 74 at enrollment. Social supporters will be able to personalize the SMS content at enrollment the default message will be This is your reminder to assist your friend XXX attend her upcoming ANC visit due soon. They will also be advised to assist study participants with problems that may affect ANC attendance or facility delivery. The interv ention is designed to build on existing supporti ve relationships of study participants within their communities. All women and their social supporters will recei ve all accredited messages included in this app for at least 4 months, including the standard routine care provided at the community maternity centers. content_chunk: For our primary effectiveness outcome, HCP-led skilled birth delivery, we will fit a multi variable logistic regression model, with study arm as the predictor of interest, and age, high-risk pregnanc y, and health facility at enrollment as a priori additional variables in the model, due to their strong association with the selected outcome 70,90,91. In our primary intention-to-treat model, we will consider women with missing outcome data, after home visits and next of kin intervie ws, as presumed to have not recei ved skilled birth ie, there will be no missing outcome data in our primary analysis. In sensiti vity analyses, we will 1 repeat the analysis after excluding women with missing outcome data and 2 include additional potential confounders in the model that may have persisted despite individual randomization eg, number of previous deliveries at a facility , socioeconomic status, distance to facility , history of facility delivery, food insecurity , alcohol JMIR Res Protoc 2025 vol. or g 2025 1 e67049 page number not for citation purposes Atukunda et al JMIR RESEARCH PROTOCOLS XSL FO RenderX use, and depression. Although not designed to detect a difference, we will also explore additional secondary outcomes, including 1 number of ANC visits completed, 2 mode of infant delivery, 3 institution-based delivery, 4 presence of one or more birth complications, 5 child mortality , 6 maternal mortality , 7 preterm birth, 8 birth weight, 9 completion of postnatal care, 10 SS, and 11 initiation of breastfeeding. Both our pilot data and other similar studies estimate that 70 of the women in Uganda deliver with a skilled attendant 15,48,49. Finally , we will explore the role of SS as a moderating effect of the interv ention through a prespecif ied stratif ied analysis among women in the upper versus lower half of SS in the cohort, as measured by the Duke-UNC Functional Social Support Scale 64. To test our primary effectiveness hypothesis, allowing for a 2-sided type I error of 5 , 90 power, and assuming a 5 loss to follow-up, we will require 824 participants to detect a 10 difference in HCP-led skilled birth delivery between arms. Data analysis will be conducted using Stata version 17; StataCorp LLC. The findings will be presented as descripti ve statistics, scatter plots, and graphs; statistical signif icance will be considered at P. While wewill ensure completed data are collected through timely cleaning and REDCap prompts, we will still be able to detect the same effect in the primary outcome with the power of 85 in the unlik ely event that we lost up to 18 of the records due to missing data.
