content_chunk: During preeclampsia, these cells present with a senescent phenotype and increased endog - enous superoxide production. Interestingly, hematopoietic stem cells from cord blood display similar characteristics during preeclampsia, with reduced colony-forming capac - ity, causing the authors to conclude that cord blood banking is not suitable for mothers with preeclampsia 87. Whether the fetal cells that are transferred to the mother during pre - eclampsia also possess these undesired properties is cur - rently unknown, but it is plausible considering they likely originate from the same populations that were examined in the studies mentioned above 85 87. This process could thereby also impact stage 2 endothelial dysfunction and inflammation in the mother. Of relevance in the context of the second stage of pre - eclampsia development, functional mesenchymal stem cells of fetal origin may have a positive systemic effect on biological function has revealed that these cells are not only multipotent, but also hold regenerative potential through rejuvenating paracrine signalling 79. In fact, Caplan recently wrote a paper urging that mesenchymal stem cells be renamed to medicinal signalling cells 80 keeping the commonly used abbreviation MSC arguing that they do not behave as stem cells in vivo 81. Instead, he argues, their main function is secretory and it is rather the resident stem cells that are responsible for reconstructing and repair - ing injured or dysfunctional tissues in response to trophic factors released by the mesenchymal stem cells 82. As it turns out, this quality may have profound implications for pregnancy complications both locally in the placenta, cor - responding to the first stage in the two-stage model, and sys - temically in the mother, corresponding to the second stage. In the context of stage 1 placental dysfunction, cho - rionic plate-derived mesenchymal stem cells have been shown to significantly increase the invasive properties of trophoblasts in vitro, an essential function for physiologic pregnancy development 83. Interestingly, simply apply - ing supernatant from umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells increased trophoblast migration 84 , demonstrat - ing that the positive effect is indeed likely due to paracrine signaling. The authors of both these papers postulate that mesenchymal stem cells could act as treatment for placen - tal dysfunction and placenta-related diseases 83, 84. content_chunk: Interest - ingly, most Tregs in the decidua are not fetus-specific 103 and while miscarriage is associated with lower overall Treg cell numbers, and thereby a reduction in the absolute number of fetus-specific maternal Tregs, the proportion of clonally expanded fetus-specific Tregs is similar to what is observed in healthy, successful pregnancies 104. In contrast, pre - eclampsia is associated with reduced clonal expansion of fetus-specific Tregs relative to the total number of decidual Tregs 104. It has been proposed that the observed decrease in maternal Tregs in preeclampsia may be due to them having a senescent phenotype associated with apoptosis 105, 106 , poor proliferative potential and functional impairment 107, 108. Hypothetically, the maternal immune system would be less equipped to downregulate a fetus-specific maternal effector cell response to the increased amounts of circulat - ing fetal microchimerism associated with preeclampsia. The fetal immune system is also exposed to allogeneic maternal antigens during pregnancy. Though increased maternal microchimerism in the setting of preterm labor was associated with an increase in fetal central memory T cells a subtype of effector T cells , the levels of fetal Tregs remained the same 74 , suggesting that fetal tolerance to non-inherited alleles may be acquired even in preterm labor as has been shown in healthy pregnancies. Specifically, the fetal Tregs that mediate tolerance towards non-inherited maternal antigens are generated when maternal cells cross the placenta and home to fetal lymph nodes Fig. However, like other CD4 T cells, Tregs require low-level antigen stimulation for long-term persistence 110 , and it has been proposed that this is achieved through the presence of maternal microchimeric cells residing in immune tissues 109. This is in line with the findings of higher success rates in solid organ 111 and bone marrow 112 transplantation when the donor alloantigens and non-inherited maternal alleles overlap. Furthermore, maintained tolerance to non- inherited maternal alleles may partly explain the observed protection against preeclampsia associated with maternal proband microchimerism during pregnancy 29. Mouse studies by Sing Sing Way s group have further expanded our understanding of the role of maternal microchimerism in pregnancy 10, 11, 92. During allogeneic mating, the proband s Tregs protect against fetal wastage when non- inherited maternal antigens and fetal alloantigens matched Fig. Experimental antibody-induced depletion of maternal microchimeric cells from the proband prior to mating reverted this protective effect, highlighting the maternal tissues, to a degree mitigating the cardiovascular burden of pregnancy. Injection of human umbilical cord- derived mesenchymal stem cells ameliorated hyperten - sion and proteinuria in a mouse model with LPS-induced preeclampsia-like symptoms Fig. In these mice, mesenchymal stem cell treatment also reversed vascular and placental inflammation. Due to the mouse model used, this effect is likely attributable to systemic effects of human umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells, rather than effects on extravillous trophoblast invasiveness. Interest - ingly, we recently reported a positive correlation between severe maternal hypertension and fetal microchimerism presence and quantity in women with preeclampsia 28.

content_chunk: It is tempting to speculate that this is due to increased natural recruitment of fetal mesenchymal stem cells in response to maternal endothelial dysfunction and vascular inflamma - tion 28. This might instigate a self-perpetuating negative cycle as recruitment of dysfunctional or senescent fetal mesenchymal stem cells could further exacerbate endothe - lial dysfunction in women with preeclampsia. However, the characterization of fetal microchimeric cell types and senes - cence markers in this setting remain to be investigated. Microchimerism and tolerance Maternal immune tolerance towards the fetus is essential for a healthy pregnancy. This is consistent with studies show - ing that a shorter period of sexual cohabitation prior to conception less than 3 months , and thus less exposure to paternal antigens to build tolerance 89 , is associated with increased risk of developing preeclampsia 90. Moreover, this acquired tolerance seems to persist over time as subse - quent pregnancies with the same partner carry significantly reduced risk of infant mortality and other adverse pregnancy outcomes 91. The same pattern is documented in mice, where repeated mating with the same paternal alloantigens grants resilience towards fetal wastage 10, 92. Extravil - lous trophoblasts do not have strong immunogenicity, but they do express polymorphic HLA-C on the cell surface 93 and HLA-DR intracellularly 94 which may act as a source of foreign epitopes when exposed by maternal anti - gen-presenting cells. In addition, HLA genotyping studies in oocyte donation pregnancies revealed that the level of HLA matching between the mother and child in multiple alleles was positively associated with successful, uncomplicated pregnancies 95, 96. This suggests maternal immune expo - sure to more than just placental cytotrophoblast cells, which is where fetal microchimeric cells transferred to maternal circulation during pregnancy might come in. As for the maternal immune response resulting in toler - ance to fetal alloantigens, Tregs Regulatory T cells , which are a subset of T cells involved in immune regulation and 1 3Page 9 of 14 21 Seminars in Immunopathology 2025 47:21 Future perspectives conclusion Here, we have reviewed the current literature on microchi - merism in healthy pregnancies and pregnancy complications related to placental dysfunction. The quantity of circulating microchimerism varies by source and cellular phenotype of the microchimeric cells across the various pregnancy com - plications, suggesting that these cells may be impacted by or play a role in their underlying pathophysiology. Based on ours and other findings, we have proposed that fetal microchimerism is associated with both stages of the two-stage model of preeclampsia, i. placental dysfunc - tion and maternal endothelial dysfunction 30. Meanwhile, mother of the proband microchimerism has been postulated to contribute beneficially to placentation as it is negatively correlated with miscarriage and preeclampsia 29, 73. Interestingly, maternal microchimerism in fetal circulation is elevated in preterm labor, and has been proposed to play a role in initiating uterine contractions 74. These hypotheses remain to be investigated.

content_chunk: One of the fetal origin cell types that have been detected in fetal microchimerism are mesenchymal stem cells 76, 77. They affect trophoblast function in vitro and might thereby impact plantation 83, 84. Investigation of fetal mesenchymal stem cells in decidua basalis in parallel with extravillous trophoblasts could shed some light on possible mechanisms underlying the evolutionary benefit of micro - chimerism. Furthermore, their function as signalling cells could have implications in maternal tissues as well. Finally, fetal mesenchymal stem cells display a senescent phenotype during preeclampsia 85, 86 , which might have an inflam - matory effect locally in the placenta as well as in the mater - nal periphery. Animal studies reveal the involvement of microchime - rism in immunological tolerization processes 10, 11, 92. This has yet to be demonstrated in humans, but is in line with the observation of increased mother of the proband microchimerism in the circulation of healthy pregnancies 29. Thorough study of HLA genotypes in three genera - tions grandmother, mother and offspring with longitudi - nal follow-up for multiple pregnancies, combined with fetal and maternal microchimerism quantification and anti-body measurements could shed some light on this issue, but is technically demanding in humans. The field of microchimerism challenges our understand - ing of transgenerational health and disease development. Our studies point to the placenta likely representing the cru - cial organ for orchestrating microchimeric processes. Our future research plan involves exploring potential avenues of fetal cell transfer during normal pregnancies and pre - eclampsia, as well as comparing fetal microchimeric cell properties in these two clinical settings. We also aim to importance of low-level antigenic stimulation in sustaining these specific Tregs. Mother of the proband microchimeric cells sequestered within the proband s immune cell niches may thus facilitate pregnancies where inherited paternal alleles in the fetus overlap with or resemble non-inherited maternal alleles expressed on mother of the proband micro - chimeric cells. Mother of the proband mirochimeric cells are depleted naturally during pregnancy, displaced by fetal microchime - ric cells 10, 113. The exact mechanism of displacement is unknown, but has been observed in both humans and ani - mals. In women, circulating mother of the proband micro - chimerism was negatively associated with parity 113. This is clearly demonstrated in mice, where pregnancy displaces mother of the proband microchimerism and thereby also erases the proband s tolerance to non-inherited maternal alleles in subsequent pregnancies 10. Fetal microchime - rism, on the other hand, was not associated with parity in multiparous women 113. The latter observation supports the concept that newly acquired microchimerism displaces previous microchimerism residing in stem cell and immune cell niches. In other words, fetal cells from multiple preg - nancies do not seem to accumulate, but rather to compete for a restricted capacity. It is difficult to assess whether birth order determines which fetal cell population will be dominant in multiparous women. In a study by Gammill et al.

content_chunk: , only four families met the criteria to evaluate fetal microchimerism from sequential pregnancies. Two of these women had measurable circulating microchimerism, and in both cases, these cells stemmed from the second pregnancy 113. Although this sample is too small to draw any con - clusions, the findings do not contradict the observations in mice, where fetal cells from subsequent pregnancies out - compete cells from previous pregnancies 10. Interestingly, displacement of fetal microchimerism in mice does not erase the protective effect of previous preg - nancies with overlapping alloantigens 10. The persistent immunotolerance towards previously encountered fetal alloantigens in the apparent absence of relevant fetal micro - chimerism and the associated Tregs is attributable to a par - ticular subset of T cells termed exTregs. These exTregs have previously been implicated in autoimmune disorders, as the differentiation from Tregs to exTregs tends to be accompa - nied by a more proinflammatory phenotype 114. However, in the context of pregnancy, exTregs may apparently be of benefit, involved in reproductive fitness. Taken together, the presence of fetal microchimerism sustaining Tregs, or the presence of exTregs in the absence of fetal microchime - rism, may account for some of the protective effect of parity against preeclampsia and other pregnancy disorders. 1 3 21 Page 10 of 14 Seminars in Immunopathology 2025 47:21 References 1. content_chunk: : 0123456789 Cardiovascular Toxicology 2025 25:325 340 Pregnancy and Postpartum Effects of Electronic Cigarettes on Maternal Health and Vascular Function in the Fourth Trimester Amber Mills1,6 Duaa Dakhlallah2 Anand Ranpara1,6 W. Travis Goldsmith1,6 Paul D. Chantler3 Yue Wern Huang4 Jonathan Boyd5 I. Mark Olfert1,3,6 Received: 18 September 2024 Accepted: 12 January 2025 Published online: 22 January 2025 The Author s 2025 Abstract Pregnancy is a vulnerable time with significant cardiovascular changes that can lead to adverse outcomes, which can extend into the postpartum window. Exposure to emissions from electronic cigarettes Ecig , commonly known as vaping, has an adverse impact on cardiovascular function during pregnancy and post-natal life of offspring, but the postpartum effects on maternal health are poorly understood. We used a Sprague Dawley rat model, where pregnant dams are exposed to Ecigs between gestational day GD 2-GD21 to examine postpartum consequences. Litter and dam health were monitored during the weaning period, and maternal vascular and endocrine function were assessed after weaning. Exposure to Ecig emissions during pregnancy led to fetal losses i. , reabsorption in utero and reduced survival of pups during weaning compared to controls air-exposed dams. We find that maternal vaping during pregnancy, with or without nicotine or flavoring results in maternal vascular and hormonal dysfunction i. , reduced prolactin, increased expression of sirtuin 1 deacetylase in the brain. Both 5 and 30W Ecig aerosol exposures resulted in significant impairment of middle cerebral artery reactivity to acetylcholine-mediated dilation decreasing 22 and 50 , respectively. We also observed an increase in the number of extracellular vesicles EVs in plasma from 30-W group that persists up to 3-week postpartum and that these EVs impaired endothelial cell function when applied to in vitro and ex vivo assays. Our data suggest 1 Ecig vaping, even without nicotine or flavorings, during pregnancy alters maternal circulating factors that influence maternal and fetal health, 2 circulating EVs may contribute to the etiology of vascular dysfunction, and 3 that the window for recovery from vascular dysfunction in the dam is likely to be longer than the exposure window. content_chunk: Adverse outcomes that occur during pregnancy, such as preeclampsia, gestational diabe- tes, and fetal growth restriction, are known risk factors for maternal health and can increase the risk for subsequent cardiovascular disease CVD in women in the postpartum window and beyond 1. While the risks of adverse out- comes to pregnancy are well established with exposure to air pollution 2 and smoking 3 , 4 , recent studies have documented similar cardiovascular concerns to vaping exposure from electronic cigarette Ecig emissions dur - ing pregnancy 5 , 6. However, to our knowledge, no stud- ies so far have investigated the effects of Ecig use during pregnancy on maternal cardiovascular or cerebrovascular health extending into postpartum window. Understanding the links between exposure to Ecig emis- sions and vascular health is important because CVD is the leading cause of mortality among pregnant and postpar - tum women 1, 7. Risk of stroke and vascular dementia are also established concerns that postpartum women face 8, 9 , but there is lack of established research evaluating cerebral vascular health in connection with Ecig use i. , vaping during pregnancy. At present, vaping is touted as a healthier alternative to traditional smoking. Still, evidence from both pre- clinical 10 16 and human 17 19 studies suggest that Ecigs adversely impact cardiovascular and cerebrovascular health 20, 21. For example, recent studies have presented that Ecig exposure increases arterial stiffening 10, 22 , impairs vascular function 18 , 23 , induces hypertension 24 , weakens immunity 25 , and alters platelet function 26, 27 , all of which can increase the risk for thrombo- genic events. Sirtuin 1 SIRT1 is among the key regu- lators known to positively influence vascular health and remodeling see review 28 , but recent reports indicate the vaping reduces SIRT1 expression 29 31. SIRT1 is NAD -dependent histone deacetylase that is known to protect blood vessels during times of stress and senes- cence via its influence on oxidative stress and endothelial nitric oxide synthase eNOS 32, 33 , but its response in the context of maternal vaping and the postpartum window is not yet known. Given the overall vascular risks con- sistently being reported with vaping, it is surprising that some public health agencies have promoted Ecig use over smoking 34 , even during pregnancy 35. As of 2021, 327 Cardiovascular Toxicology 2025 25:325 340 10. 1 of reproductive age women currently smoke and many of these women might naively believe vaping is a safer option during pregnancy 36 without realizing the potential long-term health consequences of vaping during pregnancy. Herein, we used an established rodent inhalation exposure model to test the hypothesis that maternal vaping during pregnancy compromises cerebrovascular function in the postpartum life of dams. We investigated the effect of Ecig device wattage i. , 5 vs 30 watts on the particle and chemi- cal composition of the generated aerosol and their relation- ship to the vascular and cellular e. , SIRT1 outcomes observed.

content_chunk: Lastly, we provide an insight into extracellular vesicles EVs contribution to the underlying cerebral vas- cular dysfunction caused by Ecig exposures. Materials and Methods Ethical Approval All procedures were conducted with approval from the West Virginia University Animal Care and Use Committee IACUC, protocol 16-05003053 and to the established NIH Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. Euthanasia of animals occurred while under deep anesthesia inhaled 3 5 isoflurane as part of a terminal surgical pro- cedure to obtain vital organs and blood vessels for analysis. Study Design and Exposure System Male and female Sprague Dawley rats 200 250 g, 3 months old were purchased for breeding Charles River, Wilming- ton, MA and housed in AAALAC-certified vivarium facil - ity. Rodents were provided standard rat chow and reverse osmosis drinking water and kept on a 12-h:12-h day night cycle, throughout the study at West Virginia University. Animals were allowed to acclimate to the new facility for at least seven days before breeding. Males were time mated with nulliparous females overnight, after which a vaginal smear was obtained to verify the presence of sperm and or observation of a vaginal plug as evidence of pregnancy and establishment of gestational day GD 0. Dams n 42 were randomly assigned to receive exposures in one of the following group assignments: 1. Ecig aerosol with no nicotine at 5 W atts Ecig0 5W, n 8 , 2. Ecig aerosol with no nicotine at 30 W Ecig0 30W, n 8 , 3. Ecig aerosol with 50-mg mL e-liquid nicotine at 5W Ecig50 5W, n 7 ,4. Ecig aerosol with 50-mg mL e-liquid nicotine at 30W Ecig50 30W, n 8 , and 5. Ambient air control, n 11. Complications during pregnancy occurred in 3 of the 4 Ecig-exposed groups details reported in Sect. Maternal Body Mass and Litter Survival , resulting in the loss of the dams and or offspring. Thus, the final dam numbers in these groups were Ecig0 5W n 6 , Ecig0 30W n 7 , and Ecig50 30W n 6. Air controls were housed and handled in the same manner as the Ecig-exposed animals, but only exposed to ambient air during the exposure treatment. The selection of wattage and nicotine levels for Ecig groups was based, in part, on 1 relevance to human exposure and 2 the settings applied allow comparison to previously reported results conducted with pregnancy-related exposures 5 , 6, 12. For example, 5W was chosen because it is the lowest possible operating level for most devices, and 30W is a somewhat high level that an experienced user might select. We chose nicotine at 50 mg mL, because it is equivalent to 5 solution, which is the most popular concentration of nicotine used with Ecigs in the USA 37. Maternal exposure began on GD2-4 and continued until GD21 using a whole-body exposure rat chamber exposure system Ecig Puffer v3, IEStechno, Morgantown, WV, USA which allowed 4 rats to be exposed simultaneously.

content_chunk: Dams were not restrained in the exposure chamber but were in a confined space limiting mobility and physically separated from each other. A Joyetech Ecig device i. , EXCEED D19 was used to create 60 puffs day 1 puff, 83 mL volume, every 1. 5 min for 90 min , 5 days week during the intrapartum period. Similar to our prior pub- lished work 5 , 6, 12 , puff duration was set at 5 s with an inhalation draw rate of 1 LPM, and diluent air was also continuously fed into the chamber at rate of 20 L min to create an episodic exposure pattern to more closely mimic human vaping behavior with clean air breaths between puffs. E-liquid consisted of a mixture of 50:50 vegetable glycerine VG : propylene glycol PG with no flavoring, and groups with and without nicotine were tested as noted above. Laboratory grade VG was purchased from Sigma 2143-01, Avantor, J. Baker and PG from Fisher Sci- entific P355-1. A Joyetech atomizer 1. 2 Ω Ω resist- ance for 5 W and 0. 5 Ω for 30 W was employed for the Ecig aerosol exposure. Dams were not exposed to Ecigs and not handled or disturbed during the postpartum lactation i. Assessment of dam s body and organs uterine and ovary masses, including uterine implantation sites, occurred within 24-h post-weaning. 328 Cardiovascular Toxicology 2025 25:325 340 Aerosol Analysis Aerosol concentrations from the animal chamber were logged in real-time throughout each exposure using a Casella MicroDust Pro Monitor Model CEL-712. An ionization detector miniRAE 3000 , Honeywell, USA was utilized to measure real-time levels of total volatile organic com- pounds VOCs. Offline assessments without animals in the chamber for aerosol size distribution were also made using an electrical low-pressure impactor ELPI , Dekati Ltd under the wattage conditions used in this study i. Formaldehyde CAS 50-00-0; IARC Group 1 car- cinogenic and Acrolein CAS 107-02-8; IARC Group 2A probably carcinogenic were assessed by modifying previously established water-trap method containing deri- vatizing agents 38 and then analyzed using a headspace sampler Model 7697A coupled with gas chromatography Model 8890 mass spectrometry Model 7000 GC MS from Agilent Technologies Inc. Briefly, we used 50 mL of double distilled water 17 mΩ to sample Ecig aerosol at 1 LPM for a given duration of exposure. Out of 50 mL, an aliquot 10 mL was mixed with 0. 5 mL of 1-mg mL O- 2,3,4,5,6-pentafluorobenzyl hydroxylamine hydrochloride PFBOA: Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA and 3 g of sodium chloride in airtight 20-mL volume size of headspace. This headspace vial was allowed to equilibrate for 24 h at room temperature 23 C. Then, the headspace vial was conditioned at 100 C oven temperature for 20 min and transferred at 110 C for further analysis with an HP- 5MS UI column 30 m 250 μm 0. 25 μm Agilent Technol- ogies Inc. A reagent blank was prepared, and two reagent spikes at 10 ppb and 5 ppb were also analyzed. The calibration curves had R2 values between 0. 9999, and the spike recoveries ranged from 82. The 10 ppb QC standards had recoveries ranging from 92. These metrics indicate that the ICP-MS method was robust and reliable across a wide linear range. content_chunk: Immediately thereafter, the brain was carefully removed to obtain the middle cerebral artery MCA for pressure myography. MCA was isolated from Circle of Willis, cleaned, and then placed into a microvessel chamber filled with cold physiological salt solution PSS; 4 C. Both ends of the isolated MCA were cannulated within a heated chamber 37 C that allowed the lumen and exterior of the vessel to be perfused and superfused, respectively, with heated PSS from separate reservoirs. PSS was equilibrated with a 21 O2, 5 CO2, and 74 N2 gas mixture and had the following composition mM : 119 NaCl, 4. 18 NaH2PO4, 24 NaHCO3, 0. 329 Cardiovascular Toxicology 2025 25:325 340 Following cannulation, MCAs were extended to their in situ length and equilibrated to 70 mmHg. Then, the ves- sel was challenged using 10 4 M serotonin to check viabil- ity; thereafter, vessel reactivity was assessed in response to increasing concentrations of an endothelial-dependent dila- tor EDD acetylcholine, ACh; 10 9 10 4 M , an endothe- lial-independent dilator EID sodium nitroprusside, SNP; 10 9 10 4 M , and a vasoconstrictor agent Serotonin, 5-HT; 10 9 10 4 M. Additionally, MCA responses to ACh were measured following acute incubation 30 min of vessels with nitro- l-arginine methylester L-NAME, 10 4 M; an inhibitor of nitric oxide synthase, Sigma-Aldrich to assess contributions of nitric oxide NO and TEMPOL to better understand the implication of oxidative stress and its effects on MCA reactivity. A video dimension analyzer connected to the inverted microscope was used to measure lumen diameter. Resistance vessels such as the MCA have endogenous smooth mus- cle tone therefore pre-constriction prior to assessing dilator responses is not required. Thus, dilation and constriction are assessed by subtracting the starting lumen diameter before each treatment and chambers were washed between each drug. Extracellular Vesicles EVs Plasma was obtained centrifugation at 3000 rpm, 10 min at 4 C from dam s blood and EVs were collected and puri- fied by differential centrifugation which has been described previously 39. To quantify the EVs and detect their sizes, Nanoparticle Tracking Analysis NTA was used according to the manufacturer s protocol Malveen Panalytical Inc. as previously described 39. To test the effects of EVs on vessel function, we added 50 µL of purified EVs concentrated to 1-million EV per 1-mL PBS to MCA vessels from 3-month-old naïve non- exposed males and females. content_chunk: Maternal Body Mass and Litter Survival Offspring outcomes and maternal weight gain for Ecig0 conditions have previously been reported 5 , herein we provide a comparison of those results to Ecig50 group which have not previously reported. Discussion The main finding of this study is that Ecig exposure dur - ing pregnancy leads to considerable arterial dysfunction that persists into the postpartum window. The conse- quences of vaping during the perinatal period included lower maternal weight gain, reduced litter size, and greater postpartum pup losses compared to air controls. Mater - nal vaping at a higher wattage i. , 30W led to greater arterial impairment compared to lower watts i. However, it is notable that Ecigs operating at 5W also resulted in significant 40 vascular dysfunction com- pared to controls. We also observed elevated circulating EVs and lower cerebral levels of SIRT1, which provides evidence of a mechanistic link between oxidative stress and epigenetic mechanisms underpinning the functional behavioral changes observed. It is important to note that the adverse maternal vascular outcomes seen post-weaning stem solely from emissions created by the base e-liquid solution i. , VG:PG , since no flavoring was present, and similar impairment was observed irrespective of nicotine. Taken together these pre-clinical reports provide strong evidence that vaping during pregnancy is not safe and can be expected to contribute to postpartum complications and adverse maternal health effects. These findings are crucial in shaping future policies and guidelines related to maternal health. It is critical to emphasize that our experimental model is not meant to replicate or model vaping behavior in pregnant humans, but rather provide an avenue to gain insight regarding harm or harm potential from criti- cal windows during pregnancy. Indeed, women who are not smoking or vaping before pregnancy would not be expected to start vaping once they become pregnant. However, our experimental design gives an understand- ing of the effects of exposure to Ecigs during pregnancy and provides an avenue to explore the fourth trimester in a way that cannot easily be gleaned from humans. We have previously provided reports on gestational Ecig expo- sure related to offspring outcomes when maternal vaping occurs prior to conception and during different trimester windows 5. This report extends our understanding on the effect of the maternal fetal dyad beyond gestational and into the postpartum window for dams. Recovery from Ecig Induced Endothelial Dysfunction Several studies 11, 13, 16, 23, 41 have reported vascu- lar dysfunction following acute Ecig exposure, but to our knowledge none have reported cerebral vascular outcomes Fig. 3 A Offspring loss due to reabsorption during pregnancy deter - mined by the difference in offspring litter size and number of implan- tation sites.

In the current con - text, exposure occurred for 3 weeks during pregnancy and ceased for 3 weeks during weaning , at which time we observe significant cerebral vascular impairment Fig. This level of impairment i. , 40 60 has been reported in rats and mice from prior studies after chronic exposure from 4 to 8 weeks 12, 29 , suggesting that the window for recovery may be much longer than expected. At present, it is not known what the exposure timeline is to create per - manent insult or injury, and there is very little information on when and how long recovery of vascular function will take after cessation of vaping. However, we have shown that MCA reactivity takes 3 days to return back to normal control levels following an acute i. , single 1 h Ecig exposure 23. Based on these data, it could be speculated that the window for recovery may be several fold longer than the exposure time experienced and possibly linked to expression of SIRT1. Further studies are needed better to characterize the temporal nature of acute vs chronic exposure on key molecular pathways and their associa- tion with change in vascular function to determine the temporal boundaries required for vascular recovery from chronic Ecig use. This may be especially important during pregnancy, given that it is a unique time with profound cardiovascular changes accommodating the expansion in plasma volume, increased cardiac output, and changes in peripheral resistance. Adverse outcomes during pregnancy or those occurring postpartum increase the future risk for cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease in women 42. In humans, the postpartum period is viewed in phases cor - responding to acute first 24 h , early up to 7 days , and late 6 weeks to 6 months with each phase having unique clinical considerations and challenges 43. This report is the first to provide an initial glimpse into this timeline from pre-clinical data, but emphasizes the need for further studies at different temporal windows to more fully under - stand the consequences that vaping will have on women during pregnancy.

content_chunk: Etiology and Recovery from Ecig Induced Endothelial Dysfunction We 12, 23 and others 41 have shown that vaping induces vascular dysfunction primarily via endothelial cell-depend - ent nitric oxide NO -mediated mechanism, and not altered smooth muscle function i. , endothelial-independent mechanisms. This is supported in the current study where L-NAME significantly impairs vascular function Fig. In the context of Ecig use, reduced NO bioavailability has also been widely linked to ROS activity 41, 44 and is sup - ported by our finding that the inclusion of a superoxide dis- mutase mimetic i. , TEMPOL helps to rescue Ecig-medi- ated vascular dysfunction Fig. This is also consistent with our prior work showing that vascular dysfunction in gestationally exposed offspring is ameliorated with the addi- tion of TEMPOL 45, 46. Given that SIRT1 is known to be vascular protective by inhibiting oxidative stress in vas- cular endothelial cells 28, 33 , the reduction in SIRT1 we observed indicates it as a key mechanistic pathway linking Ecigs to vascular pathology. While this study cannot establish a causal relationship to any single chemical in the Ecig aerosol, the downstream effect on biological pathways logically originates from the toxic emissions within Ecig aerosols. The size distribu- tion of the aerosol produced i. 1 is ideal for peripheral deposition in the lung and as Fig. 4 A Maternal middle cerebral artery MCA vasodilatory response to dose response of acetylcholine ACh and B maximal vessel response from 10 4 M ACh. n 5 11 offspring group. ANOVA with post hoc Tukey analysis where p 0. Mean SE 334 Cardiovascular Toxicology 2025 25:325 340 seen in Table 2 is laden with VOCs e. , formaldehyde and heavy metals e. , cadmium, chromium, lead, copper 47, 48. Both VOCs and heavy metals are implicated in ROS production 49 and thus could trigger the vascu- lar dysfunction we report in this study. Here too, SIRT1 has been proposed as a potential therapeutic target to help mitigate neurotoxic effects in pregnant women with occu- pational exposure to heavy metals 50. Indeed, metals can also influence neuroendocrine pathways, where aluminum or cadmium have been shown in both rats and humans to negatively influence prolactin levels 51, 52. These findings are consistent with the lowered SIRT1 expres- sion in the brain and circulating prolactin we observed in our Ecig-exposed dams plasma at weaning Table 2 and could in part also account for the greater complica- tions and reduced viability of pups seen during weaning from dams with Ecig exposure during pregnancy Fig. Although our metal analysis in this study was limited to aerosol from Ecig0 group, the source of metals in Ecig aer - osols is thought to come from coils and heating elements used 53, 54 and not nicotine or other chemical constitu- ents of the e-liquid. Since we used the same device, coils, and e-liquid just with and without nicotine in our Ecig50 and Ecig0 groups, respectively, the levels of metals are not expected to be different between Ecig groups.

Total VOCs, specifically formaldehyde, were three- to fourfold higher in our 30W exposure and one- to twofold higher with the 5W Ecig exposure, compared to negligi- ble levels in the air group. Levels of formaldehyde created in the daily 1. 5-h exposure used in this study exceed the OSHA permissible exposure limits PEL for formaldehyde by 2- to 3-fold. But, it is important to note that this limit is designated over an 8-h exposure, and if we calculated the equivalent level of formaldehyde after 8 h of Ecig use, our exposure would exceed the PEL limits by 10- to 12-fold. Formaldehyde, as well as other compounds like acrolein, are toxicants directly implicated in EDD vascular dysfunction. For example, Jin et al. 16 have shown that mice exposed to 5 ppm 6 h day formaldehyde have vascular impairment. Likewise, vascular function assessed via flow-mediated dila- tion FMD which is commonly used in humans to measure brachial artery function found that brachial artery FMD decreased following a 90-min formaldehyde exposure 56. There is also evidence that circulating markers of oxida- tive stress i. , malondialdehyde were increased and cor - relates with impaired MCA reactivity 57. Notably, SIRT1, a protein known to be involved in regulating oxidative stress and endothelial function, is inhibited by NADPH oxidase activation 40. Given the close connection between SIRT1 and eNOS, and that we found SIRT1 was decreased in the cerebral tissue of the dams with Ecig exposure Table 2 , it appears that SIRT1 may have a central role in the overall effect on vascular function. However, given that eNOS has multiple points of upstream regulation the relative contribu - tion of SIRT1 will require further study. Another novel observation is that EVs are likely to have a significant influence on EDD vascular dysfunction. While we have previously reported that plasma EVs are increased in rats acutely exposed to either cigarette smoke or Ecig aer - osol 23 , in this study we observed changes in EVs are still present after three weeks of vaping cessation. Here, circulat- ing EVs in plasma of Ecig-exposed dams at the higher 30W, but not 5W were significantly elevated compared to controls in both Ecig0 and Ecig50 dams Fig. This suggests that 30W exposure would cause significant disruption to cel- lular homeostasis, especially to endothelial cells, leading to increased shedding of EVs into the plasma 58, 59.

Aerosol emis - sions from Ecigs even in the absence of nicotine or flavor - ings are optimally sized and contain toxic compounds that result in altered endothelial cell function, vascular dysfunc- tion, and endocrine changes that negatively influence mater - nal health into the postpartum window. Vaping at higher wattage produces a greater concentration of chemicals and metals in the aerosol cloud and results in greater vascular impairment compared to lower wattage. However, even vap- ing at the lowest possible wattage i. , 5 watts induced sig- nificant vascular dysfunction in the MCA. Notably, our data support a role for EVs i. , exposomes and microvesicles and oxidative stress in the etiology of vascular dysfunction and suggests that the time for recovery from vascular dys- function is likely longer than the exposure window from which it resulted. Translational Relevance and Limitations Our data are the first glimpse into the effect of vaping dur - ing pregnancy and the impact on cerebral vascular health in the postpartum period. They highlight that vaping cre- ates disruption in cellular and vascular homeostasis and that changes are occurring which are known to be precursors for vascular-related disease. The current study cannot speak directly to human pregnancy timelines and therefore, any interpretation of humans must be viewed with caution. For example, in our previous reports 5 , 6 and in this study, we find decreases in litter size and loss in pups during the wean- ing in association with rodent Ecig exposure during gesta- tion. While studies in humans find vaping during pregnancy can lead to pre-term delivery and low birth weight 65 , they do not report offspring demise as we see in rodents. This dis- crepancy is likely because biological reproduction in humans invests heavily in singleton births, whereas rodents have a strategy with multiple offspring. Thus, when faced with physiological insult stress during pregnancy rodents can use fetal reabsorption during gestation and or favored selection of healthy pup during lactation weaning to optimize progeny and species survival. This strategy would not be practical to ensure the survival of humans in times of physiological insult stress with pregnancy.

content_chunk: Yet, rodent exposure models still provide significant insight toward developmental and cardiovascular outcomes for humans 66. Thus, our data demonstrate that vaping during pregnancy is not safe for the dam and provides mechanistic insight suggesting greater risk for adverse cerebrovascular events or disease. It is the first report to utilize a temporal approach where dams are studied in the postpartum period after weaning , and while not intended to fully mimic human-related behavior directly, it offers insight by isolating the exposure to a discrete win- dow of time and then evaluating postpartum effects. an endeavor that is not possible in humans. Our evidence that SIRT1 and EVs appear to play a crucial role in Ecig-induced vascular dysfunction provides an avenue for future studies to evaluate the potential for interventional strategies aimed at reducing the burden or risk for vascular injury or disease. Stutterheim2 Abstract Background In East Africa, women face significant challenges accessing maternal healthcare during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postnatal period. While several studies have examined barriers and facilitators to maternal care, there is no comprehensive review reflecting the various perspectives of women, their families, healthcare providers, and key stakeholders. We systematically reviewed qualitative literature on maternal healthcare in East Africa, synthesiz- ing insights from multiple perspectives and exploring barriers and facilitators across socioecological levels. Methods A qualitative evidence synthesis focused on studies from East Africa published between January 2015 and June 2024. We searched electronic databases, including PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Cochrane, Web of Science, and ProQuest, and used citation tracking to find additional references. Eligible studies were critically appraised using the Critical Appraisal Skills Program, and a thematic synthesis was performed to identify barriers and facilitators. Results Of the 3181 records identified, 81 studies 63 qualitative and 18 mixed method met the inclusion criteria, representing 4816 individuals from six East African countries. This review identified barriers at various levels: individual barriers included a lack of awareness and knowledge, fear of being treated poorly, and financial constraints; interper - sonal barriers comprised limited family support, communication challenges, and a lack of decision-making autonomy; health facility barriers included poor quality of healthcare, poor infrastructure, limited medical supplies, provider shortages, abusive behaviors from healthcare providers, lack of transportation, and high service costs; community- level barriers involved socio-cultural norms, societal stigma, and gender-based disparities; and policy-level barriers included poor focus on maternal health, a lack of male accompaniment policies, and conflicts.

content_chunk: Key facilitators identi- fied included improved healthcare understanding and women s self-efficacy at the individual level, family support and positive social influences at the interpersonal level, high-quality services, reliable transportation, compassionate care, and health education at the health facility level, community initiatives, gender equality, and maternity waiting homes at the community level, as well as free maternity services and health extension programs at the policy level. Correspondence: Manaye Yihune Teshale Full list of author information is available at the end of the article Page 2 of 22 Yihune Teshale et al. BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth 2025 25:111 Conclusion The synthesis identified key barriers and facilitators to the maternal healthcare in East African coun- tries, ranging from individual to policy levels. We recommend that future initiatives focus on addressing these barriers while enhancing facilitators across individual, interpersonal, health facility, community, and policy levels through woman-centered, evidence-based strategies. Moreover, fostering collaboration among governments, health- care providers, and communities is essential for improving access to the maternal continuum of care. Keywords Continuum of care, Barriers, Facilitators, Maternal healthcare, East Africa Background The global health challenge of maternal mortality contin - ues, resulting in the death of a woman every two minutes due to pregnancy and childbirth complications, most of which could be prevented with timely and appropriate care 1. The vast majority of these deaths 94 occur in low and middle-income countries 2. Sub-Saharan Africa SSA alone accounts for about two-thirds of global maternal deaths 3. East African countries have made significant steps in reducing the maternal mortal - ity ratio, experiencing a 48 decrease from 853 to 443 deaths per 100,000 live births since 2000 4. However, the maternal mortality rate in East African countries varies widely compared to other African nations, rang - ing from 3 deaths per 100,000 live births in Seychelles to 1,223 deaths per 100,000 live births in South Sudan 5. Sustainable Development Goal SDG 3 calls for an end to preventable deaths of women and children by 2030 6. In response to the global target, East African countries are working to reduce maternal mortality to less than 70 per 100,000 live births, neonatal mortality rates to 12 per 1,000 live births, and under-5 mortality rates to at least 25 per 1,000 live births by the end of 2030 6. These coun - tries need to decrease their maternal mortality rate by a minimum of 20. 3 annually from 2020 to achieve the SDG target by 2030 5. The Ending Preventable Maternal Mortality Initiative has established new coverage targets and milestones that need to be achieved if the SDGs are to be met 7. These SDGs stipulate that 90 of pregnant women attend at least four antenatal care ANC visits, 90 of births are attended by skilled delivery care SDC , and 80 of women who have just given birth access post - natal care PNC within two days of delivery 7.

content_chunk: The continuum of care encompasses the comprehen - sive maternal healthcare a woman receives throughout pregnancy, delivery, and the postpartum period, includ - ing i antepartum care with four or more ANC visits, ii intrapartum care involving SDC following ANC, and iii postpartum care with both mothers and their new - borns receiving PNC within six weeks of delivery after attending at least four ANC visits and receiving SDC 8. Nearly 71 of maternal mortality and about two-thirds of neonatal mortality could be prevented with effective maternal healthcare throughout pregnancy, delivery, and the postpartum period 9. Unfortunately, only 25. 0 of women in SSA utilize the maternal healthcare, with rates varying from 17. 9 in East Africa to 51. 5 in Southern Africa due to a wide range of determinants and barriers 10. The World Health Organization WHO has identified several main barriers to the maternal healthcare, includ - ing economic hardship, limited access to information, distance from healthcare facilities, insufficient and sub - standard maternal healthcare, and cultural customs and beliefs 11. Likewise, many prior primary studies from East African countries have identified similar barriers to accessing ANC 12 20 , SDC 21 27 , and PNC 28 31. Previous studies have also highlighted facilitators such as the empowerment of women, positive past experi - ences, family support, partner involvement, high-quality service, the availability of ambulances, and free mater - nity services 32 37. There is a significant body of evi - dence regarding the barriers and facilitators to accessing maternal healthcare. However, to date, no comprehensive review has combined the perspectives of women, their families, healthcare providers, and key stakeholders in East Africa. Such an overview is crucial for understand - ing the complex challenges at various levels of accessing maternal healthcare. By examining these diverse perspec - tives, we can identify service delivery gaps and develop targeted interventions to enhance maternal health out - comes for all. Accordingly, this review synthesizes qualitative stud - ies that explore the perspectives of women, their families, healthcare providers, and key stakeholders on the barri - ers and facilitators to maternal healthcare in East Africa. Qualitative research is especially valuable in this context, as it offers in-depth insights into personal experiences and the cultural, social, and contextual factors affecting access to maternal healthcare. By capturing diverse view - points across individual, interpersonal, health facility, community, and policy levels, we can thoroughly under - stand the challenges encountered and identify effective improvement strategies. This analysis, framed within the socio-ecological model, recognizes the complex interac - tions between individuals and their environments, high - lighting that behavior is influenced by multiple factors across these various levels 38. content_chunk: The findings of this review are reported in accordance with the guidelines of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses PRISMA 39 , Additional File 1. Search strategy We searched for published and unpublished studies on barriers and facilitators to accessing the maternal health - care in East Africa with a publication date after January 1, 2015, which aligns with the year in which the SDGs were formulated. It was thus then that East African countries committed to the aim of reducing neonatal mortality to 12 per 1,000 live births, under-five mortality to at least 25 per 1,000 live births, and maternal mortality to less than 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030 6. A step-by-step search strategy was utilized in this review. Primarily, elec - tronic databases that comprise health system research, including PubMed, Embase Ovid , Scopus, Cochrane, and Web of Science, were searched. Unpublished works were also searched from ProQuest Dissertations and Theses. Afterward, hand-searching of reference lists and citation tracking of included studies were screened for additional studies. The search was performed independently by two authors MY and AG and using three main categories of keywords related to the review question, Medical Sub - ject Headings MeSH , and employing Boolean search operators OR , and AND. The main keywords utilized for the article search included: maternal healthcare, access, and East African countries. These keywords were selected because they aligned with the core concepts of the review question. Various combinations and varia - tions of these keywords were employed. We explored synonyms for each search term in the literature to cre - ate a comprehensive search strategy. The initial database searches took place on April 10, 2024, followed by a sub - sequent search on June 30, 2024. The full search strat - egy employed and search results identified across the six databases are available as a supplementary file Addi - tional File 2. Eligibility criteria The eligibility of studies for inclusion in the systematic review was rigorously established according to prede - termined inclusion and exclusion criteria, as outlined in Table 1. The selection process followed the PICo frame - work, outlining the key components of the research ques - tion, including the Population perinatal women, their family members, healthcare providers, and other key stakeholders , phenomena of Interest maternal health - care , and Context East African countries 40. Study selection The search results were exported to Mendeley reference management software, where duplicates were removed. The remaining records were exported to Covidence https: www. org for evaluation in two dis - tinct screening steps.

Three authors MY, AB, and AG were involved in this step, with each article indepen - dently assessed by two authors. In case of disagreements, we thoroughly examined the issues and consulted a third-party SS to resolve them. One author MY cross- checked 10 n 30 of randomly selected abstracts, revealing that reviewers consistently applied the eligibil - ity criteria and made appropriate decisions, indicating that the initial review process was reliable. Each abstract was carefully read and evaluated to determine if the cor - responding article should proceed to the second step, which involved screening the full text. The same authors conducted the second step based on the full texts. Any studies that the authors agreed upon were included, and any disagreements were resolved through discussion. The full-text articles were then extracted and assessed against the inclusion and exclusion criteria. The selected full- text articles were re-evaluated for data extraction and assessed for quality. Quality appraisal All articles that passed the full-text verification were assessed for quality using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme CASP checklist for qualitative studies 41. The CASP consists of 10 questions to evaluate the research aims, methodology, research design, recruit - ment strategy, data collection, data analysis, reflexiv - ity, ethical considerations, findings, and research value. Each question has three response options: i Yes score: 1. 0 , ii Partial Yes score: 0.

content_chunk: Stud - ies were categorized as good, moderate, or low-quality if they scored 9. The quality assessment was conducted independently by two authors MY and AG , and any disagreements were resolved through discussion. It is important to note that the quality assessment was not used to exclude articles but to identify potential research limitations. Data extraction Three authors MY, AB and AG independently extracted data from eligible studies using a customized data extrac - tion form in Covidence. The system was configured to allow data from each included study to be extracted by two authors. A third author double-checked and verified the accuracy of the extracted articles by comparing the extraction outputs of two authors, which were displayed side by side in Covidence. In cases where discrepancies were observed between the two individuals, the third individual reassessed the articles to address any errors accordingly. The form was filled with information about the first author, year of publication, country of study, study aims, study-focused areas including ANC, SDC, PNC, or combined services , study design, setting, study period, data source or perspectives, sample size, sam - pling technique, method of data collection, data analy - sis, and results relevant to the review question barriers and or facilitators. In our context, barriers are obstacles that prevent women from accessing essential services and support related to pregnancy, childbirth, and postpartum care, while facilitators are factors and best practices that promote and enhance women s access to and utilization of these services during the same periods. Sample data extraction tool is provided Additional File 3. Data synthesis We conducted a qualitative evidence synthesis using a thematic synthesis approach as described by Thomas and Harden 42. Thematic synthesis is an adaptation of thematic analysis, which is a common form of analysis for primary qualitative data, and involves familiarisation with the data, coding the results of the primary studies, developing themes, and using this to conceptualize fur - ther understanding and hypotheses 42. We selected four good-quality studies from the included studies based on their robust methodology, clear results addressing our synthesis questions from various perspectives, and well- defined terminology to establish our initial code list 26, 34, 35, 37. We then conducted line-by-line free cod - ing to help translate concepts across studies and expand the code bank as we analyzed more studies and themes 42. We genereated themes and sub-themes, using direct quotes from participants and the authors data summa - ries in the findings section of the included studies. All codes, which were labels or categories used to classify similar pieces of data, were organized into categories or overlapping themes. Then overlapping themes, which are common ideas or patterns present in multiple codes, were combined into a single theme. These groups were further categorized and summarized. Finally, generated themes concerning barriers and facilitators were sum - marized using the socio-ecological framework and thus categorized into individual, interpersonal, health facil - ity, community, and policy levels.

content_chunk: The two authors MY and AG conducted the synthesis process and included selected participant quotations to support the themes. All data management and coding tasks were carried out using NVivo Version 14. Assessing confidence in the findings The two authors MY and AG used the GRADE-CER - Qual Confidence in the Evidence from Reviews of Qualitative Research approach to assess confidence in each review finding 43. CERQual assesses confidence in the evidence-based on four key components, includ - ing methodological limitations of included studies 44 , Page 5 of 22 Yihune Teshale et al. BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth 2025 25:111 coherence of the review finding 45 , adequacy of the data contributing to a review finding 46 , and relevance of the included studies to the review question 47. After evaluating each of these components, we reached an overall judgment regarding the confidence in the evi - dence supporting the review findings, categorizing it as high, moderate, low, or very low 48. This final assess - ment was based on consensus among the authors. Review author reflexivity The author MY conducted a qualitative evidence syn - thesis as part of a PhD study to address the gap in com - prehensive reviews by incorporating the perspectives of women, their families, healthcare providers, and key stakeholders within the East African context. The study operated under the assumption that women face many barriers in accessing adequate maternity services. Recog - nizing the potential influence of this assumption on data interpretation, an additional author AG was brought in for his expertise in qualitative research methods. Addi - tionally, SS, MS, and RC provided guidance and super - vision for all aspects of the work, addressing concerns about accuracy and integrity, reviewing methods, find - ings, and drafts of the coding, categories, themes, and manuscript. Results Study selection Overall, 3163 references were initially located through searching the databases, and an additional 18 were located through other sources such as checking the ref - erence lists of located papers. After the exclusion of duplicates, 1778 remained, of which 361 were retrieved for full-text review. Of these, 280 studies were excluded for reasons such as intervention-evaluation studies, the country of study being outside East Africa, studies done outside our time frame, and having primary outcomes that did not explore barriers or facilitators. A total of 81 studeies was retained for further analysis Fig. Characteristics of the included studies Despite a thorough search of all included East African countries, no eligible studies were identified for Burundi, Comoros, Djibouti, Rwanda, Seychelles, Somalia, and Sudan. This suggests that up-to-date evidence on this topic is lacking for a large part of the East African coun - tries. Nearly half 48 of the reviewed studies originated from Ethiopia. Of all the studies included, 67 aimed to explore only barriers. Meanwhile, 32 focused on SDC, and only 7 were concentrated in PNC Table 2.

content_chunk: Summary of methods and participants in included studies Most included studies 78 used an exclusively quali - tative approach, and 22 employed mixed methods. Among the eligible studies, 90 involved care recipi - ents, such as women of childbearing age, pregnant women, or postpartum women; and 30 involved the families of care recipients, such as husbands, heads of households, mothers, or fathers-in-law. In terms of sample size, 27 of studies involved 21 40 participants. Data were collected through interviews and FGDs in 47 of the reviewed studies. Also, 71 of the included studies employed thematic analysis Table 3. Quality appraisal results The CASP quality appraisal tool was employed to assess the included studies, identifying potential research limitations based on ten specific criteria. The majority of the studies demonstrated moderate to good quality. Notably, all 81 included studies presented a clear state - ment of their research aims. However, 13 studies failed to explicitly describe the research design employed to address these aims, and 22 studies did not adequately report the relationship between researchers and par - ticipants. To address these gaps, the research team adopted an inclusive approach to critical appraisal, which allowed for a comprehensive understanding of each study s strengths and limitations. This in-depth evaluation enhanced the reliability of the findings while ensuring a more thorough interpretation of the data. Detailed scoring for each domain of the included stud - ies is available in Additional File 4. Barriers to maternal healthcare Of the 81 studies included in this synthesis, 76 described barriers to accessing the maternal healthcare from the perspectives of care recipients, their families, healthcare providers, and or key stakeholders. Below, we discuss these barriers according to the socioecologi - cal level at which the barrier occurs Table 4 and Fig. Individual level barriers n 55 Lack of awareness and knowledge Of the 55 studies reporting individual level barriers, 28 indicated that a key barrier to accessing maternal care is lack of awareness and knowledge about maternal health issues and the importance of utilizing maternity care services 16, 25, 28, 29, 31, 34, 37, 49, 53, 55 58, 60, 61, 64, 67, 71, 73, 77, 80, 81, 86, 92, 96, 99 101. Personal beliefs A total of 21 studies indicated that personal beliefs affected women s utilization of maternal healthcare, often leading them to delay or avoid care altogether 19, 25, 26, 34, 49, 50, 53, 55, 56, 62, 63, 65, 68, 70, 73, 86, 88, 96, 98, 99, 103. Otherwise, what new things will the healthcare providers make for us if the pregnancy goes well. They simply examine us and tell us that we can return home if the pregnancy is going well. BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth 2025 25:111 Discussion This review synthesized existing qualitative literature on women, their families, healthcare providers, and key stakeholders perspectives on barriers and facilitators in the maternal healthcare in East African countries at individual, interpersonal, health facility, community and policy levels. The synthesis revealed that a lack of awareness and knowledge about obstetric danger signs and maternal health services hinders access to maternal healthcare, particularly for rural and marginalized women in East Africa. This lack of awareness and knowledge stems from low education levels, traditional practices, and limited access to health information 104. This finding aligns with prior reviews on barriers to obstetric care access in SSA, India, and European countries 105 107. A lack of awareness leads to delays in seeking healthcare, increas - ing the risk of adverse maternal and neonatal health outcomes and contributing to higher morbidity and mortality rates 108. Women must understand maternal health issues to ensure timely access to maternal health - care 56, 100. We recommend implementing targeted educational programs, focusing on stimulating realis - tic perceptions concerning susceptibility and severity of missing using the materinal healthcare access 109 and at the same time supporting participants to actually access maternal healthcare. These programs should be part of community health initiatives and could be deliv - ered through workshops, mobile health applications, and community health workers, using culturally relevant materials and involving community leaders for effective dissemination. This review also showed that personal beliefs shaped by cultural norms, religious values, and individual experi - ences impede women s utilisation of maternal healthcare in East Africa. This finding is consistent with previ - ous research on barriers to obstetric care in India 106. Many women prefer traditional practices and local heal - ers to health facilities because they perceive these options as safer and more accepted within their communities 19, 62. This preference often arises from a lack of awareness or trust in the healthcare system, resulting in many seek - ing medical assistance only when complications occur 19. Additionally, stigma surrounding unmarried or adolescent status complicates health-seeking behaviors by imposing societal pressures that lead to shame and limit women s autonomy in decision-making 37. Con - sequently, many women avoid or delay maternal care due to sociocultural influences, which increases the risk of complications and negatively impacts both maternal and neonatal health outcomes 74, 110. To overcome these barriers, community health initiatives should focus on education, mobilization, and collaboration between traditional healers and healthcare providers.

content_chunk: Programs must respect personal beliefs while delivering accurate maternal health information to shift perceptions, build trust, and empower women, ultimately enhancing their self-efficacy to access maternal healthcare 56. Fear of being treated poorly due to past negative healthcare experiences, such as disrespectful behaviour and perceived discrimination, also deters women from accessing maternal healthcare. This issue is worsened by systemic problems, including inadequate professional conduct from untrained providers, overwhelming work - loads that lead to burnout and reduced empathy, and poor community engagement that overlooks the unique needs of the populations served 29, 75, 102. Addition - ally, communication challenges arising from language barriers and low health literacy hinder women s ability to articulate their needs and seek appropriate care 13, 27. Prior studies support the notion that negative encounters foster mistrust, while unmet communication needs dur - ing interactions contribute to poorer health outcomes 111 113. This cycle of disengagement aggravates health disparities and undermines public health initiatives aimed at improving maternal health. To break this cycle, it is crucial to implement communication interventions that promote positive interactions, with a focus on pri - oritizing cultural competency training for providers 59, 62. Establishing peer support programs can provide emotional support, and multilingual services, including interpreter assistance, can ensure effective communica - tion and access to care. Further, this review shows that financial constraints limit women s access to maternal health services in East Africa, mainly for low-income women, due to high out- of-pocket costs, transportation expenses, and lost wages. In rural areas, the burden of domestic work and lack of family support worsen these challenges 34, 99. This emotional and financial stress undermines women s deci - sion-making power and contributes to feelings of isola - tion, which discourages them from voicing their health concerns 37. This review supports earlier studies in low-income countries, showing that economic barriers and lack of decision-making autonomy limit access to maternal health services 114. Women who do not have access to maternal care due to socioeconomic factors are at risk of complications that timely medical intervention could prevent 115, 116. Additionally, the emotional toll of financial stress and social isolation further aggra - vates mental health issues, negatively impacting women s overall well-being 117. To address these challenges, we recommend inclusive policies that subsidize maternal health services, expand health insurance coverage, and provide financial support to low-income women through cash transfers and transportation vouchers 36, 118. Page 17 of 22 Yihune Teshale et al. BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth 2025 25:111 Moreover, developing community-based support systems can strengthen social networks and encourage family involvement in maternal care, as supportive families play a crucial role in improving access 36. The poor quality of healthcare in East Africa limits women s access to maternal health services, primarily due to inadequate facility conditions and a lack of suffi - cient resources.

content_chunk: Furthermore, a shortage of trained pro - viders results in long wait times and lower quality of care, contributing to the perception that these facilities cannot adequately meet maternal health needs 82, 102. Previ - ous studies conducted in low-income countries support this finding, indicating that substandard care conditions hinder access to maternal care 105, 106. The WHO also emphasizes that workforce shortages and insufficient training of healthcare providers are critical barriers to delivering maternal care 119. Women without access to quality maternal health services face increased risks during pregnancy and childbirth, resulting in immedi - ate and long-term effects 120. To address these barriers, governments and health organizations should prioritize investments in accessible, and well-equipped healthcare facilities. Increasing the number of trained healthcare providers and ensuring ongoing professional develop - ment are crucial for improving care quality and address - ing staffing shortages. Community-based solutions, like health extension programs and maternity waiting homes, can help bridge access gaps for rural women 36, 51. Additionally, our review has shown that, a lack of focus on maternal health in policy frameworks, combined with the absence of supportive policies that engage men, impede women s access to maternal health services. Con - flicts and restrictive laws exacerbate these barriers, leav - ing women feeling unsupported in their reproductive health needs 29, 89, 99. Prior studies also show that pol - icies ignoring male involvement result in poorer health outcomes for mothers and infants, as men are crucial in decision-making regarding healthcare access 120, 121. Without targeted policies that prioritize women s health and encourage male involvement, maternal health is often seen as solely a women s issue 122. This oversight neglects the contributions of male partners and commu - nity members, potentially leading to reduced access to maternal healthcare and higher risks during pregnancy and childbirth 121. To address these gaps, it is essential to promote policy reforms that prioritize women s health and include men through family-focused initiatives. Awareness campaigns can educate men about their roles in maternal health, and engaging community leaders and male role models can enhance support and foster shared responsibility. Furthermore, providing educational work - shops and establishing support groups are crucial for encouraging open discussions on parenting. Strengths and limitations of the synthesis The strength of this review lies in its comprehensive exploration of the barriers and facilitators to accessing the maternal healthcare across individual to policy lev - els. This approach provides valuable insights for public health professionals and policymakers by incorporating diverse perspectives from women, families, healthcare providers, and key stakeholders. However, we acknowl - edge a limitation in our review, as our thorough search across all listed East African countries yielded no eligible studies from seven countries, and a significant 48 of the included studies originated from Ethiopia, which may affect the generalizability of our findings to the broader East African context.

content_chunk: For future reviews, we recommend including studies published in other commonly spoken languages in East Africa, such as Swahili, as our study centered on English-language studies. Moreover, we observed that most included articles did not adequately describe researcher-participant relationships or demon - strate researcher reflexivity. Additionally, the diversity of maternal healthcare services and variations in publica - tion titles may challenge the search and selection process, suggesting that despite our rigorous review methods, some important studies may have been unintentionally excluded. Roadmap for policymakers and future research To enhance access to maternal healthcare, policymakers should establish a comprehensive roadmap that incorpo - rates immediate, medium, and long-term actions prior - itized by urgency and impact. Initially, the focus should be on short-term actions, such as educating the com - munity about maternal health, strengthening support systems involving family members, and ensuring reliable transportation solutions. Following these, medium-term actions should improve healthcare quality by address - ing health infrastructure, shortages of medical sup - plies and healthcare providers, implementing policies for free maternity services, expanding health insurance for all maternity care, and training healthcare provid - ers to deliver compassionate and effective care. Long- term strategies must prioritize gender equality, promote community-driven initiatives, develop policies that allow male accompaniment during maternity services, and establish maternity waiting homes for women in remote areas. Continuous research and evaluation are critical for assessing the effectiveness of these interventions, iden - tifying data gaps, and enabling ongoing strategy refine - ment, ultimately fostering supportive environments that adequately address women s health needs. Scaling up targeted interventions will also require implementation research that emphasizes measurable results and trans - parent processes. Page 18 of 22 Yihune Teshale et al. BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth 2025 25:111 Conclusions In conclusion, this synthesis highlights several barriers and facilitators impacting access to maternal healthcare in East Africa. Key barriers include a lack of awareness and knowledge, financial constraints, limited family support, poor healthcare quality, distance to facilities, socio-cultural norms, and insufficient policy empha - sis. Facilitators that promote access comprise an under - standing of healthcare benefits, supportive families, high-quality services, reliable transportation, supportive community initiatives, and offering free maternal ser - vices. Future efforts should focus on overcoming these barriers and amplifying the identified facilitators through evidence-based, woman-centered interventions. Col - laborative action among governments, healthcare pro - viders, and communities is crucial for ensuring equitable access to maternal care. Recommended strategies include implementing targeted health promotion programs, optimizing medical resources, improving transportation infrastructure, and educating women about healthcare options and financial literacy. Furthermore, expanding access to maternal care through mobile clinics in under - served areas, engaging Traditional Birth Attendants for culturally sensitive care components, and training health - care providers in compassionate practices can enhance trust and improve service accessibility.

To view a copy of this licence, visit Pr egnanc y and Childbir th Determinants of well-being in pregnancy: the impact of sociodemographic and obstetric variables and maternal health literacy, cross sectional study Pınar Kara1 Abstract Background Maternal well-being is paramount in elevating maternal, fetal, and societal health. This study aimed to examine the impact of pregnant women s sociodemographic and obstetric variables, as well as maternal health literacy, on well-being during pregnancy. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted between April and October 2024 at a public hospital in a south- eastern province of Türkiye. The study was completed with the participation of 456 pregnant women who met the inclusion criteria. Data were collected utilizing the WHO-5 Well-Being Index , the Maternal Information Form, and the Maternal Health Literacy Inventory in Pregnancy MHELIP. The statistical significance level was defined as p 0. Results The study identified maternal health literacy as the most significant predictor of well-being during preg- nancy β 0. Additionally, perceiving income as insufficient B -1. 872 , residing in urban centers B -1. 708 , and the presence of pregnancy-related risks B -2. 145 were found to contribute substantially to diminished well- being during pregnancy p 0. Conclusion This study found that maternal health literacy along with various maternal socio-demographic and obstetric variables are important determinants of well-being in pregnancy. These findings may provide essential insights to better comprehend the necessities for improving well-being during pregnancy, guiding policymakers and healthcare providers in developing targeted solutions. This understanding could also inform the adaptation of existing health and community services to create a health literacy-sensitive environment more likely to address the diverse health needs of pregnant women and mothers.
